But in season three, it’s finally time for the precious. The official Prime Video synopsis says as much: “The Dark Lord toils day and night, obsessed with harnessing a power that will bring the last of his enemies to their knees: One Ring to rule them all...” The season’s key art also depicts Charlie Vickers’ Sauron wearing his signature crown and gazing at his golden creation. So we were already pretty confident that Rings of Power would at last be introducing its ultimate ring of power, and a new glimpse at the season three script proves it—almost. Entertainment Weekly has a look at the opening scene from season three, and it shows Sauron running into some roadblocks on his sinister journey. “Season three is the one where Sauron makes the One Ring in the volcano,” co-showrunner Patrick McKay confirmed to EW. “But for him, on a personal level, it’s a bit of a struggle to craft a ring more powerful than any that have ever been crafted before.” As the scene shows, Sauron has zero issues treating Orcs as his lab rats. But while he’s not putting himself at any risk, he’s still growing impatient with his failure. “Sauron has fallen back down that rabbit hole of frustration and darkness,” Vickers told EW. “In killing Celebrimbor, he has lost control and killed the person that could have helped him most on this quest. So he is doubting himself, which is a very unusual thing for Sauron when we rejoin him in the season.” We have a feeling it won’t take too long for Sauron to get what he wants—though this is Rings of Power, so it could also plausibly take the entire season to get there. We’ll start to find out when The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three kicks off November 11 on Prime Video. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: RIP to Cult Actor Gerrit Graham, Star of ‘Phantom of the Paradise’ and ‘Child’s Play 2’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.20
There are certain actors who pop up in multiple cult movies, sometimes as the lead, sometimes only in very small roles—but are always memorable, no matter where you see them. Gerrit Graham, who passed away this week at the age of 77, was one such performer; his career kicked off in the early ’70s and spanned decades of entertaining turns in movies and TV shows. If you’re a fan of Brian De Palma’s Phantom of the Paradise, Graham’s role as the flamboyant pop star Beef is forever emblazoned in your psyche. He also made an impression in the suddenly timely AI tale Demon Seed (1977); Robert Zemeckis’ satirical salesman saga Used Cars (1980), opposite Kurt Russell; the terrible but also wonderful National Lampoon’s Class Reunion, a 1982 black comedy set at “Lizzie Bordon High School;” post-Vietnam urban warriors action flick The Annihilators (1985); trashy “alien invasion by way of my satellite TV” romp TerrorVision (1986); splattery techno-horror delight Chopping Mall (1986); and CHUD II: Bud the CHUD (1989), in which he played the sewer-emergent title character. Graham also appeared in 1987 cult skateboarding film The Search for Animal Chin, endearing him to an entirely different demographic beyond midnight movie fiends. In 1990, he starred in Child’s Play 2 as a foster dad who takes in little Andy Barclay and ends up tangling with Chucky as a result. On the small screen, he had roles on Tales From the Crypt, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine and Voyager, and Babylon 5, among many others. According to Variety‘s report on Graham’s death, he was also a songwriter who collaborated with Bob Weir of the Grateful Dead and a screenwriter who penned episodes of the 1980s Twilight Zone, among additional credits. He will be greatly missed. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Nuclear Experts Offer China and US Solutions for AI Risks
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.46
Fears over the danger of artificial intelligence have literally gone nuclear. Ahead of a scheduled meeting in Washington next week between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, experts are calling for a shared framework between the two countries to mitigate the risks of an AI-triggered cyberattack or nuclear strike. They address a concern similar to the one that’s driven multiple AI industry insiders to warn about possible extinction-level events: Humans are handing over too much autonomy over critical systems to AI agents they can neither understand nor control. In a report published last week, the Brookings Institution’s Melanie Sisson and Fudan University’s Tianjiao Jiang wrote that it was crucial for both countries to ensure that critical military decisions—like when to launch a nuclear retaliatory strike—remain solely in human hands. “As militaries integrate agentic AI into their operations and AI models advance rapidly in sophistication and capability, new pathways to catastrophic outcomes are emerging,” Sisson wrote in the report. “Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping can lead in governing these dangers by agreeing that only humans, not AI, should make the decision to initiate a cyberattack against each other’s nuclear command, control, and communications systems (NC3) or critical infrastructure.” Sisson and Jiang suggested that the U.S. and China work together to establish “red lines” around the military use of AI, rules determining what “meaningful human control” looks like in practice, and a dedicated “military hotline for AI,” through which officials in both countries could quickly report “emergency incidents triggered by AI errors or AI cyberattacks.” Former president Joe Biden reached an agreement with president Xi in late 2024 that neither the U.S. nor China should allow decisions related to the use of nuclear weapons to be handled by AI. But tensions between the two countries have ratcheted up since Trump returned to office just a couple of months later, in large part over their competition to build ever-more powerful AI systems. And the current President has shown no signs that he feels beholden to honoring agreements struck by previous administrations. The Trump administration has also eagerly embraced AI tools in its ongoing military campaign against Iran, including the use of Palantir’s Maven to gather and parse battlefield information that helped military officials identify targets for future strikes. And while a growing number of AI researchers and ordinary Americans have begun to worry about the possibility of an AI-triggered doomsday, the country’s 80-year-old commander-in-chief has dismissed such fears as a “SICK conspiracy” spread to benefit China, while also posting AI-generated images to social media depicting overseas destruction and himself as a competent, imposing leader. Fears that a simple miscommunication, technical glitch, or bureaucratic hiccup could trigger an international nuclear exchange are not new. During the height of the Cold War in September 1983, a lieutenant colonel in the Soviet Air Defense Forces named Stanislav Petrov received a warning from an automated early-warning satellite system that five U.S. nuclear warheads were headed directly towards the Soviet Union. If he had alerted his superior officers in the military about the apparently inbound missiles, they very likely would have authorized retaliatory strikes. Instead, in a moment of awe-inspiring level-headedness, he reasoned that if the U.S. were going to launch a full-scale nuclear attack on its Cold War adversary, it would’ve used hundreds of bombs from its vast arsenal, not just five. He phoned his superior officers to report a false alarm. It was later determined that the satellite system had picked up flares of sunlight bouncing off of clouds and interpreted them as incoming warheads. Petrov may have single-handedly spared the world from armageddon that day. But an AI system entrusted with making similar judgment calls, based purely on analyzing real-time data, might not have made the same decision. Even when handed ostensibly routine, harmless tasks, modern AI agents are prone to all kinds of unpredictable behavior, as was dramatically demonstrated by the recent Hugging Face hack. Multiple insiders from frontier AI labs have come forward over the past week to warn that the capabilities of these agents are advancing much quicker than our understanding of how to ensure they’re aligned with human interests and values. Earlier this month, Senator Bernie Sanders—one of Capitol Hill’s most vocal critics of the unregulated AI sector—called for an international ban on the development of so-called “superintelligence,” with punishments on par with those in place around the illegal development of nuclear weapons. In July, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres urged the 193 U.N. member states to unilaterally outlaw the use of autonomous weapons systems. “Some decisions must remain forever human—none more than taking a human life,” Guterres said during his speech, delivered at the inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva.

item.title: Pessimism Reigns Over AI and Jobs, Pew Poll Finds
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.46
What do people across the globe think AI will do to the labor market? A global Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday found that in 34 out of 37 countries, the most common answer was “fewer jobs.” Across a 37-country median, 46% of respondents predicted fewer jobs, 13% said it wouldn’t make much difference, and just 9% anticipated more jobs. Roughly a quarter said they weren’t sure. The only country where more people thought AI would create more jobs than it eliminates was Nigeria (27% vs 26%), though “not sure” beat out “fewer jobs” by considerable margins in Thailand (49% vs 32%) and the Philippines (54% vs 26%). Pew identified a clear trend towards pessimism in countries with higher GDP, perhaps reflecting fears about the automation of white-collar work and/or an AI-induced collapse in wages. In the U.S., 71% of respondents predicted fewer jobs, up from 64% just two years ago. Young adults also appeared to report the most anxiety about AI’s impact on the job market in both high- and middle-income countries, Pew reported, although this trend was not universal. Pew noted that high earners and the educated were more likely to predict job loss (at least in middle-income countries), though that’s because lower earners and the less formally educated were more likely to answer “not sure,” as opposed to having a more positive outlook. “The share of adults who say they are more concerned than excited about the technology has gone up since last year in Sweden (+9 percentage points), Poland (+8), the Netherlands (+7), Hungary (+6) and Australia (+4),” Pew noted. Respondents who described their overall ideological leanings as closer to the left than right tended to be more pessimistic than their conservative counterparts on inequality. Pew found one of the widest ideological gaps of any of the 34 nations included in this part of the poll in the U.S., where liberals were 31% more likely to fear rising inequality than right-wingers. AI’s actual impact on the job market so far is unclear, although that may just be because it’s too early to tell. Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research experts found the overall consequences for the U.S. labor market had been marginal in work published July 2026, although AI may already be contributing to a harsher environment for recent graduates. Of course, Silicon Valley firms driving the frontier edge of AI haven’t done themselves any favors on the popularity front by relentlessly scaremongering as a marketing tactic and promising customers huge savings via mass layoffs. A number of CEOs have changed their tune and now insist they’re only selling productivity tools that won’t replace workers, but Pew’s numbers seem to indicate the AI hype rhetoric has won the industry very few friends among the public writ large. While respondents appeared slightly less negative about AI’s impact on inequality, that’s basically because many respondents expected more of the same bullshit. “On balance, people are more likely to say AI will increase rather than decrease the gap between the rich and the poor,” Pew added. “Still, relatively large shares in many places are either unsure or say AI will not affect inequality in their country much.” Still, about 46% of U.S. respondents said it would worsen inequality, while just 21% said it would make little difference. Just five percent of Americans said they believed it would make the country more equitable.

item.title: Dyson’s Latest Robovac Is Ideal for People Who Don’t Care About Mop-Bots
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.21
Dyson has released three new robot vacuums this week: the $550 R1 Nurovi Dry, the $700 R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry, and the $1,200 R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub. And it’s actually the cheapest of those that caught my eye the most. Robot vacuums can be a very nice thing to have around the house, but high-end floor bot pricing has ballooned out of control lately, with some encroaching on the $2,000 marker. At the same time, some of these robots—I’m looking at you, Dreame Aqua10 Ultra Roller—can whiff so hard on the basics that it’s impossible to justify spending that cash. I don’t know about you, but I long for a cheaper, simpler robot vacuum that can still map my home, navigate well, and has good obstacle avoidance. That seems to sum up the R1 Nurovi Dry. The R1 features 21,000Pa suction, a mid-tier spec compared to some other robovacs that reach into the 30,000s and higher. But as Dyson chief engineer Jake Dyson is quoted as saying in a press release emailed to me this week, “Robotic cleaning isn’t just about suction power.” I’m inclined to agree, based on all of the various robot vacuums I’ve tested. For example, the best model I’ve tested for picking up dust and dirt remains the Matic robot vacuum, which only sucks air at 3,200Pa in its standard cleaning mode. So what does the R1 do instead? A cross-section render on the Dyson site (check it out below) shows a smaller channel that brings fine debris into one chamber, while a larger channel above it collects bigger chunks in another. The company also says it can “intelligently detect dust levels and floor types in real time” to adjust its suction power and cleaning behavior, and its self-emptying dock uses a cyclonic canister instead of a dust bag you’d have to replace every few months. The R1 has other premium-style features, including a side sweeping brush that reaches out to get into tight spaces the robot otherwise wouldn’t be able to reach. The company says in its press release that this brush has been “engineered at a precise angle” with a connector that “actively controls the pressure and direction of the brushes” to keep from flicking debris away from the robot, instead directing it into the robot’s path. I’ve seen similar claims from other robot vacuum makers, and I’d be interested to see how this plays out in real-world testing. Furthermore, Dyson says the R1 can climb up to 0.79-inch floor transitions and is fairly squat at 3.78 inches tall, meaning it can get under very low furniture. That’s not the shortest, but it’s pretty good—for comparison, the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete stands at 3.12 inches tall when its periscope-like sensor cluster sinks into its body. But that’s a $1,700 vac-bot; I’ll take the extra half an inch to save $1,100. The R1 uses LiDAR for mapping and navigation, as well as “line lasers and edge sensors” for object avoidance. All of the above can be said for the R2 as well, which also features dual triangular mop pads that the company says can better get into edges and corners, while its dock washes the pads using 167-degree water. Meanwhile, the R3 adds AI vision cameras and uses UV light for “forensic checks” after cleaning “for full proof of a hygenic clean.” It also features 30,000Pa suction and a roller mop that extends to reach edges but lacks the articulating side brush of the other bots. The R1 Nurovi Dry and R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub are each available now on Dyson’s website. The R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry is exclusively available at Costco.

item.title: This little-known Android setting makes public Wi-Fi less risky
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 6.27
Public Wi-Fi is convenient, but it can expose more of your browsing than you'd expect. Android has a built-in feature called Private DNS that quietly encrypts one of the most revealing parts of your connection. Here's what it does, how to turn it on, and what else helps. What's a private DNS? Encrypting the lookups your phone makes behind the scenes As you may or may not know, every time you tap a link or open an app, your phone has to figure out where that website or service actually lives. It does this through the Domain Name System, or DNS, which translates names like google.com into the numerical IP addresses computers use to reach each other. DNS is one of the oldest parts of the internet, and it wasn't designed with privacy in mind. Traditional DNS requests travel unencrypted, so anyone between you and the DNS server can read them. On your home network, of course, that usually means your internet provider. On public Wi-Fi at an airport, café, or hotel, more people could be watching. The network operator can see every domain your phone looks up, and a malicious hotspot can go further by tampering with those responses, quietly sending you to a fake login page instead of the real one. This is called DNS spoofing, and unencrypted lookups make it easier to pull off. A private DNS is how you solve that problem. Google added support for it in Android 9 Pie, and it has been part of every version since. In the case of Android, it uses a protocol called DNS-over-TLS, which wraps your lookups in the same kind of encryption that protects HTTPS websites. Instead of sending requests in plain text, your phone opens a secure connection to a trusted resolver, checks that it's talking to the right server, and sends its queries through that connection. Neat. As a result, a nosy network can no longer read or alter your DNS traffic. Private DNS does have limits, though. It doesn't hide your IP address, and a determined observer can still infer some things about the servers you connect to. It isn't a VPN. What it does is close a common gap that's easy to exploit, and it works at the operating-system level, so it covers every app on your phone without extra software. How do you set it up? Choosing a trusted provider takes less than a minute For what it's worth, setting up Private DNS takes less than a minute, and you don't need to install anything. The exact path depends on who made your phone. On Pixels and most phones running near-stock Android, open Settings, tap Network & internet, and look for Private DNS. On some models, it sits under an Advanced menu. Samsung puts it somewhere else: go to Settings, then Connections, then More connection settings, and you'll find Private DNS there. If you can't find it, searching for "Private DNS" in the Settings search bar is usually the fastest route. Once you open it, you'll see three options: Off, Automatic, and Private DNS provider hostname. Automatic is often the default. It tries to encrypt your lookups using your network's own DNS server if that server supports encryption. If it doesn't, your phone falls back to regular, unencrypted DNS without telling you, which is exactly what you'd get on a sketchy public hotspot. For real protection, choose the provider hostname option. This makes your phone use a specific encrypted resolver on every network. You'll need to enter a hostname rather than an IP address because Android confirms the server's identity as part of the encrypted handshake. Popular free choices include dns.google for Google Public DNS and one.one.one.one for Cloudflare. Personally, I use Cloudflare myself, since I've found it to be the fastest and most reliable. There's also dns.quad9.net for Quad9, which blocks known malicious domains, and dns.adguard-dns.com for AdGuard, which also filters many ads and trackers. Type it in, tap Save, and you're done. There's one quirk to know about. Some public networks, including certain hotel and corporate Wi-Fi setups, block the port that DNS-over-TLS relies on. If that happens, Android will warn you that the Private DNS server can't be accessed, and pages won't load. Switching to Automatic for a while will get you online, but you should treat that network with extra caution. Other stuff you can do Stacking simple habits for safer public Wi-Fi Private DNS is a smart baseline, but it only fixes one of the things that make public Wi-Fi risky. If you often connect at airports, coffee shops, or hotels, a few other habits make a real difference. The most effective upgrade is a reputable VPN. Private DNS encrypts only your lookups, while a VPN encrypts all of your traffic between your phone and the VPN server, hiding which sites and services you use from the local network. Most VPN apps send DNS through their own encrypted connection and override your Private DNS setting while connected, so the two don't conflict. Choose carefully, though. A free VPN with a vague privacy policy can end up seeing more of your data than the café network ever would. You can also be stricter about how your phone joins networks. Android can remember open networks you've used before and reconnect to them automatically. That makes it easier for an attacker to set up a fake hotspot with a familiar name. Forget public networks when you're done, and turn off any setting that connects to open Wi-Fi automatically. When you don't need Wi-Fi, switching it off further reduces your exposure. Pay attention to what you do while connected. Almost every major website now uses HTTPS, but check for it before entering passwords or payment details, and never click past a browser warning about an invalid certificate. For sensitive tasks like banking, your mobile data connection is generally safer than shared Wi-Fi. If you need to get a laptop online, your phone's hotspot works too. Finally, keep your phone updated. Android security patches and Google Play system updates regularly fix vulnerabilities in the networking stack and elsewhere, but they only help if you install them. Private DNS is a small step with real benefits Private DNS won't turn public Wi-Fi into a secure network, but it closes an easy gap attackers love to exploit. Set a trusted hostname, pair it with a VPN and sensible habits, and your Android phone becomes far harder to snoop on.

item.title: I found the weirdest thing interfering with my Wi-Fi, and the fix took 5 seconds
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.62
Wi-Fi problems are a tricky thing, because they can be traced back to almost anything, and no amount of router tricks will help sometimes. Sometimes, Wi-Fi is just wonky, period. As I tried to (mostly fruitlessly) investigate where my Wi-Fi problems were coming from, I recently found the strangest culprit. Chances are that it's messing up your connection, too. USB 3.0 can really be a nuisance to your Wi-Fi 2.4GHz in particular Out of all the things that could be messing up your Wi-Fi, could you ever suspect that USB 3.0 is the culprit? I know, it doesn't make a whole lot of sense. I get something like dead zones, sure, but USB? How's that related to a router that doesn't even connect via USB by itself? Alas, it absolutely can. The problem lies in radio frequency noise. USB 3.0 moves data at high speeds, and it doesn't need to be to or from your router to cause trouble, as the electrical activity itself can generate broadband interference around the 2.4GHz range. Unfortunately, that's exactly where the 2.4GHz band operates, and it also happens to be the most congested band on most networks. A badly placed USB device, cable, hub, or port can effectively raise the noise floor around your wireless gear and make a perfectly decent signal harder to hear. That's also why the 2.4GHz band is usually more affected than the 5GHz or the 6GHz; it's not that the USB device is somehow biting into your overall Wi-Fi bandwidth, but rather that it's producing so much unwanted RF noise in the wrong part of the spectrum that nearby Wi-Fi receivers start having a bad time. This is especially true if the signal wasn't much to write home about to start with. Long story short, a tiny USB 3.0 device could be messing up your entire home network, and no amount of rebooting the router will fix this particular issue. It can make perfectly good Wi-Fi look borderline broken Slow speeds aren't the only giveaway Annoyingly, figuring this out will probably take you on a merry journey through various router settings, Ethernet cable testing, and whatever else you'll find in a typical network troubleshooting toolkit. That's because the symptoms don't immediately scream "it's the USB gear." You'll see this problem behave as bad Wi-Fi tends to do. Slower speeds, spiking latency, inconsistent performance, disconnects. It also shows up as the 2.4GHz band being utterly disappointing and unreliable. What this doesn't do is mess with your actual router, so the device itself will seem to be fine; everything else won't. One clue to look out for is when the problem seems unusually localized. Maybe the laptop that sits next to a USB hub is struggling, but your phone (far away from the USB troublemakers) is thriving. Or maybe the connection gets worse when you use your external SSD. Those signs don't immediately mean that it has to be USB 3.0, but if you know that you have such devices connected close to the router or the end device, it's worth investigating. The easiest way to prove it is to make the problem disappear Change one thing and see whether it fixes it I'm sure this will elicit a "well, duh" type of response, but the easiest way to fix this is to simply unplug those USB 3.0 devices and see if that helps. Yes, it is that simple. Leave everything else exactly as it was with zero other changes, then rerun the same Wi-Fi test from the same exact spots. Don't make any other changes, such as changing channels or rebooting the router, as we're trying to isolate the problem. If the only thing that changes is the removal of USB 3.0 devices, then congrats, you've isolated the problem. To make sure it's not a one-off, repeat the test a few times. Then, plug the device back in and go over all the tests again. If the performance drops, you've found your culprit. You probably don't need to give up USB 3.0 A little distance can make a surprisingly big difference While getting rid of those USB 3.0 devices is a logical fix, it's hard to just choose to live without any of your USB gadgets. Let's talk about workarounds. The easiest fix is usually not to remove them entirely, but to put some distance between them and the router (or whatever is using Wi-Fi and struggling). Move the hub, drive, or cable farther away and re-run all the tests. Chances are it'll help. ...It didn't help? Inspect the cable itself. A better-shielded USB 3.0 cable or an extension cable can help you keep noisy hardware farther away, preserving your connection. The only downside is that introducing an extension cable may affect charging or data transfer speeds, so it's a trade-off you need to think about. The weirdest Wi-Fi problems aren't always Wi-Fi problems When I finally figured this out, I was pretty baffled. This kind of problem is often the last thing you'll think of when investigating Wi-Fi issues, but it's also one of the easiest things to check. If you're feeling stumped, unplug a few USB 3.0 devices and try your luck.

item.title: 4 reasons some Android features are still off-limits to you
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Are you also dealing with a particular kind of Android frustration I know too well? You find out your phone can do something, get excited to try it, and then find the feature nowhere. You check Settings, Google it, follow the instructions step by step, and still come up empty-handed. No setting. No toggle. Nothing. That’s because “available on Android” doesn’t necessarily mean “available on your phone.” Android features can be surprisingly selective. Two people can have Android phones, run the same software version, and still have access to different features. Strange, right? It’s the same, same — but somehow different. I’ve learned to check a few things before wasting time digging through Settings for a feature that may never show up. So, before you blame yourself — or your phone — here are four reasons some Android features can still be off-limits for you. Region locked Not every feature is global I noticed something was off when I started looking into Gemini in Chrome. I had a perfectly capable Android phone, and the feature simply wasn’t available to me. Google currently lists Gemini in Chrome on Android as available only in the U.S., so if you’re using an Android phone in India, you won’t have access to it, even if your device meets the other requirements. Google also says the feature is still rolling out gradually, so availability can depend on more than just your phone. This isn’t limited to Google’s features. Samsung also makes some Wallet features available only in certain countries or regions. Samsung Wallet can handle payment cards, boarding passes, tickets, and digital keys, but the features and content available can vary by country, device, carrier, and firmware. That’s what makes region restrictions so confusing. Apparently, your phone has a passport too. Hardware dependent Your phone can’t fake hardware I’ve had this happen when comparing Galaxy phones: I’d see my brother using a cool feature like Auto Zoom in FlexCam on his Galaxy Z Flip 6, grab my own Galaxy Z Fold 6, and expect to find the same option right away. After all, they’re both premium Samsung foldables. But that’s when I learned not to assume every Galaxy phone gets every feature. Samsung says some Galaxy AI and camera features are available only on selected devices. Hardware can make a bigger difference than you might expect. The processors, camera sensors, display, and other components can determine whether a feature is supported. In the case of Auto Zoom in FlexCam, the feature is designed around the Flip6’s FlexCam setup, where the phone can be partially folded and automatically adjust the zoom to keep you in frame. The Fold6 has a completely different form factor. Your phone can fake a lot with software, but it can’t fake hardware it simply doesn’t have. Software limited Don’t let your phone fall behind This one has caught me more than once. Sometimes, hardware isn’t the problem at all — the required software simply isn’t there yet. It’s a bit like having a perfectly good TV but missing the app you want to watch something on. The hardware is there, but the software hasn’t caught up. For example, I’ve opened Samsung’s Settings after seeing a useful feature in a tutorial, only to realize the person in the video was running a newer version of One UI. The menus looked familiar, but the option I was looking for was missing. The same thing can happen with Google apps. You might see someone using a new Gmail, Google Photos, or Google Messages feature, check your phone, and wonder why yours looks different. Updating the app or your phone can sometimes make all the difference. Sometimes your phone doesn’t need a new feature — it just needs to catch up. After all, in life and on your phone, staying up-to-date matters. Phased rollouts Wait for your turn This is probably the most annoying one because waiting around for a feature you already know exists is tedious. A feature can be officially announced, your phone can support it, and your software can be completely up to date, yet the feature still might not appear on your device. That’s because companies often roll out new features in stages instead of switching them on for everyone at once. A little patience, apparently, is part of the deal. I’ve seen this with Google and Samsung features. Google Messages is a good example. Google says Gemini in Messages is being released gradually, so even if your phone meets the requirements and your language and country are supported, you might not see it immediately. So I’d rather wait for the feature than panic over something that isn’t even in my control. Your phone might be innocent After all this, I’ve stopped assuming a missing Android feature means my phone is doing something wrong. Sometimes the feature is restricted where I live; sometimes my phone doesn’t have the hardware for it; sometimes my software needs to catch up; and sometimes I’m just waiting for my turn. So, the next time I see someone showing off a feature I can’t find, I’m not immediately going down a settings rabbit hole. It just means: not here, not on this phone, not yet.

item.title: These 4 built-in Windows tools helped me build a self-healing PC
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.49
Windows doesn't need third-party utilities to take care of itself. With the right built-in tools and a bit of setup, a PC can check its own health, repair corrupted files, and even recover from a failed boot without much help from you. Task Scheduler The quiet automation engine behind every repair routine Task Scheduler is the piece that ties everything else together. On its own, it doesn't fix anything, but it runs other tools at set times or in response to specific events, so repairs happen without anyone having to remember them. You can open it by searching for Task Scheduler in the Start menu or by running taskschd.msc, and the Create Task option gives you far more control than the simplified Create Basic Task wizard. Triggers are where the tool gets interesting. A task can run on a fixed schedule, at startup, at logon, when the computer goes idle, or when a particular entry appears in the Event Viewer. That last option lets a maintenance script run in response to a logged error, such as an unexpected shutdown, instead of waiting for the next scheduled window. For system maintenance, a few settings matter more than the rest. Repair commands need administrator rights, so set the task to run with the highest privileges and allow it to run whether a user is signed in or not. Running it under the SYSTEM account avoids storing a password and keeps it independent of any single user profile. On a laptop, the Conditions tab can restrict the task to times when the machine is plugged in, which prevents a long scan from draining the battery. The Settings tab also lets you run a task as soon as possible after a scheduled start is missed. That's useful for a PC that isn't always powered on at the chosen hour, since a skipped weekly check simply happens the next time the machine is available. The practical result is a single scheduled task that launches a script containing the repair commands covered below. Once configured, it runs in the background, and its history tab shows when each run happened and whether it finished successfully. DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) Fixing the source Windows uses to repair itself DISM is a command-line tool originally built to prepare and service Windows images, but it has become one of the most useful repair utilities on a running system. Its value comes from what it repairs: the component store, a folder of reference files located in C:\Windows\WinSxS that Windows relies on when installing updates and restoring damaged system files. If that store is corrupted, other repair tools have nothing reliable to work from. DISM offers three levels of inspection, all run from an elevated Command Prompt or Terminal. The command DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth quickly checks whether corruption has already been flagged. The /ScanHealth option runs a deeper and slower scan of the component store. Finally, /RestoreHealth scans for problems and repairs whatever it finds, which is the command most people end up using. By default, RestoreHealth downloads replacement files from Windows Update, so the PC needs an internet connection for the repair to succeed. When that isn't possible, or when Windows Update itself is part of the problem, the /Source parameter can point DISM to a mounted Windows installation image instead. The image should match the installed version of Windows; otherwise, the repair may fail. A full RestoreHealth run can take anywhere from several minutes to much longer, and the progress indicator has a habit of pausing at certain percentages. That pause is normal, and interrupting the process is a worse idea than waiting. DISM writes a detailed record of each operation to C:\Windows\Logs\DISM\dism.log, which is the first place to look if a repair reports an error. In an automated maintenance routine, DISM should run first. Because the System File Checker pulls its replacement files from the component store, repairing that store beforehand gives the next step a healthy foundation. It also means that a problem DISM can't fix shows up clearly in the logs before anything else runs. SFC (System File Checker) Scanning protected system files for silent corruption System File Checker has been part of Windows for decades, and it remains the simplest way to verify that core operating system files haven't been damaged or replaced. It works through Windows Resource Protection, which guards critical files, folders, and registry keys. When SFC finds a protected file that doesn't match its expected version, it replaces it with a clean copy from the component store. The standard command is sfc /scannow, run from an elevated prompt. The scan checks every protected file and repairs what it can, reporting one of a handful of outcomes when it finishes. The best result is a message stating that no integrity violations were found. Other messages indicate that it found and repaired corrupt files, or that some files couldn't be fixed. For a scan that only reports problems without changing anything, the /verifyonly switch is available. SFC's biggest limitation is its dependence on the component store. If the reference copies are damaged, SFC can't restore healthy files, which is exactly why running DISM first is the recommended order. When both are chained together in a script, DISM repairs the source, and SFC then uses that source to fix the live system files. Every scan is recorded in C:\Windows\Logs\CBS\CBS.log. That file is long and noisy, but filtering it for lines tagged with [SR] isolates the entries created by SFC, making it much easier to see which files were affected. SFC can also work when Windows won't start normally. From the Windows Recovery Environment, the /offbootdir and /offwindir parameters point the scan at the offline Windows installation, so files can be repaired without booting into the desktop. There are trade-offs to scheduling it. A scan uses noticeable disk and processor resources, so running it daily is unnecessary for most people. A weekly run during idle hours catches problems early without getting in the way. Quick Machine Recovery (QMR) Letting Windows fix boot failures through the cloud The tools above can only help when Windows starts. Quick Machine Recovery covers the scenario they can't: a PC that fails to boot at all. It's a Windows 11 feature that Microsoft built on top of the older Startup Repair tool, and it became available to Home and Pro users starting with the August 2025 security update for version 24H2 and later. When Windows detects repeated boot failures, the PC enters the Windows Recovery Environment instead of looping endlessly. QMR then connects to the internet over Ethernet or Wi-Fi and checks Windows Update for a remediation that addresses the problem. If a fix exists, it downloads and applies it, then restarts the machine. If the repair doesn't work, the device returns to the recovery environment with the usual troubleshooting options. The feature is enabled by default on unmanaged Windows 11 Home and Pro machines, and its toggle lives under Settings, System, Recovery. Devices managed by an organization have it turned off by default, leaving the decision to administrators. An additional setting enables automatic remediation, which makes the PC keep checking for a solution at set intervals rather than stopping after a single attempt. When QMR is switched off, Windows falls back to the local Startup Repair process. It's important to understand what QMR is designed for. Microsoft positions it as a response to widespread boot problems, such as a faulty update or driver affecting many devices at once, where the company can identify the issue and push a targeted fix. It isn't a general-purpose repair tool for problems unique to a single machine, and it can't help if the PC has no network connection during recovery. Early testing also suggests it may not work on older hardware. Even with those limits, QMR fills the last gap in a self-healing setup by handling failures that happen before any scheduled script has a chance to run. Built-in tools that keep Windows running on its own Task Scheduler automates maintenance, DISM repairs the component store, SFC restores protected system files, and Quick Machine Recovery handles boot failures. Together, they give Windows 11 a layered, largely hands-off way to keep itself healthy without installing any extra software.

item.title: Excel Easter eggs ended 24 years ago—but this open-source Space Invaders project keeps the fun alive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.41
I've always liked the fact that older versions of Excel had hidden games tucked away inside them. Microsoft stopped doing that years ago, but Excel users never completely stopped having fun with spreadsheets. I recently found an open-source Space Invaders-style game that runs entirely inside Excel. Excel used to hide games in plain sight But the Easter eggs eventually disappeared Microsoft snuck some genuinely unexpected games into older versions of Excel. Excel 95 had the Hall of Tortured Souls, a Doom-style 3D maze, Excel 97 had a flight simulator (pictured above), and Excel 2000 had a driving game called Dev Hunter. But that tradition didn't last. In 2002, Bill Gates told Microsoft employees that Trustworthy Computing had become the company's highest priority, with a particular focus on security and reliability. Around the same time, newer versions of Excel stopped shipping with these kinds of hidden games. This meant we lost the intrigue and excitement of discovering that the spreadsheet program we use for budgets and reports contains an entirely unnecessary video game. Microsoft isn't the only company to have turned a spreadsheet into a place for games. Back in the 2000s, an OpenOffice Calc Easter egg let you play a Space Invaders clone directly in a spreadsheet. Two decades later, thanks to VBA and someone's hard work, I found myself doing essentially the same thing in Excel. Play "Space Defenders" in Excel Turn your spreadsheet into an arcade machine Evanml2030's Excel-SpaceInvader project on GitHub is an open-source VBA version of the classic arcade game. Download the macro-enabled Space Defenders workbook, open it in desktop Excel, and play directly inside the workbook. Macro-enabled Excel files can be malicious, so always double-check what you're opening first. I opened this file in Safe Mode (by holding Ctrl as I opened Excel) and inspected its VBA (Alt+F11) before I played it. For more details, scroll to the Security section below. It's much more recognizably Space Invaders than I expected. You move your ship from side to side, fire at the incoming enemies, and try to clear them before they reach you. The controls are simple: use the Left and Right Arrow keys to move and the Spacebar to fire. The game runs inside Excel's normal window, with the workbook effectively becoming the game screen. When you get hit, you're greeted with an abrupt "Uh oh, collision detected" alert, and you can click Launch to play again. On one playthrough, I did encounter a glitch where a falling object suddenly appeared next to my rocket and ended the game. Other than that, though, it worked excellently and played like a proper arcade game. How to get started If you've read the security information below and are comfortable proceeding, download the XLSM workbook from the project's GitHub page. In Windows File Explorer, right-click the file and select Properties. On the General tab, look under Security, check Unblock, and click OK. You'll also need to enable ActiveX controls in Excel for the game to work. Open a blank workbook, go to File > Options > Trust Center > Trust Center Settings > ActiveX Settings, select the option you want, and click OK. Once that's done, close the blank workbook, open the Space Defenders workbook, and enable its macros and ActiveX controls if prompted. Remember to change your ActiveX settings back when you've finished playing. This setting applies to Excel generally, rather than just this workbook, so leaving it changed can affect how Excel handles ActiveX controls in other files. There's a surprising amount of code behind it Excel is doing far more than displaying a few pictures For me, the interesting part was seeing how the game actually works. The VBA handles the game state, movement, enemies, bullets, collisions, timing, and the repeated updates needed to make everything appear to move smoothly. It uses DoEvents, which allows Excel to process other events while the game is running. Without that, a VBA routine that continually loops through the game would quickly make Excel feel unresponsive. The project also calls a couple of Windows API functions. GetAsyncKeyState, from user32.dll, is used to detect keyboard input, while QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency, from kernel32.dll, are used for high-resolution timing. The graphics are handled in an especially Excel-ish way. The game dynamically creates Microsoft Forms Image.1 ActiveX controls and uses them to display the various sprites. In other words, those things flying around the screen aren't some special Excel game-rendering system. They're controls being created and manipulated by VBA. I find that more interesting than the fact that you can play the game itself. Someone has effectively built a small arcade-game framework inside a spreadsheet app. Security: Opening a macro-enabled file from the web In this case, I didn't find anything concerning Before playing, I inspected the workbook's VBA to see what it was actually doing. I didn't find code that launches external programs, makes network requests, reads or deletes files, modifies the Windows registry, or uses obvious code obfuscation. I also didn't find an automatic Workbook_Open() or Auto_Open() routine. The Windows API calls I found are used for the game itself: GetAsyncKeyState handles keyboard input, while QueryPerformanceCounter and QueryPerformanceFrequency provide high-resolution timing. The ActiveX controls are used to display the game's images. That doesn't mean you should automatically trust every macro-enabled Excel file you download. It means that, in this particular workbook, I didn't find anything that appeared to do anything beyond run the game. Microsoft disables ActiveX controls by default in Microsoft 365 and Office 2024, so you may stumble upon additional security warnings when opening the workbook. That's another good reason to treat downloaded macro-enabled files with caution. Excel is a playground You don't need to know VBA or build an entire game inside Excel to get creative with it. I've used Excel's humble grid to get creative in some surprisingly different ways, like making pixel art, planning a room, creating a stop-motion animation, designing a board game, and even mapping out a crochet pattern. You just have to stop thinking of Excel as somewhere you only put numbers.

item.title: These 3D prints are meant to break—that's the whole point
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.38
3D prints can be brittle and weak, depending on which materials you use and how you choose to print them. But some prints are designed to be broken, either as part of their core functionality or in order to protect something else. Here are some 3D prints that you might want to break. Snap-off shims Snap to decide which size you need 3D-printed shims can be made to size and are perfect for installing and fixing doors and windows that are out of plumb. There are two ways you can go about this: draw up and design a shim that fits perfectly every time you need one, or keep a few around and break them down to size with models like the cutaway shim or easy snap waffle shim. While 3D-printed parts are weak enough that bending can cause them to separate at the layer lines, even basic PLA is tough enough to withstand the sort of compressing force that these shims are designed to endure. They’re perfect for using up those last few grams of filament, too! Tamper-evident seals and locks Designed with a single use in mind Tamper-evident seals and locks are designed to be used just once. You attach them to whatever it is you want to monitor for interference, after which you have to break them in order to gain access. There are a few models to choose from here, including the popular tamper-evident lock and the much smaller tamper-evident bag lock. Both of these models have an excellent community rating, even if they’re probably not as reliable as commercially available solutions. Assuming you’re not securing police evidence or crime scenes, they’ll probably do the job just fine. Remember that these aren’t designed to keep people out like a standard lock, but rather to break easily if someone attempts to make their way in. Breakable surprise egg Add a surprise during the pause, then finish the print This breakable egg needs to be cracked in order to get to whatever is stored within it. Send it to your printer and then, when the print pauses, fill it with a surprise: toys, candy, or anything else you want. Resume the print and the contents will be sealed up inside, ready for someone to break open. At only 8g of filament per egg, you don’t need to feel too bad about plastic waste (justmake sure that you recycle or reuse the waste filament when you’re done). Be careful about putting chocolate and other meltable items inside the egg, since the heat from the print bed will cause them to soften. The Death Box Like the surprise egg but less cheery The Death Box follows the same basic principle as the surprise egg above, with a cheeky morbid twist. This simple yet sturdy print is designed to store a piece of paper, photograph, or other thin object. When the print pauses, add your items, then resume the print to seal them up. To retrieve them—whether that’s after your death or not—the box will need to be broken. The author has included two models: one’s a bit easier thanks to a weak spot, another that’s a lot harder to break. This doesn’t have to contain your last will and testament or instructions following your demise; you could use it to enclose a private note, the answers to a quiz, or anything else you want to save for a big reveal. Alternatively, print it using something sturdy, put a photo of yourself and a small blurb about who you are, and bury it in the backyard or entombed in the walls of your house as a time capsule. Drone propeller guards Break cheap guards, not propellers 3D-printed drone propeller guards are surprisingly popular, even though drones still feel like a relatively niche gadget. There are guards for a wide variety of models like the DJI’s Avata 2, Lito, Mini 3, and Mini 2 (SE). There are many more models online, from entire protective cages to generic prop guards for other drone types. These lightweight prints shouldn’t add a ton of weight to your drone when printed using light material. Some call for TPU for added flex, but most use cheap PLA that’s easy to print and cheap to replace should the worst happen. While it’s debatable that these are meant to be broken, it’s certainly preferable to break these as opposed to a more expensive part of your drone like the chassis or propeller. Beyond protecting a flying machine you may already own, did you know you can also use your 3D printer to create your own drone?

item.title: 4 ways to repurpose an old Kindle eReader
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.77
eReaders are particularly great gadgets because they tend to stay perfectly usable for a long time. However, there will eventually come a time when you want to upgrade. So what should you do with the old one? We have some ideas for you. Turn it into a smart home display The best feature of your old Kindle is the thing that made it so great for reading—the e-paper display. Since the e-paper only uses power when the screen changes, it’s a great device for a smart home dashboard. There’s an excellent guide from Matt Healy for setting this up with an old Kindle. It essentially just shows a web page, but it’s much easier to update the web page remotely than mess around on the Kindle itself. Attach this to your fridge and it’s a great little hub. Make an E-Paper clock If a full smart display feels like too much work, you can pare it down to the essentials. An e-paper clock is one of the coolest clocks you can have, offering extreme visibility without the annoying glow of an LCD or LED display. As long as your Kindle isn’t super ancient, you can literally just open up time.is in the browser and let it run. Sure, this isn't the most mind-blowing use for an e-paper display, but we're working within the confines of the stock software. Jailbreak it for full control In reality, there’s not a lot you can do with an old Kindle in its factory state. If you want true freedom and flexibility, you're going to have to jailbreak the thing. Doing this opens the door to far more than just custom home screens and new display hacks. Once liberated, you can install custom software and use the device for things Amazon never intended. The good news is it’s probably a lot easier to do this than you might think. Check out our full guide for a general walkthrough. Trade it in for a new one Alright, maybe you're a person who doesn't want to spend an afternoon tinkering with old tech. If you want the least painful path, you can repurpose your Kindle by using it to buy a new Kindle. Amazon offers a trade-in program that gives you an Amazon gift card and a nice 20% discount on a new Kindle. The discount is the real selling point here, though—Amazon typically offers only $5 for old Kindles. Don't let old Kindles go to waste! The takeaway here is that even the simplest, most limited tech can often be turned into something useful instead of gathering dust in a drawer. You got a little more mileage out of your money, and now you’re ready to start filling up your new e-reader with all the books you can handle.

item.title: You’re probably buying the wrong hard drive, and this 341,000-HDD study proves it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.68
When shopping for HDDs, it's all too easy to focus on the price and nothing else. Sure, the biggest drives tend to have eye-watering price tags, and not everyone needs 20+ terabytes of storage anyway ... but a recent study, based on a massive sample size, reveals that those drives might be well worth the added cost. In fact, Backblaze found that some of its largest HDDs failed the least out of its entire fleet. Backblaze's biggest HDDs are currently failing less And the sample size is huge Backblaze regularly reports on how its massive fleet of HDDs is doing, but one of its most recent reports reveals some interesting insights. Namely, that larger capacity may translate to better longevity for hard drives. The company analyzed more than 341,000 production hard drives in the first quarter of 2026. A huge chunk of those drives are of the enormous kind, with capacities of 20TB and more. The sample size is crucial here, because if, out of 86,000 drives, Backblaze is seeing encouraging trends, that has to mean something. While these 20+TB drives don't make up the majority of the fleet, Backblaze seems to be betting on them right now, as out of the 10,220 drives it deployed in Q1 2026, over 9,400 were above 20TB. That's roughly 92%. The most important finding comes down to the reliability of these humongous drives: Backblaze says that their AFR, or annualized failure rate, is just 0.85%. That's well under the average across the entire fleet, which sits at 1.24%. The way AFR works is that it accounts for how many days the drives were actually in service and annualizes the resulting failure rate, so it's more revealing than just comparing raw numbers of how many drives died vs. how many made it out unscathed. Backblaze also reported that its overall AFR improved from the first quarter of 2025, when it was at 1.42%. There's one enormous catch: these drives are still very young Drives you buy on the cheap are probably not Trusting an old HDD can end poorly for many reasons, and that's one important caveat we have to discuss to not make these 20TB+ HDDs look too exciting. The 20TB-and-larger models in the Q1 2026 report range from just a couple of months old to around 16 months on average. Compared to some of the smaller drives, some of which have been running for over five years, these new 20TB+ HDDs are basically babies. That gives them an advantage that might taper off when we look at these same figures in 10 years. A brand new HDD and an older drive don't exactly have the same odds of failing, especially when they're running 24/7 (as is the case here). On the other hand, a more recent Secure Data Recovery study revealed that roughly half of all failed drives sent to the company died in their first year of operation, but even this data has an important caveat: it only talks about drives that actually failed. Those that don't fail never reach the company, and thus aren't accounted for the way they are in Backblaze's data. I digress. Despite the potential age difference between Backblaze's chonky drives and those less capacious, the data is sound, because this isn't the only instance of it. Backblaze has previously compared its 20TB+ drives against older 14TB to 16TB models at similar points in their lives, and the newer, higher-capacity drives still looked competitive, if not slightly better. One 22TB drive is doing a lot of heavy lifting here Bigger doesn't automatically mean better Fun fact: The company seems to have a favorite drive. The WDC WUH722222ALE6L4 (22TB) now accounts for over 45,000 of Backblaze's units, and it only has a 0.38% AFR, which might have something to do with that preference. It also accounts for more than half of Backblaze's entire 20TB+ fleet. The data isn't a fluke, it seems. The drives averaged 16.1 months old, and the model's lifetime AFR was still only 0.58% across more than 22 million drive days; an impressive result when compared with the overall data. Still, there's a model that has an even better failure rate, although the sample size is much smaller, too. Toshiba's 24TB drives posted an excellent 0.22% AFR that quarter, measured across 7,203 HDDs. A cheap hard drive can still end up being the expensive choice Price per drive isn't the number I'd optimize for Going through these numbers does make me rethink my storage strategy a little bit. Most of my own strategy boils down to using what I already own. For instance, I've harvested HDDs from old consoles and laptops. I also tend to think that even tiny drives, such as a 120GB SATA, can have some use, provided you take good care of them and back up your files (those drives tend to be old, bordering on ancient, after all). When it comes to buying new drives, though, it's just not a good time to buy any, so when I did buy, I settled for 8TB. But looking at the prices now, as well as Backblaze's data, it does seem that those bigger drives might be the play. Of course, an important caveat: Do you even need 20TB+ of storage? Many people don't, and if you can't see yourself ever filling such a drive to, say, 70%, there's no need to spend more. These AFRs are low, no matter how you spin it, so it's not like a pricier drive is bound to live a longer life. The biggest drives are far from a gamble, they're just pricey I've heard people say that big HDDs are more prone to failure. I can't tell you based on my own experience, as I've been lucky enough to see very few drive failures in the last 20 years, and they've all been way smaller than 20TB. But Backblaze's data is just about the best sample size you can officially find, and it does reveal that 20TB+ HDDs are doing exceptionally well for now—so, at the very least, don't be afraid to buy them if you actually need them. Seagate Exos 22TB Buying a refurbished/recertified drive is a good way to get yourself lots of terabytes for cheap (well, relatively). The only issue is that those drives might not last as long as a brand-new drive would, so check and make sure they're in good condition.

item.title: You don't need CAD skills to customize 3D models anymore
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.28
Have you seen the slew of new customizable 3D models that are on sites like MakerWorld lately? It's all thanks to a word you might never have heard of before — parametric. Parametric modeling has done more to improve the 3D printing world than almost anything else, and here's everything you need to know. Normal 3D printing files are one-size-fits-all And we all know how one-size-fits-all rarely actually fits well If you've been 3D printing for any length of time, then you've probably run into the problem where a 3D print file from a site like MakerWorld, Thingiverse, or anywhere else almost works. The hole is slightly too small, or the grid is a little too large. While you can easily scale a project in your slicer, that's often not the best solution. The problem with scaling is that everything scales equally. That might not sound like a problem, but for something like Gridfinity, that means the entire thing no longer fits the Gridfinity bins. So, the only option used to be trying to pull the model into a 3D CAD program and update it manually. It was cumbersome, never worked well, and it always took way more effort than it should have. However, parametric modeling completely changes that. Parametric modeling allows you to change parameters to fit your project It adds a level of customizability that just wasn't there before Parametric modeling isn't new. It's been around for years, but it was typically found only in CAD software. Still, though, I always loved it when I found someone who had a parametric 3D model I could just load into Autodesk Fusion and start changing parameters. The way parametric modeling works is by assigning a parameter to a dimension in the model instead of a dimension itself. Then, you define the dimension in a separate table. This is great because you can define something like "plyThickness" for the thickness of your plywood and use that for extrusions. Then, you can change that from 1/8 to 1/4 to 1/2 inch, and it just updates the model accordingly. These parameters can be used anywhere in the model, and they update dynamically. So, if you parameter affects. There have been a few instances where that hasn't happened for me, but it's typically because I did something wrong. But in the world of 3D printing, this is a much better way to design in CAD. You can make a parameter called "smallMagnet" and then print a test print, and if you need to change the size, you can just change the parameter instead of having to update each magnet hole individually. The problem was that, to use parametric modeling, you had to use the software that the model was originally designed in. Thankfully, in 2026, that's no longer a requirement. You no longer need CAD knowledge to edit parametric models It can be done right in your web browser now These days, you'll find parametric models right on sites like MakerWorld. This allows someone to design parametrically and then upload it to MakerWorld, and you just have to enter a few dimensions on the website. For example, take this screw generator. With it, you can generate just about any screw or nut you might need to 3D print, all from your browser without having to know CAD. Or there's this parametric post cap generator. All you have to do is insert the post size you have, and it designs the cap to fit your post. The sky is the limit here, and I love that parametric generators are now available in the browser. One of the best places to use parametric modeling is with Gridfinity. Instead of having to find dedicated websites to generate your grids, you can simply navigate to this customizable Gridfinity project on MakerWorld and input the dimensions you need. Need custom-sized Gridfinity bins? There's a parametric project for that, too. Parametric modeling also lets you do more than just customize dimensions. For instance, there's this custom LED name light box project where you can type a name in, and it generates the whole project for you. Or, this custom name pen holder project where you, again, just type a name and it creates a custom pen holder with the name. If . 3D printing has never been easier When I first started 3D printing around five years ago, it was still a tinkerer's hobby. In some ways, it still is. But these days, 3D printing is much more user-friendly and easier to get into than ever before. 3D printers now tune themselves out of the box in a matter of minutes, and there are more places to download files than ever before. So, if you've been wanting to try out 3D printing, there has never been a better time than now to give it a shot.

item.title: I started keeping an "offline" NAS. It’s the only backup I actually trust
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.03
Most home NAS units are designed to stay powered on and available 24/7. After all, if you want to ensure a backup is made, the best way to do that is keep your backup solution available all the time. However, I also run a small NAS that stays powered off and completely disconnected except for a backup that I run every month or so. As strange as it sounds, it is actually the backup that I trust and rely on the most. This is why. An offline NAS is my backup of last resort Disconnected and offline 95% of the time My offline NAS is my "backup of last resort." It isn't what I use to handle backups of the data that I use day to day for work or in my hobbies. Rather, it stores copies of irreplaceable photos, copies of important tax forms going back a decade or so, digital copies of my social security card, and other things like that. An offline NAS isn't a replacement for your regular NAS or cloud backup. It is a supplement to ensure that your most important files aren't lost. As such, I keep it offline unless I'm actively creating or using a backup. The hardware doesn't need to be anything fancy. You can use an old PC, a Raspberry Pi with a USB drive enclosure, an old Synology unit, or even just a bare drive in a dock. The most important thing is nothing can write to the drive without your direct intervention. . It can't be corrupted by a bad update or botched sync Always-on backups back up mistakes One of the problems that can occur with always-on backups is actually how good they are at mirroring exactly what you do. If you make a mistake and delete something from your PC or a file gets corrupted accidentally, that change can be backed up within minutes, depending on your settings. We've occasionally seen cases where a bad software update to either the NAS or the backup file system can break something too. An offline system mitigates all of those risks. It is almost certainly going to be offline when an unexpected update rolls out, and your file and folder updates are similarly insulated. If I were to corrupt a document with my current setup, I'd have weeks to spot the problem. Moreover, I deliberately don't update files that I haven't manually changed. That way, if a sync bug or a botched migration overwrites my entire photo library, I don't have to panic. I can just fire up the offline NAS, copy over my "cold storage" backup, and everything is fine. Ransomware and malware can't affect a drive that isn't connected Network isolation can be protection Unfortunately, some modern ransomware is specifically designed to find and infect networked storage. Some NAS manufacturers have features designed to mitigate that risk, but it still isn't a risk I want to take. An imperfect implementation can still leave you vulnerable. On the other hand, a device that is disconnected from power and the internet can't be hit with ransomware. The only window where my backup solution could be infected is during a backup phase, but that risk is easy to mitigate—double-check your PC before you perform a backup. It isn't affected by random power surges or wear and tear A disconnected device doesn't care about a power surge There is a physical safety advantage as well. Power surges and brownouts can damage electronics, but if your device is disconnected completely, you don't need to worry about it. You reduce wear and tear Mechanical hard drives are also subject to wear and tear, especially if they spin 24/7. On the other hand, a NAS that is only active for an hour or two every month (or whatever your backup window is) will have a much longer lifespan. SSDs need to be powered on intermittently or their risk of data loss increases. Mechanical hard drives are basically safe to leave off—it doesn't meaningfully affect their data retention. An offline backup is my version of cold storage Always-on backups are designed to protect your regular files against loss. I back up my work and hobby project files to a cloud server and a separate NAS daily. While losing them would be inconvenient and frustrating, it wouldn't devastate me—none of it is irreplaceable. On the other hand, the offline NAS shines when you need a backup that you want to insulate against every possible risk or attack avenue. If you have photos you can't replace, critical documents that you don't want to lose, or anything else like that, I'd recommend creating an always-offline NAS. So long as you're careful with it, and selective about the files you choose to back up, it'll be reliable and cost-effective for years. The only real tradeoff is convenience. You need to remember to transfer your latest f1040 during tax season or those pictures you scanned from a relative.

item.title: 4 innocent-looking Linux commands that can ruin your day
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.89
If you use Linux, you'll eventually want to get comfortable with the terminal. It streamlines your workflow and opens up a whole new way of computing that graphical apps simply can't match. This includes writing Bash scripts for system management and automation or administering a remote machine over SSH. That said, if you're just getting started and relying on online guides or AI chatbots for help, you need to be extra careful. Some commands can look completely harmless, but will break your system in seconds. Here are my top five picks for innocent-looking commands that you wouldn't think twice about but can completely ruin your day. rm -rf ~ /Downloads/old The most expensive typo you'll ever make The traditional dangerous version of this command goes like this: sudo rm -rf / Here, you're essentially running the remove (rm) command with elevated privileges and telling it to recursively (-r) and forcefully (-f) delete everything under /, the root of the filesystem. So, clearly, rm -rf can be dangerous, but it's not some forbidden command you should never touch. In fact, it's a standard way to delete a directory and everything inside it. Say you have an old Downloads folder you want to get rid of. The quickest way to do that is: rm -rf ~/Downloads/old The problem is that a single misplaced space can change everything. In the correct command, the tilde (~) and the path form one continuous string: ~/Downloads/old, which the shell expands to a path under your home directory, such as /home/dibakar/Downloads/old. But let's say you accidentally add a space after the tilde: rm -rf ~ /Downloads/old Now the shell sees two separate arguments. The first is ~, which expands to your entire home directory. So the command will now happily wipe out your documents, photos, configuration files, and everything else in your home directory, and then move on to the other path you specified. echo "a new line of text" > imp.config The difference between appending to a file and overwriting it If you're working in the terminal, one way to add a new line to a configuration file is to open it in a text editor like Nano or Micro and type it in. However, a faster way is to echo the same line straight into the file with a single command: echo "a new line of text" >> imp.config This command adds “a new line of text” to the bottom of the imp.config file. However, let's say you were in a hurry and mistyped it as: echo "a new line of text" > imp.config Now you've replaced the contents of your old imp.config file with a new file containing just one line: “a new line of text.” The only difference is that you typed “>” instead of “>>”. That's because the “>>” operator means append — it adds the command's output to the end of the file while leaving the existing contents intact. The single-arrow “>” operator, on the other hand, means write or overwrite. It creates a new file and writes the output to it, or, if a file with the same name already exists, replaces its contents with the new output. So, say imp.config originally had 10 lines of carefully written configuration, and you run the echo command with “>” instead of “>>”. Those 10 lines are gone. The file now contains exactly the one line you entered in the last command. I've personally done this to my .bashrc, which had hundreds of lines of customization built up over time. I'm not saying “>” is more dangerous than “>>”. Each operator has its place, and it's important to understand the difference so you can use them appropriately. sudo ufw enable It's the equivalent of locking yourself out of your own home This command is about as harmless as it gets on paper. It enables the firewall, which is genuinely good practice from a security standpoint and part of many routine setup checklists when configuring a new system. The problem shows up when you run it over SSH. Say, you're setting up a remote machine and type sudo ufw enable to start the firewall. If your SSH connection isn’t already allowed — which is unlikely on a new setup — the firewall will kick you out and prevent you from reconnecting. You'll need console or physical access to the machine to fix it. This can be a mild annoyance if the machine is in the next room, but a disaster if you're managing a server from another city, or worse, remoting into your home lab while on vacation. To avoid the mishap, first allow your SSH service through the firewall with sudo ufw allow ssh (or explicitly allow your custom SSH port), and only then run sudo ufw enable. This creates the firewall rule before the firewall is activated, so your SSH connection can continue through the firewall. :(){ :|:& };: Just don’t paste a command you can’t read Last but not least, we have the fork bomb. It's about as famous as rm -rf in the Linux community, but if you're a new user, you might have no idea it exists and could carelessly type it in. In fact, I've personally seen this used as a prank in online forums. Someone asked how to get fancy lettering (font ligatures) rendered in their terminal instead of the boring default text, and this evil–evil person told them to enter the fork bomb. On the surface, it almost feels logical that a weird string of symbols would render itself as fancy characters. However, what it'll actually do is rapidly consume system resources, slowing everything to a crawl and potentially making your system unusable. To understand why, here’s a quick overview of how it works: - :() declares a function with the name “:” - { :|:& } is the function body. Every time the function runs, it executes “:|:&” - :|:& creates a pipeline containing two calls to the function and runs that pipeline in the background - ; ends the function definition. - The final : calls the function for the first time. So it's essentially a function that keeps calling itself — where the first call becomes two, then two becomes four, then eight, then sixteen, and it just keeps going. The number of processes grows extremely rapidly until the system hits its limits. You’ll notice a severe slowdown or the system becoming entirely unresponsive. Now, the command itself doesn't delete your files or install malware, but recovering from the resulting lockup will require a hard reboot. This can cause problems if your system was in the middle of writing data — for example, during a system update, backup, or file transfer. Likewise, anything you opened but didn't save will likely be lost. It's rarely catastrophic, but it certainly turns into a nuisance.

item.title: These are the cheapest GPUs that can run DLSS 5 (you probably own one already)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.56
The first game with official DLSS 5 support, NBA 2K27, came out recently, and modders quickly took the DLSS 5 DLL file from the game and made it available to gamers around the world who own a newer NVIDIA GPU, allowing them to use DLSS 5 in a bunch of PC games with tools such as OptiScaler and DLSS 5 Swapper. While only the RTX 50 series is officially supported, at least for now, the two aforementioned utilities allow you to use DLSS 5 on older NVIDIA graphics cards as well. While a good chunk of NVIDIA GPUs can run DLSS 5 at playable frame rates, either officially or with mods, I've created a list of the most affordable NVIDIA cards that are widely available new and that you can run DLSS 5 on. Naturally, most are RTX 50 models, but I've also included a few RTX 40 cards as well. RTX 5050 The cheapest official route to DLSS 5, but it only just manages 1080p You can get an RTX 5050 new for about $300, but I recommend opting for a different card because the 5050 isn't that great, even for 1080p gaming. If you already own one, that's a different story, and you should definitely test DLSS 5 in games you own just to see the technology for yourself, even though it has a drastic frame rate hit. Now, while NBA 2K27 can run at playable frame rates at 1080p on an RTX 5050, reaching almost 60 FPS, you'll have to settle for 30ish frames per second or less in many other modern games. You'll also have a hard time using multi-frame generation along with DLSS 5 due to the card's limited 8GB memory buffer. But hey, the RTX 5050 can run DLSS 5, and at playable frame rates in some games, so why not try it out if you already own the card? RTX 5060 The minimum for a playable 1080p experience The RTX 5060 is the first decent choice for a 1080p experience. PC gamers have managed to get almost 60 frames per second running DLSS 5 at 1080p in a number of titles, which should be more than playable for many people. Some more demanding games will run slower, though, at about 40 FPS or lower. While this card's much more expensive than the RTX 5050, with the most affordable configs starting just north of $450 as of this writing, you're getting much higher performance that's enough to play many games with the modded DLSS 5 DLL.
