The only caveat, again, is that the card only has 8GB of RAM, which won't be enough for multi-frame generation running on top of DLSS 5 in games that use lots of video memory. That said, you should be able to run both frame gen and DLSS 5 in a wide range of games that aren't memory hogs. GIGABYTE GeForce RTX 5060 GAMING OC V2 - Memory Clock Speed - 2602MHz - Graphics RAM Size - 8GB A no-nonsense option for 1080p gaming, the RTX 5060 pairs 8GB of GDDR7 with NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture, while Gigabyte's triple-fan cooling setup keeps temperatures and noise in check through long gaming sessions. RTX 5060 Ti 8GB A bit faster than the RTX 5060 and a serviceable option for 1080p Now, while the 8GB version of the RTX 5060 Ti wasn't a great choice back when GPU prices were sane, it now makes sense to get one since you're getting a 15% performance bump compared to the RTX 5060 for about the same price bump. When it comes to playing games with DLSS 5, the performance boost should be enough for 60 FPS at 1080p in a lot of games, and about 40 FPS in more demanding titles. You will also be able to use frame generation in many modern titles, but multi-frame gen will be a no-go in games that devour VRAM. If you ask me, at current prices the RTX 5060 Ti 8GB is a better choice than the RTX 5060 if you can stretch your budget by about $50. RTX 5060 Ti 16GB The bare minimum for the 1440p resolution Thanks to its 16GB of VRAM, the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB is the first option on this list capable of running games at 1440p with DLSS 5 enabled at playable frame rates. That said, the experience won't be perfect. You can expect about 40 FPS in most games where you can mod in DLSS 5, with 60 FPS and higher frame rates only being available with frame generation. The RTX 5060 Ti 16GB has a major downside, though. It costs only about $60–$70 less than the RTX 5070, while the latter is about 30% faster. Sure, you're only getting 12GB of memory with the RTX 5070, but even 12GB should be enough for DLSS 5 and multi-frame gen at 1440p, with the RTX 5070 being less than 15% more expensive than the RTX 5060 Ti 16GB. If you're getting a new card, the RTX 5070 is a much better choice between the two. Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 Ti - Memory Clock Speed - 2632MHz - Graphics RAM Size - 8GB, 16GB Nvidia's RTX 5060 Ti (this time made by Asus) comes in two variants: 8GB and 16GB. The 16GB is a lot pricier, but with growing VRAM constraints, it remains the better pick. RTX 5070 The first decent choice for 1440p DLSS 5 gaming The RTX 5070 is the first card I'd actually recommend for 1440p DLSS 5 gaming. It's got enough oomph to run games at playable frame rates without the help of frame generation, and its 12GB of memory will hold down the fort at 1440p in most games, even with ray tracing enabled. While its price is highly inflated compared to the MSRP, this is the case for every NVIDIA card out there, so despite it being overpriced, it's still a solid choice if DLSS 5 support is a must. If not, you should consider getting the AMD RX 9070 XT, which packs 16GB of memory, is about 25% faster, and is actually cheaper than NVIDIA's card. I've been using an RX 9070 XT for about a year and a half now and can say that FSR 4 is almost as good as DLSS upscaling and that the card is an excellent choice for 1440p and 1440p ultrawide gaming. Gigabyte GeForce RTX 5070 Windforce - Graphics RAM Size - 12GB - Boost Clock Speed - 2600MHz Nvidia's RTX 5070 graphics card is one of the more balanced options in the RTX 50-series lineup. It gives you 12GB of VRAM, which is much more future-proof than the 8GB VRAM lower-tier cards offer, while also offering more cores and higher bandwidth than the RTX 5060 Ti. RTX 4060 and RTX 4060 Ti These RTX 40 cards aren't officially supported yet, but you can run DLSS 5 on them with mods Now, DLSS 5 isn't officially supported on older NVIDIA cards, but you can make it work with OptiScaler and DLSS 5 Swapper. When it comes to older NVIDIA cards you can still buy new, the RTX 4060 and RTX 4060 Ti are the cheapest out there that can run games with DLSS 5 at anything resembling playable frame rates. The RTX 4060 Ti is in a much better situation since it's about as fast as the RTX 5060, meaning you will get a playable DLSS 5 experience at 1080p in a wide range of modern games. On the flip side, the RTX 4060 is just a tad faster than the RTX 5050, meaning you shouldn't expect much more than 30 FPS with DLSS 5 enabled at 1080p, with more demanding games running even slower than that. Still, this is high enough to check just how DLSS 5 looks in action, so if you own an RTX 4060 and are interested in checking out NVIDIA's latest tech, feel free to test it. But if you want to get a new GPU for DLSS 5, neither the RTX 4060 nor the RTX 4060 Ti is worth it, unless you're ready to peruse the used market. You can run DLSS 5 on any RTX 20 card or newer, but most won't deliver playable frame rates Thanks to tools such as OptiScaler, RenoDX, and DLSS 5 Swapper, and the patched DLSS 5 DLL files, you can actually run DLSS 5 on every NVIDIA GPU starting with the RTX 20 series. Sure, the performance will be quite poor on many of the older cards; in fact, DLSS 5 will barely run on a good chunk of them. But hey, at least you can experience neural rendering firsthand and see what the fuss all is about.

item.title: MediaTek's first 2nm flagship chip is here — meet the new Dimensity 9600 Pro
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.43
What you need to know - MediaTek's Dimensity 9600 Pro is the company's first 2nm flagship chipset, promising better performance and efficiency. - The new 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU delivers up to 17% faster single-core performance while using significantly less power. - MediaTek's upgraded NPU supports on-device AI models with up to 30 billion parameters while improving AI power efficiency. MediaTek has officially taken the wraps off its latest flagship smartphone chipset, called the Dimensity 9600 Pro. And it's the company's first flagship chip built on a 2nm process. The new flagship smartphone season is almost upon us, and chipset makers have started unveiling their next generation of processors. Qualcomm is set to announce its next flagship Snapdragon chipsets later this month, but MediaTek has beaten it to the punch by unveiling its first 2nm chipset. Called the Dimensity 9600 Pro, MediaTek says its new chipset combines flagship performance and power efficiency with advanced agentic AI experiences. The chip features a 2+3+3 All Big Core CPU design, which MediaTek says delivers an impressive 61% reduction in multi-core power consumption. The architecture consists of two C2 Ultra cores clocked at up to 4.55GHz, three C2 Pro cores running at up to 4.35GHz, and another three C2 Pro cores clocked at up to 3.1GHz. MediaTek says single-core performance has improved by up to 17%, while multi-core performance is up to 15% higher than the previous generation, all while consuming less power. Of course, there's also a big focus on agentic AI experiences. MediaTek says the chipset's new dual-NPU architecture and Agentic AI Engine are designed to power the next generation of on-device AI. Its second-generation Super Efficient NPU reportedly reduces AI power consumption by up to 40%, while delivering 51% higher LLM prefill performance and 55% higher token generation per watt. The Dimensity 9600 Pro can also support AI models with up to 30 billion parameters directly on the device, which should allow more complex AI tasks to run without constantly relying on the cloud. There's also a larger 34.5MB cache, alongside support for LPDDR6 memory and UFS 5.0 storage for the first time. MediaTek says its new Scheduling Engine can intelligently allocate computing power and memory resources between hardware and software, allowing multiple apps to continue running smoothly in the background while using fewer resources. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Gaming is getting a significant upgrade as well. The new G2-Ultra NX GPU delivers up to 27% higher peak performance while consuming 24% less power. MediaTek says the GPU can deliver what it calls console-grade gaming on-device at up to 185fps. For cameras, there's a new Imagiq 1290 ISP, which MediaTek says will enable more advanced computational photography and content creation features on upcoming smartphones. There aren't any smartphones powered by the Dimensity 9600 Pro just yet, but we shouldn't have to wait long before the first devices arrive. Apple's 2nm A20 Pro has already launched inside the iPhone 18 Pro series, while Qualcomm is expected to reveal its answer at Snapdragon Summit later this month. item.title: Meta’s Phoenix mixed reality headset is finally starting to look real
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.12
What you need to know - Meta’s Project Phoenix is finally coming into focus after more than a year of rumors about a lightweight, high-end mixed-reality headset. - Phoenix looks more like smart glasses than a traditional VR headset, using nose pads and temple-mounted sensors. - An external compute puck appears to be part of the design. Whispers about Meta working on a lightweight, high-end mixed reality headset codenamed Project Phoenix have floated around the tech sphere for over a year. Now, we finally get our first real look at what Mark Zuckerberg's hardware team has been cooking up, and it seems Meta accidentally left the key under the mat. The images were revealed through Meta’s HorizonOS Prescription Lens package, which first appeared in August as a mostly blank system package, as noticed by UploadVR. An update in September showed detailed pictures of how prescription lens inserts attach to the Phoenix and how users scan a QR code to set them up. Interestingly, the hardware looks less like a traditional VR headset and more like chunky glasses. Phoenix uses nose pads instead of the bulky face interface of the Quest 3 and other XR headsets, with sensors along the temples. There’s also a cable coming from the left temple, seemingly confirming previous reports that Phoenix will use an external compute puck. It's a design that could change the way people think about wearing a mixed reality headset. If you’ve been using more traditional XR headsets, you’ll probably find it comforting to realize potential benefits here, like less weight on your face, but the compromise moves elsewhere: you’ll need to deal with a separate computing unit and a cable. For Meta, the greater challenge might be getting that extra hardware to feel invisible enough that Phoenix still feels like something you can casually wear, rather than another device you have to gear up for. There's another interesting clue here. The leaked setup stuff seems to be based on prescription inserts and controller-free interaction. Meta hasn’t officially announced Phoenix yet, but Meta Connect 2026 starts September 23 and has a session dedicated to controller-free interaction on its agenda. If Phoenix shows up there, we might finally learn whether Meta’s push toward lighter mixed reality headsets is a real shift in headset design, or just a clever way to move the weight somewhere else. item.title: Google just put the latest AI models through a brutal coding test — here's how they did
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.93
What you need to know - Google has launched Android Bench 2.0 to test AI models on complex Android development tasks that can take days. - The new benchmark includes tasks like upgrading dependencies, adding major features, and building Android apps from scratch. - GPT-6 Astra currently leads Google's new benchmark with a 28% pass rate, while Gemini 3.8 Flash scored just 8%. Google has announced Android Bench 2.0, an updated version of its benchmark for evaluating how well large language models (LLMs) and AI agents handle complex Android development tasks. Earlier this year, Google introduced the first version of Android Bench to measure how AI models perform on real-world Android development work. The company has now updated the benchmark with Android Bench 2.0, which is designed to evaluate models and agents against more complex tasks that better reflect actual software development. One of the biggest additions is what Google calls long-horizon tasks (LHTs). These are significantly more complex development jobs that could take a human engineer several days or even a week to complete. Google says the first version of Android Bench, along with many other early AI coding benchmarks, focused primarily on smaller, incremental changes. Android Bench 2.0 is designed to raise that bar with tasks such as upgrading dependencies, adding major new features, and even building Android apps from scratch. With Android Bench 2.0, Google has changed how models are graded. Rather than relying entirely on a binary pass-or-fail system, Android Bench 2.0 uses "continuous scoring." The company says this provides a more "meaningful indication" of how well a model performed, even when it wasn't able to fully complete a task. Google has already tested several of the latest AI models using the new benchmark, including Gemini 3.8 Flash, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, among others. According to the results, GPT-6 Astra currently sits at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate. Gemini 3.8 Flash, meanwhile, scored just 8%. Google says testing models against the LHT dataset should give it a better understanding of their strengths and weaknesses, while also providing developers with more practical guidance about which models are better suited for different Android development tasks. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The updated Android Bench 2.0 leaderboard is available now, and Google says it plans to continue expanding it with more models and results over time. item.title: iQOO 16 display leaks were true: Samsung's 2K 165Hz panel is official
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.87
What you need to know - The iQOO 16 is set to debut as the first smartphone with a 2K resolution OLED display running at a 165Hz refresh rate. - Co-developed with Samsung Display on a dedicated production line, the panel marks the Android debut of Samsung's latest M16 luminescent material and LEAD 2.0 architecture. - The screen reaches 2,800 nits global peak brightness (10,000 nits local peak), features 508 PPI, and delivers sub-pixel-level calibration for color accuracy. Rumor has it that the iQOO 16 will be released soon, and iQOO has now confirmed one of the upgrades that could make this gaming-focused flagship stand out from the crowd. The next phone from the company is said to be the first to sport a 2K OLED panel with a 165Hz refresh rate from Samsung, which iQOO is calling a smartphone first. The announcement also confirms earlier reports that the iQOO 16 would sport Samsung’s newer M16 OLED technology. The company says the phone will be the first Android smartphone to use the material, along with its new 2K LEAD 2.0 technology. For context, we saw the original LEAD OLED panel debut with the iQOO 15. LEAD 2.0 has been developed in partnership with Samsung, built on a dedicated production line just for iQOO’s flagship. The two companies also designed a custom high-refresh-rate display IC and a dedicated production line for the phone. The panel is rated at 2,800 nits for global brightness and 10,000 nits for local brightness. It also offers 508 ppi, wide P3 color coverage, DC dimming, and better brightness and color uniformity than the iQOO 15. iQOO also claims sub-pixel-level calibration leads to extremely tight color accuracy. There is also a less obvious upgrade here: Samsung recently said the new display uses roughly 31 percent less power at 150 nits than a similarly sized 1.5K panel. That’s particularly useful, as improving both resolution and refresh rate often comes with a battery cost. The target is clearly gaming. The display features 500Hz multi-touch sampling and 5,000Hz instantaneous sampling rate, while iQOO’s Q-Flex technology focuses on reducing input lag. There’s also 3,300Hz PWM dimming and many eye-comfort features. item.title: Google Photos could soon be built much deeper into Samsung Gallery
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.70
What you need to know - Samsung's OneDrive Gallery integration is ending soon, but Google Photos appears ready to take its place. - A new Gallery Cloud Sync service has appeared on the Galaxy Store with support for backing up to Google Photos. - Samsung hasn't announced the Google Photos integration yet, but it could start rolling out within weeks. Samsung has started laying the groundwork for what appears to be the replacement for its outgoing OneDrive integration, and unsurprisingly, it's Google Photos. Earlier this year, Samsung announced that users would no longer be able to use OneDrive to back up photos and videos directly through the Samsung Gallery app. Until now, Galaxy users have been able to automatically sync their Gallery photos and videos with OneDrive without needing to use another app or service. However, that partnership is coming to an end later this month. And now, Samsung appears to be preparing its replacement with none other than Google Photos. X user Sandeep Adap has spotted a new Samsung service called "Gallery Cloud Sync" on the Galaxy Store, which appears to be designed to take over from the existing Gallery OneDrive Sync integration. The app listing says Gallery Cloud Sync will safely back up your memories, including photos and videos, to "Google Cloud" so you can access them across your devices. The mention of Google Cloud might sound slightly confusing, but it appears Samsung is actually referring to Google Photos here. User That Josh Guy on X was able to preview the upcoming functionality, which isn't live just yet, and found that Samsung Gallery will offer an option to sync directly with Google. The Gallery settings will reportedly show your available Google storage, let you choose which albums to sync, and offer controls to sync over Wi-Fi or while roaming. This could be a big change if you currently rely on OneDrive for Samsung Gallery backups, since you'll likely need to switch to Google Photos. That said, the overall experience should remain pretty similar, with the sync controls still built directly into the Gallery app. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The OneDrive sync option has already started disappearing from Samsung Gallery for some users and is expected to be discontinued completely later this month. Thankfully, Samsung's upcoming Google Photos integration looks like it could be an even more natural replacement. Samsung hasn't officially announced Galaxy Cloud Sync or started rolling out the Google Photos integration just yet. But with OneDrive support ending soon, we expect the new option to become available sometime later this month or in early October. item.title: Steam Frame costs $1,059, but Android games could give it an edge
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.70
What you need to know - Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, while the 1TB model jumps to $1,299. - Android games are supported, giving the headset access to existing Android APKs without requiring completely separate ports. - Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 + 16GB RAM powers the headset, with SteamOS handling native games and compatibility layers. Valve has finally put a price tag on the Steam Frame, its new wireless VR headset that aims to blur the line between a standalone gaming device and a PC accessory. The catch? It won’t be as simple as clicking “buy” to get one. The Steam Frame starts at $1,059 for 256GB, with the 1TB model costing $1,299. Each headset has tracked controllers, and Valve is bundling Half-Life: Alyx with the device, the company announced. It can play supported games locally or stream more demanding titles from a PC. It’ll also support Android games, with developers using the same Android APKs they already use to bring mobile titles to the Meta Quest. This could give the Frame access to a much larger game library without developers needing to build entirely separate versions for Valve’s headset. The Frame also supports wireless PC streaming with the 6GHz dongle that Valve bundles in. Under the hood, the Frame is packed with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 and 16GB of RAM, with native software and compatibility layers handled by SteamOS. The storage options are also worth a closer look. You can upgrade from 256GB to 1TB for $240, but the Frame also has a microSD slot. So if your main game stream is from a PC, there may be little reason to pay extra for the bigger model. Valve had originally said it wanted the Steam Frame to cost less than the $999 Index, but the final starting price puts it $60 above that benchmark. Rising memory and component costs have complicated the pricing strategy of Valve’s hardware, as seen with the Steam Machine. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Availability will also be controlled by a reservation system, with sign-ups running until September 17 and purchase invitations starting September 18. The Steam Frame is clearly not aimed at the budget VR crowd at $1,059. Valve is betting its Steam library, Android support, wireless PC streaming, and standalone abilities will justify the premium. item.title: Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Software matters
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.58
Heavyweight The iPhone Duo is heavier and thicker than Android foldables, but that isn’t going to make too much of a difference in day-to-day use. The plus point is that it has IP68 ingress protection, and a build quality that’s different to anything else we’ve seen on Android. Also, the software is the biggest differentiator, and the little I’ve seen of this makes me highly interested to use the iPhone Duo. Sublime Make no mistake: the Xiaomi 18 Fold has the best design of any wide foldable, and Xiaomi deserves credit for slotting in a dedicated tele lens into the device. It is a full 35g lighter than the iPhone Duo, but you still somehow get a huge 6,000mAh battery. The custom Xring 03 silicon is intriguing, and the only issue with the 18 Fold is that it is limited to China, so you don’t get the best software — there’s no Play Store or other Google services. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Design and display I like the design of wide foldables as they’re much easier to hold and use than traditional book-style devices like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The iPhone Duo looks interesting thanks to the 5.4-inch outer panel, and it unfolds to a 7.6-inch inner panel. The Xiaomi 18 Fold has similarly-sized displays as well, but when it comes to resolution, the iPhone Duo comes out ahead. That said, the biggest issue with the iPhone Duo is the weight; at 254g, it is the heaviest of any 2026 foldable, and the Xiaomi 18 Fold is 35g lighter. Now, to give you some context, it is 5g heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, but the point stands that it is a hefty device. Obviously, we’ll need to see how that makes a difference in daily use; weight distribution matters a lot on a foldable, and I’ll share findings once I used the Duo. What I like is that the Duo gets IP68 dust and water resistance. It is the only foldable other Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold and 10 Pro Fold to have this feature, and it will make a genuine difference in regular use. The 18 Fold has IP58 and IP59 ingress protection, and it should do a good enough job in outdoor use. Also, the design itself is exquisite on the Duo, and the blue color looks stunning. Something you don’t see (but will make a difference) is the inner panel. The iPhone Duo uses layers of ultra-thin glass sandwiched over the panels, and it should give it much better resilience against deformation — which is an issue with most foldables. Xiaomi, to its credit, delivered what is arguably the best-looking wide foldable in the 18 Fold, and the svelte design along with the bright red hue is brilliant. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Hardware What’s notable about the internals is that both foldables use custom silicon. The iPhone Duo uses the latest A20 Pro, and the 2nm platform has much better power than last year, and it should deliver meaningful upgrades on the battery side of things. Xiaomi is using the Xring 03 silicon with the 18 Fold, and I’m excited to get my hands so I can test it — it’s not often we get a new player that can beat Qualcomm at its own game. Xiaomi also has a distinct advantage with the battery, and the 18 Fold has a 6,000mAh battery that easily lasts over a day. the iPhone Duo should last a day as well, but this is something I’ll need to test. The 18 Fold has 67W USB PD charging tech, but what I like is that the iPhone Duo has 25W MagSafe, making it that much more convenient to use. Annoyingly, Xiaomi doesn’t have built-in magnets, so you can’t just use a Qi 2.2 charger with the device. | Category | Apple iPhone Duo | Xiaomi 18 Fold | | Display | Outer: 5.4-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED, 2034x1398 Inner: 7.6-inch ProMotion LTPO OLED, 2670x1878 | Outer: 5.38-inch LTPO AMOLED, 1712x1168 Inner: 7.58-inch LTPO AMOLED, 2364x1672 | | Operating System | iOS 27, at least seven updates | Android 17 | | Chipset | Apple A20 Pro, 2nm | Xiaomi XRing O3, 3nm | | RAM | 12GB | 12GB/16GB | | Storage | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB, 2TB | 256GB, 512GB, 1TB | | Rear cameras | Main: 48MP f/1.6, sensor-shift OIS Wide-angle: 48MP f/2.2 | Main: 200MP f/1.7, OIS Tele: 50MP f/2.8, 3x tele Wide-angle: 50MP f/2.4 | | Front camera | 12MP | 16MP | | Ingress Protection | IP68 | IP58/IP59 | | Battery | 4,700mAh | 6,000mAh | | Charging | 40W, 25W MagSafe/Qi 2 | 67W PD 3.0, 50W HyperCharge | | Dimensions | Folded: 117.8 x 84.1 x 11.3mm Unfolded: 117.8 x 164.6 x 5.2mm | Folded: 83.6 x 117.8 x 10.7mm Unfolded:163.8 x 117.8 x 5.0mm | | Weight | 254g | 219g | | Colors | Night Sky, Star White | Red, Rose gold, Silver, Grey | The iPhone Duo has two 48MP cameras — a main camera and wide-angle lens — but you don’t get a telephoto lens. This is annoying, as the tele lens is the one I use the most. That’s why it’s refreshing to see Xiaomi providing the lens on the 18 Fold; its foldable has a 200MP main camera, 50MP tele lens with 3x optical zoom, and a 50MP wide-angle lens. Just having a tele lens gives the device a huge advantage, and Xiaomi is the only brand doing so on a wide foldable. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Software Where the iPhone Duo has a sizable lead is the software; it’s clear that iOS 27 has plenty of custom features to maximize the real estate on the foldable. What’s great to see is that the toggles and the taskbar are oriented on the right, and while it’s a small thing, it makes a difference in usability. The main problem with the Xiaomi 18 Fold is that it is limited to China, so you have to use the Chinese iteration of the brand’s skin. There are issues with push notifications, aggressive memory management, and there’s no Play Store or Google services out of the box. If you're an enthusiast and have used Chinese software previously, you can wrangle the 18 Fold to work the way you want (I plan on doing that), but it is a hassle. Apple iPhone Duo vs. Xiaomi 18 Fold: Which should you buy? I’ll make this easy: if you like the look of a wide foldable, you should get the iPhone Duo. Although the Xiaomi 18 Fold has arguably better internals, the software is not ideal, and I wouldn’t recommend getting it as a result. Xiaomi needs to do a better job bringing its foldables to global regions, because the 18 Fold deserves a wide rollout. Of course, the iPhone Duo is costlier than any other iPhone, but not by too much than the latest Pro models. There's no doubt that the 18 Fold gives you a better overall value (as these things go), but with Xiaomi choosing not to launch the foldable globally, this is a moot point. Heavyweight The iPhone Duo is the default choice if you need a wide foldable. The Xiaomi 18 Fold has better internals, but the Duo arguably has the better software, and it is launching in over 75 countries. item.title: Google continues to fix Android 17 issues with a QPR2 Beta 5 release for Pixels
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.42
What you need to know - Google is rolling out Android 17 QPR2 Beta 5 to Pixel testers, solving several issues, such as an unexpected reboot problem. - The company is also fixing another Bluetooth problem; however, this one involves a bug when changing device type. - Beta 4 at the end of August marked QPR2 entering Platform Stability, meaning we're headed down the final stretch toward launch. Get your Pixels ready. Google is rolling out another beta for its next quarterly Android 17 update. The company detailed everything enrolled testers will find on Reddit. If you're looking for the update, you might find one of two build numbers. Google states users with a Pixel 6a, Pixel 7, 7 Pro, 7a, Pixel Fold, or Pixel Tablet will download vCP41.260828.005.A6. If you have any other eligible Pixel device, you will find vCP41.260828.004.A8. The company is fixing a few problems users have reported throughout QPR2's testing. One fix is coming in for a system instability issue. The patch notes state this fix should solve the "unexpected device reboots during continuous UI scrolling in media-heavy applications." Another fix aims to solve an issue with the Pixel's side buttons for volume control. Users noticed that while casting media, pressing these buttons wouldn't surface the volume slider UI. Google states a fix for this issue is rolling out. Additionally, enhanced HDR was stuck for several users on the Issue Tracker. Google says its fix should solve the issue of the feature "remaining enabled despite being turned off in user settings." The remainder of the patch notes is as follows: - Changing a Bluetooth device type in settings failed to update its icon visually - Fixed a text-rendering issue that caused unexpected background highlights to appear when typing in search fields, and resolved a navigation routing issue that prevented Private Space from unlocking correctly - Launching Google Wallet via the power button shortcut caused the touchscreen to become unresponsive - Camera crashes during panorama processing - Bluetooth audio experiences noise and distortion after completing or answering a call The Final Stretch Beta 5 is fixing up some lingering issues, but it was QPR2 Beta 4 that we were really excited about. The end of August saw Android 17 QPR2 enter the Platform Stability phase. This is a standard milestone for Google's software development. It locks in the OS' APIs, ushering it down the final stretch. We're starting to wrap things up, but there's still work to do—for everyone. Similarly, Google was fixing quite a few bugs last month. Pixel Bluetooth is apparently still giving it some trouble. In August, Google fixed a Bluetooth call audio issue that saw user calls getting erroneously put through the phone's speaker. Other issues included a broken gesture problem and strange UI freezing. item.title: A mysterious Google Wear OS fitness tracker just appeared at the FCC
item.description:

What you need to know - A mysterious Google-made wearable has appeared at the FCC with clues suggesting it could run Wear OS. - The device reportedly skips Wi-Fi and relies on Bluetooth LE, suggesting it may be a fitness tracker. - GPS support and a metal frame are also listed, while ADB testing suggests some form of Wear OS software. - The device could sit between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch, potentially filling the gap left by Fitbit Charge. A mysterious new Wear OS fitness tracker has been spotted at the FCC, and there are a few clues suggesting it could be an upcoming Google Pixel or Fitbit-branded device. Google has been enjoying success with both the Pixel Watch lineup and the recently launched Fitbit Air, and it looks like the company could be preparing to expand its fitness tracking lineup even further. As spotted by 9to5Google, a mysterious new Google-made device has now appeared in an FCC listing. The device, described as a "Wireless Device," carries the model number G8BL6 and is manufactured by Goertek, a company that has previously manufactured several generations of Pixel Buds. Interestingly, the FCC listing suggests there's no Wi-Fi connectivity onboard. Instead, the device appears to rely entirely on Bluetooth LE. There are also clues suggesting the device could run some form of Wear OS, as the EUT operation test setup specifically mentions ADB testing. In terms of other connectivity, the mysterious device reportedly supports GPS or GNSS and features a metal frame that will also act as its antenna. The lack of Wi-Fi is particularly interesting, since most traditional Wear OS smartwatches have supported Wi-Fi. That could suggest we're looking at a different type of wearable altogether, potentially a more traditional fitness tracker rather than another Pixel Watch. And there might already be another clue. During the Pixel 11 launch, Google briefly showed an unannounced fitness tracker with a small display in one of its teasers, and there's a chance this FCC listing could be related to that device. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If so, the new wearable could potentially sit somewhere between the Fitbit Air and Google's more expensive Pixel Watch lineup. It's also worth remembering that Fitbit hasn't updated its Charge lineup since 2023, so this device could fit quite nicely into that missing middle ground. item.title: Ultrahuman, HealthEx team up: your medical records step forward for 'always-on' insights
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.72
What you need to know - Ultrahuman and HealthEx partner to bring the HealthEx PowerPlug for $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr in the app. - HealthEx brings your official medical records into the app, and Ultrahuman's biomarkers/Ring data is placed alongside it for better insights into your wellbeing. - Ultrahuman states this PowerPlug will also generate a "Visit Pack" full of data that's listed with your records to make your next visit more insightful. Medical records are often a tricky obstacle to navigate. This week, Ultrahuman announced a partnership that streamlines appointments, tests, and even surgeries. This morning (Sept. 17), Ultrahuman announced a partnership with HealthEx in a press release, bringing the HealthEx PowerPlug to its app. The company states the PowerPlug will "combine a member’s medical records with continuous biomarkers" from its smart ring "in a secure, transparent, and consented manner." This will roll out over the week; however, Ultrahuman shared details on how this new PowerPlug will work. Ultrahuman members will need to verify their identity to activate HealthEx's capabilities. This will automatically locate your health records from places you've received care before. Ultrahuman states HealthEx has nationwide reach, thanks to the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA). Additionally, users can choose which care sites the HealthEx PowerPlug accesses. This is done via your consent, and you can stop sharing any records at any time. Priyanka Agarwal, M.D., MBA, co-founder and CEO of HealthEx, said, "When members choose to connect the two through HealthEx, they arrive at their next appointment with the most complete health picture, helping them arrive better prepared for that conversation." Getting down to brass tacks, the HealthEx PowerPlug aims to place your entire medical history in one convenient place for you and your doctor. Ultrahuman states this new feature "maps 532 conditions" based on your medications and procedures. Incorporating your biomarkers only enhances its usefulness. Your previous diagnosis and new medications will be displayed alongside the daily measurements your Ultrahuman Ring captures of your heart. Your resting heart rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, and deep sleep are all factored in. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android If a follow-up has been missed, or a condition/medication record hasn't been checked, the HealthEx PowerPlug will surface it for your attention. Users can bring this up as a question during their next doctor's visit. Additionally, Ultrahuman highlights its "Visit Pack." This is a collection of your medication information—a "doctor-ready summary"—tied to your wearable data. The company states, "The PowerPlug also flags questions and tests to raise with their doctor based on their reports." Take care I've had to deal with medical records, or medical information in general several times. This hasn't been for me, but for family. And it can be a headache at times. The long waits, the misinformation because someone got their wires crossed. I can appreciate what Ultrahuman is trying to do by bringing in HealthEx. Its smart ring already captures a wealth of data about your body. It kind of sounds like a no-brainer to put that side-by-side with your records Research states the average doctor's visit lasts ~15 minutes. What's more, the information about your health is typically scattered. This PowerPlug with HealthEx aims to make that process a little less strenuous. The HealthEx PowerPlug has started rolling out today (Sept. 17) for users in the U.S. Users can access this PowerPlug from the Ultrahuman PowerPlugs tab in the Ultrahuman app. However, it costs $4.99/mo or $45.99/yr. If you're interested in viewing your "longitudinal health history," Ultrahuman states this is free through HealthEx Wallet. Ultrahuman and HealthEx plan to do more following the PowerPlug's debut. Vitamin D, GLP-1, and Respiratory Health should arrive sometime in the future. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.39
What you need to know - Galaxy SmartTag 3 rumors continue, suggesting Samsung could redesign the little tracker into a squircle shape, like the Galaxy Watch 8 and 9. - The tracker is reportedly arriving in white and black; however, Samsung has removed the built-in loop, meaning consumers may have to shell out more cash for a case with a loop. - Recent rumors suggested the SmartTag 3 could debut with the Galaxy S26 FE, but that never happened as the phone showed up solo late last month. Samsung's next smart tracker has been long overdue—three years, to be exact. Rumors continue in September, suggesting a reworked design is in the cards. Alleged renderings obtained by SammyGuru claim Samsung has redesigned the Galaxy SmartTag 3 with a familiar shape (via 9to5Google). The publication mentions this, too: the SmartTag 3 might take on a squircle shape, similar to the Galaxy Watch 8 and 9 series. A thicker, colored outer portion encases a silver (metallic) center. Rumors add that the SmartTag 3 could arrive in white and black. The latter trades in a silvery metallic center for a black, almost brushed metal aesthetic. The post highlights a few expectations, such as (improved) Bluetooth and UWB (ultra-wideband), like its previous model. What's more, the "NFC-based Lost Mode" is also suspected to continue in this next generation. The tracker's battery specifications are still unknown, but here's hoping that the SmartTag 3's longevity hasn't taken a hit. There's no dodging the elephant in the room. While the SmartTag 3 appears to take on a squircle shape, the alleged renderings highlight that it's missing a built-in mounting solution. According to the publication, consumers might have to shell out extra cash for a "separate case with an attachment loop." As far as pricing is concerned, the publication cites alleged "retailer listings." The SmartTag 3 could stay ~$30 in the U.S.; however, consumers in Europe might see a slight price increase of a few bucks (or... euros). This change is certainly a choice We've been playing around and tracking with the Galaxy SmartTag 2 since 2023. What's interesting is that the tracker also reworked its design from the original tag. It brought in a wider attachment loop. Consumers could get a case for it that would provide another loop (more of a keyring-style). But rumors from July finally got us thinking about a SmartTag 3 after three years. A tipster on social media claimed the next tag could debut sometime in September, alongside the Galaxy S26 FE. That didn't end up happening. The S26 FE debuted late in August. So there's a chance we're looking at a solo launch for the SmartTag 3, or perhaps something closer to the Galaxy Tab S12 debut this year. item.title: Moto's teases Snapdragon for Signature 27, and it's giving nothing but Elite
item.description:

What you need to know - Motorola teased its upcoming Signature 27 successor to the original Signature that debuted at CES 2026. - The company states there will be surprises ahead at Snapdragon Summit, as it teases work with Qualcomm. - Qualcomm states we can expect to see "Dual 8 Elites" at Snapdragon Summit on September 22, and this is a chip that would mark a change from the O.G. Signature's midrange SoC. Motorola started teasing its upcoming Signature 27 on social media, and what it has to say is so interesting that we're not sure what to think. The company posted a short clip about the device on X this morning (Sept. 18), and it's got us thinking flagship in a big way. The video starts off saying, "Every material. Obsessed." We see the phone in what looks like a moss green before an artisan takes a knife to a long stretch of leather (or fabric). This is where things get interesting. Motorola confirms the name of the device—Signature 27—alongside a date: September 22, 2026. This is important. Motorola's post reads, "There’s more to discover with Motorola and Snapdragon." Qualcomm's annual Snapdragon Summit is set for September 22-24. If Motorola and Qualcomm have come together for something regarding Snapdragon, and at this event no less, perhaps we're looking at a true flagship chip for the Signature 27. Motorola's teaser was brief, but it's given us enough to think about. For context, the Motorola Signature launched at CES 2026 in January. It's a premium, "ultra-thin" phone from Moto with a 6.8-inch screen. The Signature stood out to us as one of Motorola's best flagships. However, the phone features one tiny little drawback: its chip is for midrange phones. The Signature features Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Gen 5. The chip, while good, offers flagship-level performance for affordable phones. It misses the robust strength you'd get from the Elite Gen 5. Motorola's current Signature 27 teasers have us excited—for two reasons, mind you. Going flagship Moto's original Signature surprised me when I saw it. That's the kind of phone that I expect from the company but it never actually delivered. Not in the way I wanted. The Edge was a nice phone; though the curved display could get tiring after a while. Snapdragon Summit is coming up, so we'll have all our answers then. Mid-August held Qualcomm's teasers for what we can expect from the Snapdragon Summit this year. The company said we can expect "Dual 8 Elites" this year. Rumors claim the company is working on an 8 Elite Gen 6 and a Gen 6 Pro. Qualcomm's summer teaser mentioned connectivity enhancements and "advanced camera functionality." Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android What's more, "immersive gaming experiences" were mentioned. The major upgrades Qualcomm has planned are headed to both its 8 Elites this year. Its teaser was brief, but it gave us enough to think about heading into September. Now that we're here, we've got Dual 8 Elites on the mind and Moto's Signature 27. A flagship chip could definitely solidify its premium ambitions for the Signature 27. The original was good and gave that premium/flagship feel we enjoy, but it could've been more. Hopefully, if what we're thinking is true, Motorola will reach for a flagship Elite from Qualcomm to put the cherry on top. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. item.title: Nothing's Headphone 1 is going Pro? Rumors allege upgrades and a 'premium' feel are possible
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.06
What you need to know - Rumors now say Nothing is getting closer to a new audio product launch dubbed the "Headphone 1 Pro" late in September. - The device could enter a more premium aesthetic for consumers with a $399 price tag, 60 hours battery life, improved ANC, and a triple audio driver setup. - The original Headphone 1 were pretty good, and could've arguably been one of the best (if not the best) audio product of 2025. Nothing's first over-ear headphones made a splash when they debuted. Now, rumors suggest the company wants to make even more noise with a "Pro" model. Late this week, a post by Dealabs suggests Nothing is developing a "Headphone 1 Pro" model, and a launch could be closer than we think (via 9to5Google). As with any device, especially one marked by "Pro," design changes/improvements are possible. The publication claims the Pro headphones could feature "aluminum and glass" on their body. The idea could be to not only separate the Pro from the base model, but also to solidify a "premium" aesthetic, as the post notes. White and black colorways are supposedly likely once this (allegedly) hits the market around September 29, 2026. However, rumors claim Nothing plans to make the Pro tag matter with a triple audio driver. Improved bass, sharper audio precision, and improved treble were mentioned. Whispers allege real-time "adaptive" ANC that could outshine the original's. Battery life is another highlight. The Pro model could offer 60 hours of playback time. What's not clear is whether this is with ANC active or not. The original model could run for 35 hours with ANC on and 80 hours with it off. If this higher number concerns the former, that could be a huge boon to consumers. There's nothing official, but rumors claim the Headphone 1 Pro could run consumers $399 in the U.S. The original model was good The idea of a Pro headphone from Nothing sounds intriguing. I'm not really a fan of wearing over-ear headphones out or away from my computer. I'm a gamer, so that's usually when I'll ever wear something like this. But there's a huge market for over-ear headphones. Music is probably the best thing for them. You can connect them to your phone, get a workout in, or hop on the bus or train and immerse yourself in sound. That's what I'd like from Nothing. If it's going Pro, go immersive, too. If you take a quick step back to when the Headphone 1 launched, Nothing stuck them with a $299 price tag in the U.S. The Pro model would ask for ~$100 more, if we're to believe these early rumors. Anyway, Nothing wanted to make a bold statement with these headphones. The device brought back real, physical buttons, rollers, and paddles that make the experience more manageable. There were pieces of aluminum that accented the Headphone 1. The Pro version could take that up a bit, and with more glass, too. In our experience, the Headphone 1 was a good piece of hardware. In fact, it was arguably one of the best audio products of 2025. Considering the positioning of the controls, the Headphone 1 made it easy to control our music. What's more, since these buttons are physical, we avoided those accidental song skips or pauses. item.title: The ASUS Googlebook looks like the anti-dongle laptop we asked for
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.86
What you need to know - Leaked images of the ASUS Googlebook show a distinctive dark gray chassis, slim display bezels, a giant trackpad. - We're also seeing a dedicated Google "G" key and a signature glowing, multicolored light bar on the lid. - The physical hardware looks practical, packing two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, a headphone jack, and a fingerprint sensor. Google’s first Googlebooks will be available for preorder on September 21, and a new set of ASUS images is giving us a much better look at what one of these new laptops will actually look like. The ASUS model has a familiar laptop shape, but it’s clear Google is trying to give the new category a visual identity of its own. Leaked images from The Mac Observer reveal that the new Chromebook features a dark gray body, a large touchpad, thin display bezels, a dedicated Google "G" key, and a multicolor light bar on the lid. There’s an ASUS logo at the bottom of that glowing strip and “Googlebook” branding on the palm rest. The hardware looks refreshingly practical too. Side views show at least two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, and a headphone jack, giving users plenty of options for peripherals without immediately having to reach for a dongle. There’s also a fingerprint sensor and a keyboard that appears to have a reasonable amount of key travel. From the leaked renders, it looks like ASUS is using active cooling on the inside with a fan and heat pipe visible. That implies this particular Googlebook could be aimed at heavier workloads than today’s average Chromebook, although the processor and other specs are unknown. Googlebook is Google’s new premium laptop class that blends Android tech with the familiar desktop feel and Gemini features like Magic Pointer, Create My Widget, Cast My Apps, and Quick Access. ASUS is one of five launch partners, alongside Acer, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. The big missing pieces are price, exact specs, shipping dates, and whether this ASUS model will be available on September 21. Those answers should be coming soon, as Googlebook moves from leaked hardware to something you can actually order. item.title: BMX's GaNsta 140W may just be the 4-port GaN travel charger you need
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.63
It was when I started running out of storage boxes that I realized I may have too many GaN chargers. I joke that if you casually throw a GaN charger in my home, you're bound to hit another one. Anyway, I have dozens of these things lying around, and having tested just about every major charger released in the last three years, I know what a good charger needs to offer. So when I got started with the BMX GaNsta 140W (as puns go, the name gets an 8/10), it was clear that the charger ticked a lot of the right boxes. It has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, foldable blade pins with EU, UK, and AU converters that make it easy to travel with, and 140W power over USB PD 3.1. Oh, and it gets an LCD panel that shows real-time charging details out of each port, which is a must-have in a GaN charger in 2026. The GaNsta costs $89 as of writing, which is $10 pricier than Anker's charger, and $30 more than the last-gen 160W UGREEN Nexode Pro, both of which also have LCD screens. The GaNsta is a little smaller than other 4-port chargers, but not enough that you'd notice the difference. Build quality is decent, and I didn't see any issues in the two months I used it. I tested the charger with my Find X9 Ultra, Pixel 11 Pro XL, iPhone 17 Pro, iPad Pro M4, and a dozen or so accessories — including 160W power banks — and it turned out to be reliable in day-to-day use. I like that each port's power output is clearly labeled, and it takes a lot of the guesswork out of figuring out which port to use. The USB-C1 and C2 ports individually go up to 140W over the USB PD 3.1 protocol, and I tested this using a standalone power meter (Power-Z KM003C). I also like that the area around the ports has a slotted design to prevent scratches; this is a thoughtful design choice that makes a difference. The LCD screen is the real star of the show. It shows real-time charging details, power going out of each port, and heat levels. The latter isn't quite as useful as you don't normally see thermal issues on a 140W charger, but it's there. And as AI needs to be shoehorned into every product these days, this thermal management feature is assisted by AI (however that works). Anyway, what you need to know is that even with all ports in use, the GaNsta doesn't have any issues with overheating. You also get emoticons on the panel, and you can easily cycle through the various menus via the button at the bottom. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android With four ports available, you get the ability to charge four devices at once. Of course, the total power budget is limited when all ports are in use, and with the GaNsta, you get 125W cumulatively: 65W + 45W + 7.5W + 7.5W. I would've liked to see 65W on both the C1 and C2 ports — like the latest Nexode Pro 160W charger — but that isn't the case. That said, if you're just going to leave four devices to charge overnight, the GaNsta 140W does a decent enough job. The inclusion of a USB-C to USB-C cable along with travel plugs is a good move, and the size of the charger means you can easily throw it into a travel bag. What I'm not too sure about is the pricing; it is costlier than its rivals, and if you're willing to shell out $89, the new Nexode Pro 160W is a better deal at $99 as it has a retractable cable. If you don't need the built-in cable and like the travel-related accessories, the GaNsta 140W is a good choice. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd. Looking at what Samsung did with the Galaxy Z Fold 7 (and 8), reducing the thickness of that phone, this rumor strikes a chord. What's more, the idea of a "more durable" TriFold likely concerns its hinge/display for longevity. Right now, these rumors suggest Samsung is sticking to its "original schedule" of releasing this "TriFold 2" in 2027. Additionally, rumors say Samsung might reveal a "slideable" phone, too. That's gaming PC money. That's money put toward something far more important. This is going to be interesting. It's interesting to hear this rumor. We all remember Huawei's Mate XT surprise. It beat Samsung to the world of tri-fold phones. It's even more interesting since Samsung effectively stopped selling the Galaxy Z TriFold after three months... Maybe this wasn't so surprising. Samsung always positioned the Galaxy Z TriFold as a "limited release." These rumors about a TriFold sequel mention something Samsung struggled with before: components. Developing the Galaxy Z TriFold was already incredibly strenuous due to high manufacturing and rising component costs. If Samsung is considering a TriFold 2, in the current climate, that might be difficult (on our wallets). Nevertheless, it remains to be seen how Samsung would treat a TriFold 2. Another limited release might seem strange, but we'll have to see. The Galaxy Z TriFold debuted with a huge, tablet-like 10-inch internal display and a 6.5-inch cover. item.title: Tiny Dutch startup enlists Samsung as backer as it seeks to dethrone Nvidia AI GPU — but Euclyd won't get its inference chip out till 2028
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 6.18
- Samsung has backed a tiny Dutch chipmaker targeting Nvidia - Euclyd raised $231 million before shipping its first commercial chip - Euclyd plans to sell complete AI systems directly to enterprises but will not deliver its first hardware until 2028 Samsung has joined a group of investors backing a small Netherlands-based chip designer aiming to challenge Nvidia's dominance in artificial intelligence hardware. The startup, called Euclyd, closed a funding round worth $231 million, drawing support from several firms beyond the South Korean electronics giant. According to Bernardo Kastrup, Chief Executive of Euclyd, commercial hardware from the company will not reach customers until 2028 A chip built to rival Nvidia's grip Euclyd's Series A round totalled €200 million and was co-led by Somerset Capital Partners, the Scaleup Europe Fund, and Innovation Industries, alongside Samsung. In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Kastrup said that the capital would support two separate lines of business going forward. One involves selling physical hardware and rack systems directly to enterprises wanting to run their own AI inference securely on-site. The other involves licensing the underlying intellectual property to firms that want to build their own chips using Euclyd's designs. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Founded in 2024, the company is developing a chip system built around a different architecture than conventional graphics processors, covering both the processor and memory layers. Nvidia's GPUs were originally built for video games but became central to AI training and inference and pushed the company to become the world's most valuable. That dominance now covers the market for the very highest performing chips available today, though rivals are emerging quickly. “AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery and national competitiveness, but its potential will remain constrained unless we fundamentally change the infrastructure beneath it,” Kastrup said. Why Samsung's involvement matters beyond cash Kastrup revealed that Samsung's contribution extends well past the money it committed to the round. "Samsung can help us in more ways than money. They are one of the biggest memory manufacturers in the world,” said Kastrup. “They do a lot of engineering, they know a lot about systems, they know the supply chain, they have a huge network." Although Euclyd expects to commence shipping its chips in two years, the company plans to serve thousands of enterprise customers by 2030. The company's systems remain unproven at any meaningful commercial scale so far, leaving real-world performance an open question. Several major technology firms are pursuing similar paths away from dependence on Nvidia's processors for AI workloads. OpenAI announced in August that its first in-house AI chip, named Jalapeño, delivered industry-leading speed and efficiency. Google, Amazon Web Services, and Meta are each developing their own chips for internal AI use as well. Whether a small Dutch startup with no shipped product can meaningfully dent Nvidia's position remains genuinely uncertain given the scale involved. item.title: New Android malware can deploy AI to automate device control — and it can even bring itself back from the dead
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.64
- Zimperium zLabs discovered RedHat, a Chinese‑origin Android banking trojan with AI assistant - AI interprets screen layouts in real‑time, enabling credential theft and bypassing app redesigns - Distributed via third‑party stores, social media, malvertising, and SMS; persistence blocks uninstall attempts There is an Android malware out there that comes with an AI assistant that tells it what to do. The assistant seems to be independent of the malware’s operator, allowing the tool to work without requiring the operators to be present in real-time. The malware in question is called RedHat. It was discovered by security researchers Zimperium zLabs, who believe it is of Chinese origin. It is currently being distributed via third-party app stores, social media, malvertising, and SMS spam, and requires Android’s Accessibility permissions to work. The malware itself is a typical banking trojan - it creates an invisible overlay every time the victim brings up a banking app, capturing login credentials and one-time passwords, and thus giving attackers direct control over people’s banking accounts. AI-powered eyes But what makes RedHat stand out from a sea of Android banking trojans is its AI-powered component. The model serves as a kind of remote “eyes and hands” for controlling the victim’s phone. Usually, when criminals develop banking trojans, they need to code exact coordinates of the layout for it to work. They need to code where the password is entered, or where the login button is. If the banking app gets redesigned and changes its layout, the malware breaks. With AI, that is no longer a problem. RedHat gets a picture of what’s on the screen, sends it to the AI assistant, which then instructs the malware on how to proceed. "RatHat uses AI to intelligently navigate and control the device interface in real-time, making its operations more adaptable and harder for security software to detect than traditional, scripted automation," Zimperium explained. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The tool also has a few advanced persistence mechanisms, being capable of reinstalling deleted components, and intercepting the uninstall process to cancel it while displaying a fake error message to the victim. So far, there is no word on who the targets are, or how many people might have been compromised. item.title: China’s UBTech opens world-first factory that builds a humanoid robot every ten minutes — 14,000 square meter plant will deliver army of 10,000 robots a year
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.50
- China's UBTech has revealed its new robot factory - The facility can produce 10,000 androids a year - It uses many autonomous robots in the production process Forget AI agents and ChatGPT, fully autonomous robots are the next high-tech frontier, with companies across the globe racing to perfect their android creations. And Chinese firm UBTech has taken a big step in that direction with its new smart factory that can produce 10,000 robots a year — and it might change manufacturing forever. The factory is the first of its kind in the world, according to the Seoul Economic Daily. It’s located in Liuzhou, in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region and is focused on producing UBTech’s Walker S and Cruzr robot series. And the factory itself makes heavy use of humanoid robots and driverless vehicles, perhaps providing a glimpse of the future of production and manufacturing. Cruzr Y1 and Cruzr S2 androids unload materials and stack, load and transport them, while collaborative robots take part in the final assembly process that finalizes each product. These final-stage robots work in tandem with human operators and include autonomous vehicles and rotating workbenches. In a separate development, UBTech says it has launched “the industry’s first fully automated three-dimensional warehouse,” according to the Seoul Economic Daily. This can store 112 robots in 65 square meters of space, supposedly utilizing 50% more space than a facility with similar floor space. Expanding capacity UBTech said it has been able to create its robot factory thanks to the strong supply chain that exists in China. According to UBTech vice president Fang Jianxin, “This foundation is rooted in the many engineers, scientists and application scenarios China has accumulated over the past 10 to 20 years, which has formed a very strong supply chain base, manufacturing capability and research and development capacity.” China has been ramping up its robot production in recent years, with the National Bureau of Statistics of China noting that output hit 98,677 units in July, an increase of 30.2% on the previous year. And 635,056 robots were created between January 2026 and July 2026, an uptick of 28.5% year on year. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Agibot today claimed its A3 Ultra robot is "moving from mass production into real-world deployment", posting a video on X showing it working in "hotels, auto dealerships, supermarkets and metro inspection scenarios, with more deployments underway". And with UBTech’s factory paving the way in terms of robot creation, it might not be long before autonomous factories start expanding across the world. item.title: Seagate finds 'AI is increasing the value of data' but warns that 43% of businesses lack proper data storage infrastructure — 99% expect AI storage (and storage costs) to explode
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.36
- Seagate study finds 99% of firms expect AI to increase their storage requirements within three years - Only 38% of organizations consider themselves fully prepared for future demands - Storage infrastructure ranks among the biggest obstacles facing AI deployment New data from Seagate has claimed AI is increasing the business importance of stored information while exposing weaknesses in infrastructure readiness. The company's research found 99% of respondents expect AI workloads to increase their storage requirements in the next three years. Yet only 38% describe their organizations as completely prepared, while 43% identify storage infrastructure among the leading obstacles to wider AI deployment. AI is raising the stakes for storage planning The survey gathered responses from more than 2,700 technology decision-makers and found that 86% reported moderate or significant returns from AI investments. Among those respondents, 33% said their organizations were already seeing substantial measurable financial or operational benefits from AI initiatives. Those returns increase the importance of retaining information that can support future models, applications and decisions across changing business requirements. Nearly 7 in 10 respondents expect storage requirements to increase by at least 26%, including 32% anticipating growth exceeding 50%. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Furthermore, 98% of respondents regard storage as strategic infrastructure rather than simply an administrative technology function. The survey nevertheless shows that preparedness remains incomplete, with data quality and readiness identified by 53% as another major deployment difficulty. Storage therefore ranks ahead of compute availability, cited by 27%, and energy constraints, which were identified by 24% of respondents. The figures indicate that adding computing capacity alone does not resolve the infrastructure limitations organizations encounter when deploying increasingly data-intensive AI systems. Sustainability is becoming part of the storage equation Infrastructure expansion is also encountering sustainability concerns, with 77% of respondents reporting delays or changes to planned growth. Within that figure, 36% said investments had undergone major changes, while another 41% experienced smaller postponements linked to sustainability considerations. Power consumption was the most frequently considered environmental factor for storage hardware, cited by 62% of respondents. Equipment lifespan followed at 55%, while respondents broadly connected longer hardware service periods with improved sustainability across data center operations. Current confidence remains below future expectations, with 39% describing their storage operations as highly sustainable under present conditions, according to survey responses. That proportion rises to 61% when respondents assess where their organizations expect storage sustainability to stand five years from now. Funding levels also influence those expectations, with 70% of organizations holding sustainability budgets above $100 million expecting highly sustainable operations within five years. By comparison, 48% of organizations with annual sustainability budgets below $1 million anticipate reaching that same level during the period. Training material, active datasets, model checkpoints and retained outputs can impose substantially different infrastructure requirements throughout an AI system’s lifecycle. For organizations expanding AI operations, those differences make storage architecture, equipment lifespan, energy consumption and capacity planning increasingly interconnected decisions. The survey does not establish that every organization will face identical costs, although its findings indicate that storage growth is widely anticipated. item.title: 'Bringing the game to console for the first time' means that ArenaNet 'can reach a much wider group of players' as devs say they want to offer an 'invitation' for everybody to play Guild Wars 3 together by bringing it to PS5 and PC — but not Xbox
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.16
- Guild Wars 3 is the first game in the series to launch on both PC and console - Studio head Colin Johanson says it will allow the game to "reach a much wider group of players" on PS5 and PC - ArenaNet wants new players to take their first plunge into Guild Wars with the upcoming game Guild Wars 3 will be the first game in the MMORPG franchise to launch on both console and PC, and ArenaNet thinks it will encourage newcomers to take their first steps into the Guild Wars series. "With us bringing the game to console for the first time, [and] with us launching on Steam from day one on our own platform, we can reach a much wider group of players," said studio head Colin Johanson during a guided presentation TechRadar Gaming attended at Gamescom. Speaking about the game's setting, which takes place 1000 years before the first Guild Wars game in the ancient land of Orr, Johanson explained that the game will appeal to hardcore fans who have been eager to learn more about the lore for years. Exploring this highly anticipated era means ArenaNet could welcome new players with no Guild Wars experience, since the game is essentially a prequel and newcomers won't be required to play the first two games to understand what's going on. "Everyone's going to learn it all together, and if you're a big Guild Wars fan, you'll know what some of the species are and some of the characters or some of the locations," the studio head said. "But for the most part, everybody is on equal footing." The direction also means the studio could draw more players by launching the game on both PC and PlayStation 5; it's unclear right now whether the game could eventually get an Xbox release as well. "We really wanted to have an invitation for everybody to come play Guild Wars 3 together and feel like this could be their first Guild Wars game that they haven't played before," Johanson added. item.title: Will Samsung and Qualcomm’s organic bridge technology make AI processors more powerful and cheaper to produce?
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.12
- A collaboration between Samsung and Qualcomm aims to harness 'organic bridge' technology to reduce costs for AI CPUs - The process is being developed for 2.1D packaging, a lower-cost integration than 2.5D , where silicon, glass, or ceramic materials are used - Resins and composites are among the organic materials typically used in semiconductor integration Samsung and Qualcomm have collaborated on a new type of CPU that takes advantage of organic materials for integration between layers, rather than silicon or its alternatives. Described as an “organic bridge,” the technology is intended for AI semiconductors. The development of what has been named 2.1D packaging is aimed at reducing costs in AI chip fabrication, where 2.5D packaging is typically used. 2.5D chips rely on silicon, glass, or ceramic for connectivity between layers of microcircuits. With 2.1D, however, the use of organic material improves bandwidth. The organic bridge The key element of the 2.1D packaging is the organic bridge. It’s a technology adopted (and shrunk down) from PCB manufacture, and can reduce reduce production costs while boosting assembly. In short, it is a mass producer’s dream. Rather than the silicon (or an inorganic alternative), the organic bridge is a layer cut from resin or polymer. Its purpose is to connect multiple microcircuit dies, while providing insulation, as with silicon. However, the organic bridge has been proved to be more efficient, and can be produced more easily at scale. In addition, the organic bridge solves the supply chain issues surrounding silicon. Development of the technology for die fabrication appears to have commenced around October 2024, when a patent for “interconnected bridge” technology was filed. With the drive towards increased AI data centers in full swing, the 2.1D processor packaging could prove pivotal in delivering the predicted benefits of artificial intelligence. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Multiple partners Qualcomm isn’t the only partner Samsung is working with on organic bridge technology. Various other companies have also expressed an interest in developing chips with 2.1D packaging. The significance of the drive to build 2.1D packaging for AI chips has not gone unnoticed by other companies in the tech industry. Korean magazine TheElec suggests that other Samsung customers are interested in working with the giant’s Samsung Electro-Mechanics subsidiary to develop 2.1D. If true, this would suggest that 2.1D is being widely considered as one solution to the the cost and energy demands of AI processing. Samsung isn’t the only chip maker working on 2.1D packaging. Intel Foundry Services has its own process in development, as does TSMC, which has expanded into 2.1D packaging after dominating the 2.5D market. It seems that work between Samsung and Qualcomm has been ongoing for the past year, which indicates that it might be some time before any production-ready AI chips with 2.1D packaging are available. item.title: 10 boats in one van: Russia goes DIY with a plywood vessel that can be built in 4 hours and can carry 4 fiber-optic UAVs
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.12
- Russia's Scientific and Production Center Ushkuynik says ten disassembled Skorlupa hulls fit in one GAZelle van - Each hull can be assembled in an estimated four hours (by Russian estimates) using a cordless screwdriver and can travel up to 200 km while carrying up to 250 kg of payloads - The Skorlupa comes with up to four communication modules and can carry up to four fiber-optic drones, allowing it to serve as both a mothership for attack or recon drones and a one-way attack craft Russia's Scientific and Production Center Ushkuynik has released new details on Skorlupa, a light uncrewed surface vessel whose headline feature isn't speed, stealth, or sensors. According to www1.ru, company CEO Alexey Chadayev says ten of the boats fit into the cargo bed of a single GAZelle light van when broken down, and that one hull goes together in about four hours with an ordinary screwdriver. The hull is cut from water-repellent plywood, and Chadayev told the Russian government daily Rossiyskaya Gazeta, in an interview published on September 8 (RU) around the International Technological Congress 2026, that the craft can be produced at any furniture factory and costs roughly a fifth of a conventional naval drone. A low-cost alternative in an increasingly asymmetrical war? As the Russia-Ukraine conflict enters its fifth year, both sides have innovated, focusing on drones and autonomous vehicles to save lives, operate remotely, and minimize costs. The Skorlupa does just that: the developer cites a 200 km range and a 250 kg payload, letting operators use it remotely while cutting costs as Russia and Ukraine struggle to fund their war efforts. It can also be used in two ways: as a one-way strike platform, delivering an explosive against a ship's hull; or as a mothership, carrying four fiber-optic aerial drones housed under a deck skin that folds open on command. As the war drags on, it's increasingly becoming one that demands practical and cost-effective solutions that do not endanger lives, with Ukraine also often pulling off similar approaches, including retrofitting remote-controlled kits to Humvees and Operation Spiderweb, which ingeniously launched attacks from within Russia's borders on its airfields, dealing damage that amounted to billions of dollars. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Skorlupa does something similar that makes it immune to jamming: it is controlled by a physical fiber-optic cable that lets it function even in areas where it would otherwise be cut off from wireless communications. This is also why the KVN has become one of Russia's most-used FPV drones. A non-emitting boat carrying non-emitting drones is effectively unjammable and hard to counter, and with millions of Russia's KVN drones already in play, it would be a well-supplied Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) to build up a naval and aerial threat in a region where Ukraine regularly takes the initiative on the former. As Alexey Chadayev pointed out in his interview, "With a Skorlupa like this, you can wreck any seaport without missiles," while noting that it can be made at any furniture factory.
