item.title: Safari Keeps Getting Better. Try These 21 Hidden Tricks Now That iOS 27 Is Here
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.77
You might take Safari for granted as Apple's default web browser on the Mac, iPhone, and iPad, but have you actually checked out all of its features and settings? Standard options like Private browsing, Reader view, and file downloads are part of the package, but there are many more things you can do. Upgrading to iOS 27 or iPadOS 27 kicks in a few more features, including automatic tab groups, custom extensions, and live page tracking. Be aware, though, that several of the new tricks in Safari use Apple Intelligence, which requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, or an iPad Pro (M1 or later), iPad Air (M1 or later), or iPad mini (A17 Pro) or newer. Here's what you can do. 1. Navigate the Tab Bar Beyond entering a URL, you can use Safari's address bar, also known as the Tab bar, to easily access all your tabbed web pages. This works whether the bar is at the top or bottom of the screen. To navigate your open tabs, simply swipe left and right on the Tab bar to cycle through them. 2. Customize the Tab Bar You can pick three layouts for the Tab bar—Top, Bottom, and Compact. To set a preference, head to Settings > Apps > Safari, then choose your preferred option under the Tabs section. 3. Sort Open Tabs You’re able to view and sort all your open tabs. Tap the Tabs icon on the Tab bar, then the ellipsis icon in the upper left. Select Arrange Tabs By and sort them by title or website. iPad users will need to open tabs from the Sidebar icon. 4. Organize Tabs into Groups Ever feel like you’re juggling too many tabs? One solution is to organize them into groups. On an iPhone, tap the Tabs icon on the Tab Bar, select the ellipsis icon, and then tap Manage Tab Group. From there, select New Empty Tab Group to create a new group and populate it with pages, or select New Tab Group with X Tabs to create a group from all the existing tabs. Name the new group and tap Save. The group will now be selectable from the Tabs screen. On an iPad, tap the Sidebar icon and then select the Tabs icon. Tap the icon at the top right of the sidebar (the one with two pages and a plus sign). Select New Empty Tab Group to create a new group or New Tab Group from X Tabs to create a group out of all existing tabs, then name it. You can also press down directly on a thumbnail and tap Move to Tab Group to create a new group or move it to an existing group. An even easier method is to long-press the Tabs icon and tap Move to Tab Group to access the tab group options. With iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, Safari can automatically organize your open tabs. To try this in Safari, tap the Tabs button, then choose the three-lined menu icon in the upper left, and then select Organize Tabs > Automatically Create Topic. Related tabs are then sorted into a new group that the AI automatically creates and names. To view any of the tabbed pages at any time, go to Tab view, tap the thumbnail of the tab group, and then tap the page you want to open. 5. Pin a Tab Pinning a tab lets you save a page on the Tabs screen, making it easier to open again. To pin a tab, tap the Tabs icon. Press down on the page you want to pin, then select Pin Tab from the menu. The next time you want to access that page, tap the Tabs icon and then tap the pinned tab to open it. 6. Auto Close Open Tabs The pages you open in Safari have a way of growing until the browser gets cluttered with dozens of open tabs. To prevent this, set a certain amount of time before tabs are automatically closed. Go to Settings > Apps > Safari > Close Tabs and set tabs to close manually, after one day, one week, or one month. 7. Customize the Start Page The Start page is what you see when Safari first opens, but it can be customized by adding, removing, or moving certain sections and choosing a background image. Swipe to the bottom of the Start page and click the Edit button. Disable any sections you don’t want to see or drag and drop sections to rearrange them on the page. Under the Background Image section, select a background or upload your own, then tap the X button to see your new Start page. 8. Turn a Web Page into a Web App Instead of always firing up Safari to access your favorite web pages, you can turn them into Web apps, accessible as regular apps from your Home screen. To set this up, open the page you want to turn into a Web app, tap the Share icon, and select Add to Home Screen. Name the app, make sure Open as Web App is enabled, and tap Add. You can then open the page as an app by tapping its Home screen icon. 9. Create Your Own Extensions Safari has supported extensions on mobile for several years now. To install some, go to Settings Apps > Safari > Extensions > More Extensions, and then choose the ones you want. You'd open the Extensions setting screen to enable and disable installed extensions or enable Share Across Devices to sync them across multiple Apple devices. To remove an extension, press down on its icon on the Home screen and tap Remove App. With iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, you can now create your own custom extensions using Apple's AI systems. To do this, open a web page in Safari that you might want to use as an example for the extension. Tap the three-lined menu icon to the left of the address bar and select Describe Extension. At the next screen, you can pick the option that best describes your desired extension. You can also tap the field at the bottom to describe the extension yourself. If you choose one of the options, a list of possible descriptions appears. Choose the one you want or describe something else. Tap Create to submit the description and then wait for it to be generated. When it’s ready, tap the Try button at the top and then tap the checkmark to launch it. To turn it off, tap the three-lined menu icon, swipe down the list of items, and tap the name of the extension. To launch the extension in the future on any other page, return to the menu and tap its name. To modify the extension, open the menu and select Manage Extensions. Select it and describe a change you wish to make. You can also allow the extension in Private Browsing windows, set its permissions, or delete it. 10. Browse Privately Don’t want Safari to keep track of the sites you visit or the AutoFill information you enter? Private Browsing mode will keep this information hidden (though you won’t be completely anonymous). With iOS 17 and iPadOS 17 or later, the feature automatically locks when you’re not using it to protect any open tabs from other people who have access to the device. You can then unlock Safari with Face ID, Touch ID, or a passcode. To enter Privacy Browsing mode on an iPhone, tap the Tabs icon and then tap Private. On an iPad, open the Sidebar and select Private; any page you launch now opens in Private mode. Exit Private mode by returning to the Tabs screen and selecting the previous tabs or page. 11. Check a Privacy Report If you’re concerned about online privacy, Safari blocks the cross-site trackers that monitor your web-based activities. You can also see which sites and trackers have been blocked from Apple's Privacy Report. Tap the Tool icon to the left of the address bar (the one with the square and two horizontal lines), select the ellipsis icon at the bottom, and then tap Privacy Report. The Websites tab shows which sites contacted trackers, while the Trackers tab shows which trackers were blocked. 12. Hide Distracting Elements Ever get distracted by intrusive pop-up ads and other annoying elements on a web page? With iOS 18 and iPadOS 18 or higher, you can hide these distractions. Tap the Tool icon at the left of the address bar and choose Hide Distracting Items. Select the items you wish to hide, then tap Hide to make them vanish. Tap Done at the top to browse the page without seeing those annoying elements. Tap the Tool icon again and select Show Hidden Items to restore them. 13. Translate Websites Safari is able to translate websites displayed in a foreign language. The feature supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Russian, Korean, Portuguese, Brazilian Portuguese, Arabic, and Simplified Chinese. When you open a website in one of these languages, tap the Tools icon and select Translate to [your language] on an iPhone. If it's an iPad, tap the ellipsis icon at the right of the address bar and select Translator in the menu. The site will then be translated. 14. Listen to a Web Page Read Aloud Safari has a built-in text-to-speech feature. Tap the Tools icon and select Listen to Page to have the browser read a web page aloud. To stop the reading, tap the Tools icon again and select End Listening. Siri can also read the text if you say “Siri, read this” and stop when you say “Siri, stop reading.” 15. View Highlights of a Web Page With the Highlights feature introduced in iOS 18, you can view AI-generated summaries, previews, and suggestions for supported web pages. To set this up, head to Settings > Apps > Safari and turn on Highlights. In Safari, select the Tool icon, and turn on Highlights. Now, when you open a supported web page, a small sparkle appears over the Tool icon in the address bar. When this appears, tap the Tool icon to see key information on the page. 16. View Compromised or Reused Passwords If you use Apple’s Password app to sync your passwords across devices, Safari can issue a warning when it detects compromised or reused credentials. To set this up, go to Settings > Apps > Passwords > Security Recommendations and enable Detect Compromised Passwords. At the bottom of the screen, tap Open Passwords. In the Passwords app, tap Security to see a list of compromised passwords, then choose one to view the recommendation. 17. Edit Suggested Website Passwords The Passwords app also offers an option that suggests a strong password for you to use when you create a new account on a website. Just tap the password field, and a potential password appears. You can then edit the suggested password as you see fit. Tap Other Options below the Use Strong Password button, then choose Edit Strong Password to change it. 18. Read a Web Page Offline No time to read now? You can save a web page or article to read offline. At the page you want to save, tap the Share icon, and then tap Add to Reading List. To access pages in your reading list, tap Bookmarks, select the Eyeglasses icon, and choose the page you want to read. By default, the page disappears from the list after it's been read. To see all pages, including ones that have already been read, tap Show All at the bottom of the menu. 19. Use Reader Mode Reader Mode, as its name indicates, makes a web page easier to read by stripping out distracting elements like ads and excessive formatting. Tap the Tools icon and choose Show Reader on an iPhone or tap the ellipsis icon and choose Reader on an iPad. Tap the icon again to change the text size or hide the Reader. Tap the Reader icon in the address bar to change the color and font, or to exit Reader mode. 20. Get Notified of Website Changes Safari can notify you when a website changes. To do this, navigate to the website, tap the menu icon to the left of the address bar, and select Notify Me. Type the change for which you’d like to be notified. For example, if you’re looking at a product page on a retail site, you might want to be informed if the price drops. By default, you're notified each day at a specific time, but you can tap Edit to change this. Select the checkmark to allow Safari to send you notifications. 21. Manage Your Privacy Settings Looking to further control your privacy? Apple gives you plenty of options in Safari. Head to Settings > Apps > Safari and turn on Prevent Cross-Site Tracking, Require Face ID to Unlock Private Browsing, and Fraudulent Website Warning. You should also tap Hide IP Address and set it to From Trackers. Go to Advanced > Advanced Tracking and Fingerprinting Protection and set it to Private Browsing or All Browsing. You can also try turning on Block All Cookies, but be warned that you’ll likely bump into problems with many websites. If you don't want websites to enquire whether Apple Pay is enabled on your device, leave Check for Apple Pay disabled. About Our Expert I've been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. Beyond PCMag, I've written news stories and tutorials for a variety of other websites and publications, including CNET, ZDNet, TechRepublic, Macworld, PC World, Time, US News & World Report, and AARP Magazine. I spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site’s East Coast reporters. I've also written two books for Wiley & Sons—Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. I've used Windows, Office, and other Microsoft products for years so I'm well versed in that world. I also know the Mac quite well. I'm always working with iOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and Android on my various mobile devices. And these days, I write a lot about AI, so that's become another key area for me. My wife always jokes about all the tech products we have around the house, but I manage to put them to good use for my articles. I like Lenovo computers, so I own a couple of Lenovo desktops and several laptops. I have three MacBooks and a Mac mini. For my mobile life and work, I use an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. But since I write about Android, I own several Android phones and tablets. Like any tech person, I have a cabinet full of cables, wires, and assorted mysterious gadgets. And when it's time to take a break from writing, I have an old Xbox 360 and Nintendo Wii, both of which I use for exercise and fitness games.

item.title: iTorrents.org Compromised To Spread Windows Malware, Kaspersky Says
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.65
A hacker appears to have hijacked iTorrents.org, a public repository for torrents, to spread a new Windows-based malware, according to the antivirus provider Kaspersky. Kaspersky flagged the issue on Thursday after discovering the malware infecting “several hundred victims, including both individual users and organizations” in countries such as Russia, Japan, Spain, the Netherlands and Colombia. Kaspersky’s investigation discovered the malware was circulating through disguised popular and pirated movies, including Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, which has only been released in theaters. The company’s report added, “our initial analysis revealed a common factor among the victims: all had used torrent trackers,” which can be used to download pirated films and TV shows. Kaspersky’s researchers then spotted user reports connected to the issue. This included one on Reddit about torrents on the site 1337x —which is frequently used for online piracy— delivering an executable file, rather than a media file. However, Kaspersky took a closer look and says the malicious torrents have actually been coming from iTorrents.org, a free service that caches torrent files and can be used as a backup for piracy providers. “As a result, torrent trackers that relied on this repository began inadvertently distributing malicious torrent files to their users. This approach is particularly powerful because the threat actors can reach users of multiple trackers without compromising each platform individually,” the antivirus provider’s report says. Kaspersky even warns that iTorrent.org “remains compromised.” “When a user attempts to download a torrent using a magnet link, the legitimate torrent archive instead returns a different torrent file. This malicious torrent leads to the download of the malware loader. It is used to deploy a framework that we dubbed MovieReaper.” After Kaspersky published its report, we visited iTorrents.org in an attempt to replicate the issue. At first, the site redirected us itorrents.net, which appeared to be safe. But when we visited iTorrents.org again, it immediately triggered our browser to download "AAC402C085D3DCB8B9348FDEC001CD8ECBFDCC862.exe.torrent" for a mysterious .exe file 865MB in size. Microsoft's Windows Defender later flagged the executable file as a severe malware threat, specifically "Trojan;Win32/Sonbokli.A!cl" iTorrents.org doesn’t have any contact information, so it’s unclear if the service is trying to rectify the issue. Attempts to visit itorrents.net have also started to trigger the same malicious download. In the meantime, Kaspersky says the malicious torrents will download a .exe file with a long file name, likely to hide the executable nature of the payload. The resulting MovieReaper malware communicates back to the hackers by tapping the Solana blockchain, and contains 21 different functions, including the ability “to download, upload, read files on the system,” and manipulate and exfiltrate files. Kaspersky’s investigation also found the malware infected organizations spanning “a wide range of sectors, including enterprise, government, IT, consulting, retail, transportation, and agriculture.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: HubSpot Smart CRM Review: Comprehensive Contact Management for Bigger Businesses
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.53
HubSpot is one of the biggest names in CRM providers for large-scale companies, but it also offers the simpler, SMB-focused Smart CRM tool. The service, which you can now purchase independently of the company's other products, benefits from an excellent automation builder and several AI tools that streamline contact management. Moreover, the seemingly endless number of available add-ons makes Smart CRM easy to integrate into your existing business operations. However, the base plan is expensive, and some areas of the user experience could be more intuitive. HubSpot is worth considering for bigger businesses, but the extremely flexible Apptivo, the cost-effective Bigin by Zoho, and the exceptionally user-friendly Freshsales remain our Editors' Choice winners. HubSpot Smart CRM offers two plans: Professional and Enterprise. A free trial isn't available for either. Keep in mind that although you can pay monthly, that still locks you into an annual contract, with no option to cancel early. As such, you should subscribe only if you’re confident that you will use it for at least a year. HubSpot's free Marketing Hub plan lets you create contact lists and use their information to personalize marketing campaigns, but it only includes one deal pipeline, so it's not a viable long-term CRM solution. The Professional tier ($45 per user per month, billed annually) includes the full-featured AI agent hub, intent signals to enrich high-value customers, and contact enrichment to improve contact profiles. You can create 1,000 custom properties to connect specific data points to companies, contacts, or deals, with up to 40 calculated properties that roll up data from other fields to calculate things like commissions. Team management tools include the Breeze Assistant, 15 deal pipelines, up to 100 shared inboxes, and up to 75 reporting dashboards with the option to create up to 100 custom reports. Advanced AI agents and collaboration tools, such as a shared inbox, are also available, along with integrations with Slack and Salesforce. Enterprise ($75 per user per month, billed annually) adds AI insights on CRM index pages (in beta) and more advanced user management tools, such as multi-level team creation. Custom objects let you track virtually any passive data point in the CRM, while custom events let you track actions unique to your business. You also get a sandbox account for experimenting with aspects of the user experience. The calculated properties limit increases to 200; deal pipelines go up to 100; shared inboxes increase to 200; and the reporting dashboard limit increases to 100 dashboards with 500 custom reports. Both plans include access to an AI data agent for analyzing CRM data, a customer AI agent for answering customer questions, and a prospecting agent that builds personalized outreach for specific leads. However, each of these tools requires HubSpot AI credits. You get monthly allotments of AI credits with both plans (3,000 for Professional and 5,000 for Enterprise). If your company exceeds those allotments, you can buy more at a rate of $10 per 1,000 credits. HubSpot Smart CRM’s Professional tier is pricey for an entry-level plan on paper. Apptivo's and Zoho CRM's equivalents, respectively, cost $15 and $14 per user per month, billed annually. Even Insightly, one of the more expensive CRMs I’ve tested, maintains a base plan for $29 per user per month. However, the Professional plan's AI and automation features put it on par with—and in some cases, ahead of—similarly priced, high-end plans from other companies. Large businesses will likely find value in the sheer number of features you get with the Enterprise plan, but smaller companies should likely turn to more affordable plans from Apptivo, Bigin by Zoho CRM, and Freshsales. To sign up for Smart CRM, you need to create a HubSpot account using your name, email, and business name. HubSpot’s AI will ask you some basic questions to set up the core customer platform, with the option for you to configure things yourself. You can then request the upgrade to the Smart CRM product. Next, HubSpot’s AI will ask you additional questions and generate a custom CRM center based on your answers. This process is slightly more involved than signing up for other CRMs I’ve tested, but it's still largely straightforward. To add users, you can enter email addresses one at a time or via a CSV file. You can also set up permissions; a wide range of prebuilt options are available, such as sales reps and sales managers. You can create custom permissions presets in the settings area, too. HubSpot lets you import contacts from both CSV and Excel files. It won’t import contacts unless the spreadsheet contains specific fields, however, so your file must have separate columns for first and last names, for example. Otherwise, the requirements are pretty typical. Once you upload contacts, HubSpot maps them automatically to existing categories. The process is similar to what I’ve come to expect from top-ranking CRMs, such as Apptivo and Freshsales. The platform also supports advanced import options, meaning you can pull all of your existing CRM data—including deals and tasks—using a similarly automated mapping process. This can save you a significant amount of time if you’ve collected extensive and varied data. Of all the CRMs I’ve tested, only Pipedrive offers something similar, and its advanced import process isn’t as simple. Alternatively, you can sync data from dozens of other apps in the HubSpot Marketplace, such as MailChimp, Shopify, or Zoho CRM. Both one-way and two-way sync options are available. You can also hire a HubSpot CRM Data Migration Specialist for $500 to assist you. This process can take up to three weeks, but it might be worth it if you are bringing over a lot of data. The last setup step includes attaching an email address. This is a two-click process for Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 email addresses. You have to enter POP/SMTP settings if you use a different email provider. Adding a business VoIP system or any social media accounts is optional. The internal HubSpot Home page uses a simple black-and-white color scheme, with easy-to-read boxes displaying information about upcoming meetings and tasks. Navigating the site is simple, thanks to easily identifiable icons for key areas, such as contacts and reporting, in the left-hand toolbar. The “...” at the bottom of the toolbar lets you access other areas, such as the HubSpot Inbox. You can pin the tools you use most often to the main menu, as well as get rid of others you don't need. HubSpot displays quick digital tours and tutorial videos when you first log in to your account; you can skip them if you already have experience with CRMs. After that, you can get support 24/7 via email, live chat (with both an AI bot and human support options), or phone for both plans. Alternatively, you can consult HubSpot’s extensive knowledge base. Many CRMs, including Apptivo and Freshsales, limit some or all support channels to 24/5 access, making HubSpot noteworthy. Unlike Insightly CRM, HubSpot doesn’t separate leads and contacts. Instead, every contact receives a deal-stage indicator (such as New, Open, or Unqualified). By default, Smart CRM displays a table with all the key information about your contacts, including a column for recent updates that HubSpot's AI pulls from contact records. You can also add a Kanban view to understand the health of your pipeline and a calendar view to see your upcoming events at a glance. Contact profiles use a standard layout, with basic contact information on the right and a central area with more detailed records, including AI insights based on the contact’s interaction history. A collapsible sidebar displays companies, deals, and (if you’re also using HubSpot’s help desk system) tickets connected to the contact. Within a contact profile, you can modify contact records, move contacts through the pipeline, add a new deal or task, and send an email or make a call (if you have set up VoIP). Before you get into deals, it’s best to square away your pipelines. I found this the most confusing part of the Smart CRM experience, since there’s no individual tab for pipelines within the main area or the settings. I ended up asking the AI support bot for help, which directed me to the pipeline editor in Settings > Objects > Deals. Thankfully, the pipeline editor is highly intuitive, with options to edit the default pipeline or create a custom one. Deals, meanwhile, are simple to navigate even if you’ve never used a CRM before. This section uses a Kanban view by default, which means you can easily move deals forward in the pipeline just by dragging them. You can add calendar, report, or table views to see pipelines in different ways. Apptivo offers similar options. Both the card- and table-based views let you modify data directly and save whatever lists or views you need most often. That’s convenient for deals across multiple pipelines, deal packages, and long deals. And, as with contacts or companies, you can filter particularly long lists and create new data filters as you go. Breeze is what puts the “Smart” in HubSpot Smart CRM. It uses both in-house large language models and those from OpenAI to conduct company research, perform mundane tasks, trigger workflows, unify and enrich your data, and write blog posts, among many other functions. HubSpot divides functionality into two parts: Breeze Assistant and Agents. Breeze Assistant is available on both CRM plans. You can either select a prompt (such as “generate a report” or “summarize deal”) or type a custom request. Over time, Breeze Assistant learns about your company’s CRM needs. Additionally, it can perform data and contact enrichment, gathering information from your communications and the wider web to add key attributes, such as location and social media links, to contact profiles. I tested Breeze Assistant by asking various questions about my contacts, outside companies, and the platform itself. I found it helpful for researching potential and existing clients. The minimal information on my sample contacts somewhat limited my ability to test this feature, but Breeze Assistant still impressed me with excellent suggestions for nurturing leads. You can even ask Breeze Assistant to generate graphics and images for blog posts and collateral. However, since it relies on OpenAI's DALL-E, expect some of its infamous hallmarks to appear, like garbled text and people with more than five fingers. Compared with Zoho CRM’s Zia AI, I found the Breeze Assistant easier to talk with and more capable of understanding nuance. Of course, like any AI-powered assistant, you get back what you put into it. Note that some tasks are free, while others require varying amounts of AI credits; be sure to read up on AI credit usage for each task before using Breeze Assistant. Breeze Agents are what they sound like: AI-powered agents you can train to provide personalized outreach to prospects and clients. The Data Agent’s primary purpose is to create smart properties that generate specialized insights based on the information you select, such as a contact’s previous interactions or their public-facing website. Each prompt response from the Data Agent costs 10 AI credits. Other agents are available through HubSpot’s broader customer platform plans. All of these agents use AI credits per interaction, with the cost per credit varying by agent type and interaction complexity. HubSpot Smart CRM lets you set up multi-step workflows for automating various marketing tasks, with the option to start from a template, create a workflow from scratch, or build one with AI. Most templates are available only with a paid subscription to HubSpot’s broader customer platform, except for the “Create and assign tasks when a new deal is created” option. As such, you’ll likely end up creating most of your workflows. The workflow builder is a visual designer with a left-hand toolbar for adding elements such as triggers and actions to a flowchart. You can also ask AI to find and enter elements for you. The system is fairly intuitive and doesn't require coding knowledge. It’s also pretty similar to what I’ve found in other CRMs, such as Pipedrive. My one frustration here is the inclusion of templates you can’t actually use if you’re on the CRM-only plan. Clicking on these templates opens an upsell page in a new tab, which is highly distracting. The Inbox conveniently integrates all communications channels you’ve synced with HubSpot into one spot, including email, phone calls, and chats. You can sort through all of it here, and the list updates dynamically as new messages arrive. However, this area focuses on team communications, with no clear option for separating individual agents’ inboxes—something common in other CRMs like Freshsales. The email composer appears in an unusually small box in the right-hand corner and won’t let you enter your email’s subject or content until you’ve selected a recipient. After that, you get plenty of options, including typing out the email yourself, inserting a template or other content (such as articles from a knowledge base), or generating copy via HubSpot’s AI. The last choice is the least useful; it doesn’t offer the same range of tone or length options as similar tools from Pipedrive and others. The emails it created for me were highly generic. Template creation and bulk emailing are possible through Smart CRM, but both have severe limitations. You need to pay for HubSpot’s email marketing suite or purchase a third-party tool to create dynamic campaigns. Reports and dashboards are essentially the same thing in HubSpot. You can select one of several canned reports, modify it, and save it under a different name. Unlike many competing CRMs, HubSpot lets you create reports entirely from scratch. The custom report builder takes a little time to grasp, but it’s essentially a two-stage process. Stage one covers the basic data you’re looking to access (sales, marketing, service, and so on), as well as which subcategories you want (contacts or deals, for example, if your report is for sales). For the second stage, you move to a fairly intuitive report builder that lets you customize how data fields appear (e.g., a pie chart versus a bar chart). Additionally, you can use Breeze AI to generate custom reports. One oddity here is that there’s no immediately visible option for exporting your dashboards. Nonetheless, if you click the Share button and choose to email your report, the composer includes an area to select the file type (such as PNG or PDF) to convert it. I would prefer a one-step export option, something you get with Freshsales and Zoho CRM. You can get Smart CRM as part of the complete HubSpot customer platform or bundle it with individual HubSpot tools for email marketing, content management, and customer support. Together, these tools let you manage most of your business tasks in one place, though the cost of running them can be quite high. HubSpot Smart CRM also connects with various third-party apps, including email marketing tools (such as MailChimp), financial apps (such as QuickBooks and Stripe), Google and Microsoft Office apps, and social media platforms (such as Facebook and LinkedIn). Over 2,400 app integrations are available in the HubSpot Marketplace, making it one of the most versatile CRMs I’ve tested. HubSpot uses application-layer encryption to protect all user data, though it doesn’t state the specific protocol. HubSpot’s software and data centers also go through regular penetration testing and third-party audits to ensure its protocols are effective and meet the requirements of various security certifications, including HIPAA. You can see the details about certifications and incidents here. As mentioned, HubSpot’s permissions settings give you granular control over what each user can see and modify. You can also set up two-factor authentication and single sign-on to ensure the security of individual accounts. Additionally, you can control the data that HubSpot’s AI can access (though limiting this access may also reduce its functionality). Final Thoughts HubSpot Smart CRM - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. HubSpot Smart CRM offers effective tools for contact, lead, and deal management at scale. Its automated workflows and extensive Breeze AI tools are excellent for larger businesses looking to improve their customer management processes. We're also fans of its customizable report builder, comprehensive library of integrations, and excellent support resources. However, we recommend HubSpot only for expansive or growing organizations due to its high starting costs and occasional complexity. Smaller companies should instead choose among our Editors' Choice winners, including the highly customizable Apptivo, the very affordable Bigin by Zoho CRM, and the particularly intuitive Freshsales. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert I've been building websites and marketing campaigns for small businesses since 2010. I also run two businesses of my own: Hired Gunn Writing & Consulting and the Weeknight Writers group. I'm obsessed with testing new tools to improve and expand these businesses, and I've written about those I've tried for sites like CNET, CodeinWP/WPShout, and WinningWP.

item.title: Asus's New Mini PC Uses Qualcomm's X2 Elite Chip to Run AI Agents
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.31
A new mini PC that can run AI agents locally has entered the market, this time from Asus, which is harnessing chips from Qualcomm. On Thursday, Asus launched the Ascent QN10, a compact desktop PC that features Qualcomm’s recently-launched X2 Elite processors, which have already been popping up in laptops. X2 Elite chips stand out for nearly doubling the AI performance from 45 TOPS to 80 TOPS, a mathematical measurement of the AI processing. Hence, Asus is touting the Ascent QN10 as the “world's first agentic AI mini PC with 80 TOPS” capable of running AI tools and AI agents, such as OpenClaw or Hermes Agent. Specifically, the mini PC contains a X2E-88-100 chip, which also features 18 CPU cores, and integrated graphics. The 1.65-pound compact PC promises to run cool and quietly while offering sustained performance, Asus says. The Ascent QN10 runs Windows 11 Copilot+ and arrives with 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM at $1,349. It can also be bought with 32GB of RAM at $1,699. But because its uses a Qualcomm chip, the mini PC uses the Arm-based architecture, rather than the x86 computing associated with Intel and AMD silicon. The product arrives when some AI enthusiasts have been buying up mini PCs to run AI agents locally at home or in the office. Companies including Apple and Nvidia have also been preparing pricey mini PCs with even more RAM at 96GB and 128GB, capable of running larger AI models directly over the hardware. Asus’s Ascent QN10 looks more like an affordable offering, and a potential alternative to Apple’s Mac Mini, which was recently upgraded with new processors. Asus says the $1,349 is already available on Best Buy. Meanwhile, the $1,699 model is already being sold on Amazon, Newegg, and Asus’s own online store, but it looks like supplies are running out fast. Asus adds: "For storage, it offers strong expandability with a dual SSD design: one M.2 2280 PCIe Gen 5 slot and one PCIe Gen 4 slot, supporting up to 4TB total capacity." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. item.title: Google Home Now Lets AI Agents Control Your Smart Home Devices
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.30
Google on Wednesday announced it’s adding support for Model Context Protocol (MCP) on Google Home, meaning you’ll soon be able to let your preferred AI agents interact with your smart home devices. Google already allows Gemini to respond to questions about your smart devices. The new integration adds support for other MCP-supporting tools, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes, OpenClaw, and others, according to a blog post. The AI agents can fetch information about all devices in the Google Home ecosystem, including Nest doorbells, security cameras, thermostats, and smart bulbs. Once connected, you can ask your AI agents questions like when your kids returned from school, how long the lights were left on, or how many loads of laundry were done in a week. The agents can also summarize your security camera feeds and highlight important clips. If an agent is in the middle of a task you’ve just assigned, you can expect it to leave an audio message via your speaker when the job is done. Google Home’s MCP support is currently rolling out in early access to subscribers of the Google Home Premium Advanced plan, costing $20 a month. You’ll need to create a Google Cloud project to set up your Home MCP and provide your AI agent with the necessary permissions. More setup details can be found on a separate developer support page. In both its announcement blog and introduction page, Google warns that connecting an AI agent to your devices and letting it control them “can result in unexpected or even undesired behavior.” We’ve already seen glimpses this year of the harm AI agents can cause when they act autonomously. OpenAI’s unreleased agents, for example, went rogue and carried out a cyberattack against Hugging Face in July. The same month, Anthropic’s Claude also hacked into three organizations. Interestingly, Google Home’s MCP support for AI agents arrives just days after the company backed Anthropic’s appeal to slow down AI development. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: FCC Opens Door to Starlink Mobile’s Global Roaming Ambitions
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.27
SpaceX has received the regulatory green light to offer US to international telecommunications services, which the company plans to use for Starlink Mobile, its satellite-to-phone service. On Thursday, the Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s application to offer international telecommunications, a process that requires a US company to go through regulatory review. The application specifically mentions using the authority “to support Starlink Mobile service offerings.” Back in May, SpaceX originally filed the application to request “global facilities-based and resale authority.” The application also noted that the company planned on offering “international telecommunications services to all of the destination markets” where dozens of Starlink subsidiaries reside in Latin America, Europe, Asia and Africa. Currently, Starlink Mobile is available through T-Mobile as T-Satellite, which can offer connectivity in dead zones, although bandwidth is constrained. However, SpaceX plans on upgrading Starlink Mobile with next-generation satellites that promises to beam 5G service, but from space, enabling users to receive downloads rates up to 150Mbps. Despite partnering with T-Mobile, SpaceX has also been positioning Starlink Mobile as a future rival to the big three carriers in the US. Last week, the company’s CFO Bret Johnsen said that Starlink Mobile could stand out by both eliminating cellular dead zones and offering global roaming, thanks to the orbiting satellites. A year earlier, SpaceX’s CEO Elon Musk himself also mulled Starlink Mobile possibly becoming a global carrier. But outside the US, SpaceX has been talking up partnerships. On the same day, the company tweeted about its deal with Japanese telecommunications company KDDI to offer “Starlink Mobile V2, saying it’ll offer “100x the data density, and will enable native calls, high-speed apps, streaming and more.” Meanwhile, T-Mobile and AT&T have been playing down the threat of Starlink Mobile, arguing the company’s satellites will struggle to offer robust coverage competitive with their own cell towers. However, SpaceX has plans to develop a ground network using small cost-effective radio equipment called femtocells, although industry experts have been dismissive of the approach as well. item.title: Alienware Gaming Laptops in Canada (2026): Specs, Prices, and Upgrade Paths
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.25
Quick Answer: In Canada, the Alienware 15 is the entry point to the Alienware lineup, with up to RTX 5060 graphics and up to 32GB of user-upgradeable memory, at 2.25 kg — a single device for everyday gaming alongside work, school, and other productivity. Stepping up, the Alienware 16X Aurora tops out at up to RTX 5070 Ti graphics and Intel Core Ultra 9 processors, the configuration to look at for demanding games and creative work. Canadian gamers already know that not every gaming laptop spec sheet travels well across the border. Frustratingly, a configuration or price listed in the US may not be available in Canada, and even the GPU or Windows edition can differ north of the 49th parallel. So, it’s worth checking the local lineup before getting your heart set on your dream rig. From there, you can narrow your choices based on your priorities for performance and upgrade potential, as well as practical considerations like size and weight. For Alienware buyers, the choice comes down to the capabilities you care about most. Dell’s Alienware 16X Aurora is the more performance-focused machine, while the Alienware 15 is the smaller and lighter of the two, offering an accessible entry to the Alienware experience without sacrificing high quality and performance at a lower starting price. Below is an overview of the specific details Canadian shoppers need to know before they buy either the Alienware 16X Aurora or the Alienware 15. What Should Canadian Shoppers Look for in a 2026 Alienware Gaming Laptop? Start with the configuration that’s actually available in Canada, then work backward from your budget and the games and other workloads you plan to run, as well as the upgrade paths available for each option. A few quirks and considerations to sort through up front: - The configurations on offer in Canada: Laptop makers don’t always offer the same processor, GPU, memory, or display combinations in every market, so check the Canadian product page rather than assuming a US configuration is available locally - The price of your preferred configuration: Use the starting price as a baseline, then check how your specs and preferences affect the total - What you can upgrade later: Both Windows laptops give you some flexibility to make changes down the line (for example, adding more RAM or expanding SSD storage), so it’s prudent to prioritize components that are harder to replace or upgrade later (e.g., the processor or display) - How the laptop fits into your routine: Features such as Stealth Mode, USB-C charging capabilities, and chassis size become more relevant if the same PC also has to show up at school or work Alienware Gaming Laptops in Canada: Key Specs at a Glance Here’s a quick chart for seeing how each option stacks up. How Do Canadian Alienware Configurations and Prices Compare? The Alienware 15 sits at the lower end of the price range, while the 16X Aurora offers several higher-performance configurations. This entry-level configuration pairs an Intel Core 5 210H processor with RTX 4050 graphics, 16GB of DDR5 memory, a 512GB SSD, and a 15.3-inch 165Hz WUXGA display. It’s the lower-cost route for buyers focused on portability and a multi-use device for gaming and more. This configuration steps up to an Intel Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, RTX 5070 graphics, 16GB of DDR5 memory, a 1TB SSD, and a 240Hz WQXGA OLED display. It’s a stronger fit for buyers who want more gaming performance and a higher-end display. At the upper end of the current Canadian lineup, this configuration combines an RTX 5070 Ti with a Core Ultra 9 290HX Plus processor, 32GB of DDR5 memory, a 1TB SSD, and the same 240Hz WQXGA OLED display. The extra spend primarily gets you the higher-tier GPU and twice the memory of the RTX 5070 configuration above. Can a High-Performance Gaming Laptop Double as an Understated Work Machine? Both Alienware models are designed for settings where you may not want your laptop to look or behave like a stereotypical gaming rig (like a Monday-morning status meeting or an afternoon working from your neighbourhood cafe). The Alienware 15 is especially easy to picture as part of a hybrid-work routine. Its polycarbonate-resin chassis and Nova Black finish keep the aesthetic classic and understated. At a minimum weight of 2.2 kg (4.85 pounds), it slides easily into a backpack for class or work tote for the commute. The device’s 180-degree hinge is another practical feature for anyone working at an awkwardly small desk or sharing their screen with a colleague across the table. The 16X Aurora has that same crossover appeal. An anodized aluminum exterior and clean silhouette keep the styling restrained. And when the work itself gets demanding, the laptop has the processing and graphics power for tasks like video editing or casual work in CAD or 3D software. On both laptops, Stealth Mode—activated by tapping F7 on your keyboard—lets you tone down the lighting and fan noise when you’re in a meeting or shared space, so your laptop doesn't draw unwanted attention from nosy classmates or coworkers. Are Entry-Level Alienware Laptops Easy to Upgrade Down the Line? Both laptops offer options for user upgrades to memory and storage, although the 16X Aurora offers more expansion flexibility than the Alienware 15. Some important details: Memory Both models use two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, so RAM is replaceable rather than soldered in. The Alienware 15 supports up to 32GB, while the 16X Aurora supports up to 64GB, so you can start modestly and add memory later if your games or creative applications get more demanding. Storage The Alienware 15 has one M.2 SSD slot, so increasing storage means replacing the existing drive with a larger capacity. The 16X Aurora has two M.2 SSD slots, which gives you the option to add a second drive as your game library or project files grow. Which Canadian Alienware Laptop Fits Your Budget? For Canadian buyers, the Alienware 15 is the lower-priced of the two, and the Alienware 16X Aurora is where the higher-tier GPU and display options live. The decision on how far to stretch your budget will depend on your needs and gameplay preferences: if your laptop has to move between classes, meetings, and back to your home or dorm room, the Alienware 15 may offer a more enticing balance of cost, performance, and portability. If 1440p-class gaming or heavier multitasking are higher on your list, the 16X Aurora gives you more room to scale up. What is the maximum GPU ceiling on the Canadian Alienware 16X Aurora? The Alienware 16X Aurora is currently available in Canada with up to an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 Ti Laptop GPU. Is single-channel RAM on the Alienware 15 a performance bottleneck? Single-channel RAM can limit memory bandwidth in some workloads, but the Alienware 15 has two user-accessible DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, which leaves room to add or replace memory later. How does Stealth Mode work on the Alienware 16X Aurora and Alienware 15? Stealth Mode turns off AlienFX lighting and switches the laptop to Quiet mode; simply hit the F7 key on your keyboard to activate the feature. Can you power the Alienware 15 using a standard USB-C charger? Yes. The Alienware 15 supports USB-C Power Delivery charging at up to 100W, so a general-purpose 100W (5A) USB-C charger works as a backup to the AC adapter for productivity, not gaming. USB-C Power Delivery on the Alienware 15 supplies enough power for writing a paper, building a presentation, or taking notes when the main adapter is out of reach. Gaming and other demanding workloads draw more than 100W, so those sessions need the dedicated AC power adapter included with the Alienware 15. Does the Alienware 16X Aurora feature Element 31 thermal cooling? No. Dell Technologies specifies Element 31 for its Area-51 laptops; the 16X Aurora instead uses a Cryo-Chamber cooling design. How much can Canadian shoppers save during Dell seasonal promotions? Savings vary by specific promotion and configuration; Dell Canada is currently advertising gaming PC deals of up to CAD $1,500 off select systems.

item.title: Sunnier Days Ahead? Solar Panels Are Now So Cheap It's Upending the Business World
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.16
Solar panels are so cheap now that in many places around the world, if a business isn't running on solar energy, it's going to struggle to compete. But as the Financial Times reports, the influx of cheap panels is placing new strains on the grid, and the underlying business model of utility companies which see shrinking profits alongside an explosion in self-generation. At the start of this century, solar panels were priced around $5 per watt they generated. Today, that's more like $0.12 per watt, almost entirely driven by China's enormous production of solar panels, which are currently estimated to be in the region of 1.36 terawatts per year. But where this more affordable form of green energy was initially mostly used in hard-to-reach places or in economies where decarbonizing was attractive, the low cost has now made it a fundamental part of some businesses. The FT cites a cement producer in Northern Pakistan that sees solar energy as a necessity to survive. With its rivals already using solar, it is struggling to compete on price because the others' low energy costs allow them to be more competitive, regardless of fluctuations in fuel pricing impacted by global trade and conflict. This is becoming increasing prevalent in developing countries. Estimates from the green-energy-focused think tank Ember suggest that African countries will jointly bring online over 17GW of solar power generation in 2026. This in turns helps them replace otherwise carbon-generating sources, like kerosene lamps and charcoal-cooking fires. Although the US government has stymied some attempts to accelerate solar roll out, plug-in solar is still making inroads, allowing for smaller solar setups, even on balconies, to flourish. The UK recently legalized these new plug-in systems and they are expected to see swift adoption under the looming shadow of the US-Iran war and its ongoing energy turbulence. But while some businesses are buoyed by the technology, traditional utility companies face new challenges. With so many homes and businesses switching to solar, often those with larger energy usage, utility firms are contending with reduced revenue, and less reliable demand. Cloudy days suddenly see millions more homes and businesses demanding energy from the grid, where otherwise they would rely on their own solar power. On top of that, national grids not designed with two-way power transmission in mind are straining under the exploding solar generation capacity. Day-long blackouts in Spain and Portugal in 2025 have been linked to the grid not being adapted to the increasing capacity for solar generation from individual homes and businesses. As more and more people move off-grid for the majority of their electricity, too, it raises questions about who should be paying for grid infrastructure and maintenance. But raising prices on remaining customers further risks punishing those who can't afford or physically fit solar panels on to their home. Part of the solution may be using AI to better manage grid loads and the influx of solar energy, with smart forecasting that uses weather patterns to provide a more responsive energy grid. While designing a modern power grid may be more complex and remain costly in the near-term, the genie is not going back in the solar bottle. As global disturbances push up fuel prices and increase uncertainty, a growing majority of people just want stable, affordable power. Solar looks set to be the best way to achieve that. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Waymo Robotaxis Are Coming to Singapore, But Not Any Time Soon
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.90
Autonomous taxi rides run by Waymo are coming to Singapore, with testing in the country set to begin early next year. This announcement comes days after Waymo confirmed its launch in Tokyo, Japan, and a month after it detailed plans for Munich, Germany. Riders will have to wait until 2028 for Waymo to become available in Singapore. Alphabet has yet to say when in the year the service will be available, but it would mark Waymo's first launch in Southeast Asia. In the early months of next year, a series of Waymo test vehicles will be sent to Singapore to map locations and help accumulate data in what it calls “validation driving.” It begins its research process with manual driving, before moving to autonomous driving, with specialists available behind the wheel in case of emergencies. Waymo said, “We are confident that we will be able to meet Singapore’s high AV regulatory standards based on the significant real-world experience we have to-date and look forward to seeking the corresponding government approvals for future phases.” This comes days after Waymo announced plans to launch in its first Asian market: Tokyo. The ride-hailing service is set to launch in the Japanese city next year, made available through a partnership with Nihon Kotsu and GO. Testing in Tokyo first began in 2025, which explains the long wait for Singaporeans. Both Japan and Singapore differ greatly from US roads, where Waymo vehicles were first trained, including in weather conditions and traffic systems. Late last month, Waymo announced plans for robotaxis in Munich, Germany, marking its first European Union expansion. It is aiming to be up and running by the end of 2027. Waymo’s first international market is expected to be London, England. The brand says it’s on track to hit its target of launching vehicles in the city by the end of this year, but regulatory approval may delay Waymo and its robotaxi rivals' plans. In late August, Waymo’s head of policy and government affairs for the UK and Europe, Ben Loewenstein, told the Financial Times that the brand was “working through the safety approval process.” He said Waymo was waiting on Transport for London’s guidance on “how to earn their consent.” Earlier this year, Waymo launched in additional US cities, including Denver, Las Vegas, Tampa, and San Diego, bringing its total to 15. The wait for international Waymos on your next vacation may continue, but that’s not stopping it from keeping up with rivals like Tesla and Zoox. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Valve's Steam Frame Orders Begin Today. How to Snag the $1,059 VR Headset
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.67
Following a memory-related delay, Valve’s Steam Frame is finally ready to launch. The company will begin taking orders for the VR headset today. A 256GB version will be $1,059, and a 1TB model will cost $1,299. Both come with 16GB of Unified LPDDR5X RAM. How to Order the Steam Frame VR Headset To thwart resellers and bots, Valve is using a waitlist/reservation system. If you signed up and you're selected, you'll receive an email today with the option to purchase. “Based on the results of that randomization, you'll receive an email on September 17th letting you know you're either in the reservation queue or on the waitlist,” the company says. “If you're in the reservation queue, the model you signed up for has been reserved in your name. As units become available to ship, you'll receive an email with the option to purchase. The first batch of these emails will begin going out on September 18th. “You'll then have 72 hours to complete the purchase before we cancel your reservation and move on to the next person in the queue,” the company added. The product will be available on the Steam store for buyers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australia. Customers in Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong will be able to purchase through Valve’s partner, Komodo. Valve's Steam Frame VR Headset Features Although the Steam Frame isn’t cheap, Valve is touting an array of enhancements and capabilities, including its design for both VR titles and non-VR games. “Designed for streaming, it can handle your entire Steam library. And it supports standalone play too, with over 100 games (and growing) already Steam Frame Standalone Verified,” it wrote in a blog post. The headset also features a 4-nanometer Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor and two 2,160-by-2,160 LCDs, each with a 72-144Hz refresh rate. In addition, the product relies on “inside-out tracking,” ditching external sensors, unlike the older Valve Index headset. Ahead of the launch, a few tech publications reviewed the headset. IGN notes, “The Steam Frame is probably one of the first VR headsets that can do everything right out of the box, from standalone gaming to streaming 2D games from your PC.” However, both IGN and CNET flagged the short battery life as a weakness. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Adobe Lightroom Classic Review: The Leading Photo Workflow App for Pros
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.66
Adobe's Lightroom Classic is the longtime benchmark for photo workflow apps, thanks to its best-in-class organization and nondestructive Raw processing features. Hobbyists can get creative with a range of unbeatable color tools and quickly find photos of loved ones using robust keyword and face recognition filters. Meanwhile, pros who need to sort through large volumes of images should appreciate its recently improved assisted culling features. And despite the app's monthly subscription model, the cost is reasonable for photographers who want immediate access to its latest features. We've lowered Lightroom Classic's rating by half a star because it’s no longer head and shoulders above its competitors, but it's still a clear Editors' Choice winner. It shares that distinction with the more streamlined non-Classic Lightroom (which you get as part of the same subscription) and Adobe Photoshop, our top pick for pixel-level retouching and editing. Lightroom Classic is available only via subscription, starting with the Lightroom (1TB) plan. The plan is available for $17.99 per month, $11.99 per month (with an annual commitment for a total of $143.88), or $9.99 per month (billed annually at $119.88). A seven-day trial is available for all plans. Each plan comes with 1TB of cloud storage and both Lightroom Classic and Lightroom. The apps have the same core functionality but differ in their interfaces and some features, including their approaches to storage. Lightroom Classic works especially well with local photos on your computer (but can sync images to the cloud), while Lightroom puts your catalog in the cloud by default (which can add to your monthly bill if it swells beyond 1TB). For more details, read our in-depth comparison. The Creative Cloud Photography Plan (1TB), which costs $29.99 per month or $19.99 per month with an annual commitment, includes Photoshop. It's a better deal than paying for Photoshop à la carte—Adobe charges $22.99 per month (with an annual commitment) for Photoshop and a meager 100GB of storage. Photoshop provides pixel-based, destructive (also called raster) editing tools that aren’t available in Lightroom. Photographers who prefer to retouch images by hand or use more esoteric techniques like macro focus stacking will want to add Photoshop to their toolkit, but Lightroom does so much that Photoshop is no longer a strict requirement for many creative workflows. Naturally, Lightroom Classic is part of the full Creative Cloud suite, which costs $54.99 per month for the Standard edition or $69.99 per month for the Pro version, which includes more AI tools and credits. Both of those rates require an annual commitment. If you find Adobe’s subscription model distasteful, look into getting a perpetual license for Capture One ($349), DxO Photo Lab ($249.99), or Skylum Luminar ($129). Choosing an app with a perpetual license can reduce monthly subscription costs, but you miss out on the regular feature updates that a subscription model provides. It's also worth noting that Capture One's base Pro subscription plan ($18 per month, billed annually) costs more than Lightroom Classic. Adobe regularly updates Lightroom Classic with new features and support for the latest cameras and lenses. The app typically gets new features three to four times per year, with more frequent camera and lens compatibility fixes. Adobe does a fantastic job of keeping up with support for the newest digital cameras. The current version of Lightroom Classic at the time of writing is 15.5.1, released in August 2026. Here's what's new since the last time of the last review in July of 2025: - Assisted Culling improvements: Lightroom Classic uses face recognition to select photos where subjects’ eyes are open and sharp, helping you find the best portrait or group shot in a sequence. - Better identification of AI-edited images: You can now filter images based on AI Edits, with granular options for Has AI, Has Generative AI, and Needs AI Update. - Broader support for HDR file formats: The app lets you send 16- or 32-bit HDR images to an external editor (like Photoshop) with your choice of an sRGB, HDR Rec. 2020, or HDR Display P3 color space. - DNG rendering: Lightroom Classic now lets you render and export a DNG version of a photo with adjustments applied, a plus for creators who want to make additional adjustments in another application. - Improved Generate Remove: The software's generative remove and distraction removal tools now run faster and perform better, helping you target dust spots, distracting objects, or reflections in photos. Most of the updates from the last year are enhancements to existing features rather than all-new concepts. That’s a reflection of the software’s maturity; Lightroom Classic debuted back in 2007. Adobe also typically trots out new features in full version releases. Given previous development cycles, we expect a major release later this year. To install Lightroom Classic, you need a fairly up-to-date, 64-bit OS. It supports macOS 14 or later, Windows 10 (version 22H2 or later), and Windows 11 (version 21H2 or later). It works with both Intel- and Apple silicon-based Macs, but not natively on Windows on Arm PCs (unlike the other Lightroom). Otherwise, you need about 2GB of storage for installation, and a minimum of 8GB of RAM. Adobe recommends 16GB and an SSD for the best performance. Don't ignore these recommendations. Some advanced features take a while on 8GB systems, and physical disks can also be a bottleneck. I use a LaCie 6big Thunderbolt 3 RAID 5 hard drive array for my image archive, and I typically notice a delay when drives need to spin up and load an image. A Lightroom subscription includes access to mobile apps for Android, iOS, and iPadOS. With these apps, you can edit images you’ve synced to the cloud or photos on your mobile device. If you spend a lot of time editing on mobile, non-Classic Lightroom makes more sense on desktop, thanks to its more seamless cloud integration and a more consistent interface. However, you can still sync photos with Lightroom Classic. Lightroom Classic’s user experience hasn’t changed that much over the last couple of decades, even as its feature set has grown significantly. It breaks up its main screen into seven tabs: Library, Develop, Map, Book, Slideshow, Print, and Web. A cloud icon shows how much of your Adobe cloud storage you’re using and lets you sync on demand. The app puts folders, develop presets, and templates on the left, shows the image you’re working on in the center, information and tools on the right, and a film strip on the bottom so you can scroll through images. Most of Classic’s functions live in the Library and Develop tabs, so you'll spend most of your time there. The other tabs handle less frequent tasks. Map shows a global map and populates it with images that have GPS metadata, Book lets you create photo books that you can buy from Blurb, Slideshow replaces the old Kodak Carousel and lets you create MP4 movies with titles and transitions, Print prepares images for printing, and Web helps you publish a gallery website to show off your images. I’ve used Lightroom Classic regularly since its debut, first as a hobbyist photographer and, for the past 15 years, as a camera reviewer, so it’s fair to say I know Classic better than any other piece of software. I’m old and set in my ways, so I tend to struggle with photo apps with dramatically different layouts (I’m looking at you, Capture One). But even when I was starting out, I felt comfortable in Lightroom and struggled with its contemporary competition, Apple’s long-discontinued Aperture—and I say that as a dyed-in-the-wool Mac person. Don't forget about the top bar drop-down menu. If you’re ever trying to figure out how to do something and can’t find it, the searchable Help menu is worth a visit. Just type in the feature you’re looking for, and the menu will take you right to it. If you can’t figure something out, Adobe has an extensive library of support documents on its website, along with an active user group forum. If you’re still stuck on something after that, drop me an email, and I’ll do my best to assist. Lightroom uses a catalog system that imports and sorts images into its Library, leaving the organizational structure up to you. I sort everything into year-based folders with subfolders, but you might want to take a different approach. Wedding photographers, for example, might choose to organize by client name or even create a separate catalog file for each client. Lightroom loads only one catalog at a time, but it lets you freely swap between as many as you want to create. I like this approach—I prefer to keep just one huge catalog as I often need to go back and look at images from the various cameras I’ve reviewed over the years, but I can see why working photographers would want to spin up a different catalog for each client or start fresh each calendar year. Importing photos into the catalog is required; you can’t just edit directly from a drive or memory card. The Import screen pops up automatically when you insert a memory card into your computer, or you can load it manually by clicking Import (in the bottom-left corner of the app). You can select what you bring in and choose to add keywords during the process. Lightroom gives you flexibility on where you import them, though—you can spread a library across multiple folders, as well as internal or external drives. You can opt to convert proprietary Raw formats to Adobe DNG during import, though I don’t see much point in that. If you end up switching to a different photo editing app down the road, you’re better off with original files. You can also bring images into your catalog by using Tethered Capture, a mode that lets you connect and control a digital camera from your computer screen. Tethering is available for many major brands, and photos go straight into your computer and the Lightroom catalog. It’s a must-have feature if you work in a proper studio, but not super useful for hobbyists and event photogs who take pictures out in the world. The Library tab shows your catalog’s folder structure in its left panel, along with Collections (groups of images organized independent of the folder structure). This panel also provides quick access to supported Publish services, such as Adobe Stock and Flickr. Additional services are available via plug-ins. The right panel lets you access the Assisted Culling tool, add comments and keywords to images, and make quick exposure and color adjustments via the Quick Develop tool. The film strip at the bottom lets you page through images (tap the left or right keys to move back and forth) and includes tools to add a star rating, assign a color code, and flag images as picks or rejects. If your camera lets you assign star ratings to photos, Lightroom reads those automatically. All of these features genuinely help you pare down the photos you want to edit. Assisted Culling is a big hit for sports and wildlife photography, disciplines in which you often capture a high volume of images, intending to edit and publish only a few. Event photographers should find the star-rating and color-coding features handy for picking out the best images from the day. You can also quickly compare two photos (tap ‘c’), and click on an image to zoom in and check focus. One quick, but important note: Lightroom Classic won't import images it doesn't support. Adobe is quick to accommodate new Raw image formats, but if you get a brand-new camera on day one, you might have to wait a few weeks for Lightroom to read its file format. Among its competitors, Adobe is usually the first to support newly released cameras, but not always. The Develop panel, which resembles the Library tab, is the heart of Lightroom Classic. Its right-hand editing panel has a Histogram on top, with a row of six icons (Edit, Crop and Straighten, Remove, Red Eye Correction, Masking, and AI Edit Status). The Edit section includes slider-based tools for adjusting exposure and color, applying noise reduction, adding film grain, and more. It covers a lot of ground, but puts the features you’ll use most often (exposure and white balance) toward the top, and lets you suppress other options to one line so they don’t take up space. You can’t reorder them, however. It's crucial to understand that the changes you make to photos in Lightroom are nondestructive. Instead of changing information in an actual image, the software records changes in its catalog instead and only renders a finished photo with all of your edits baked in when you export it. This matches how pretty much every workflow application behaves, and I think it's the best way to go. Since Lightroom Classic never alters the original camera file, you can always go back to rework and freely experiment with an image. That's important because if you stick with photography long enough, your style and tastes will likely evolve—I recently looked at some photos I shot in my early days and was horrified by my early, garish processing. With Lightroom, I was able to rework my edits and am now happier with the results. And when you’re ready to share your photo with the world, you can easily export it in a wide variety of file formats (AVIF, DNG, JPG, JPG XL, PSD, PNG, TIFF). The Edit panel starts with a color profile, Adobe Color by default. Some preset options (such as RNI All Films 5 Pro) give images a stylized look, but Adobe also supports camera-matching profiles that mimic the colors of straight-out-of-camera JPGs from major brands. I especially like using the latter with Fujifilm cameras as Lightroom supports all of the company’s stylized Film Simulation looks. I appreciate the flexibility. You can either find or create a profile that matches your aesthetic. Or you can stick with Adobe's or your camera manufacturer's profiles. Raw images contain an incredible amount of color data, more than most screens can display, and the strength of Lightroom Classic (or any Raw converter for that matter) lies in its ability to tone exposure after capture. And you’ll want to make some adjustments—a Raw image is not a finished product, it’s a starting point that’s meant to be edited to taste. That said, you may be happy with what Lightroom shows right after import, since its default Adobe Color profile is naturalistic. Adobe puts Lightroom Classic’s exposure panel right near the top of the develop tools. It’s your starting point, with sliders to adjust the overall Exposure and Contrast of an image, or independently change the brightness of Highlights, Shadows, Whites, and Blacks. Everyone tones images differently, but I tend to go for a lower contrast look by moving Highlights and Whites to the left and Shadows and Blacks to the right. For a punchier photo, lower Shadows and Blacks and brighten Highlights and Whites. You can also go for a cool or warm tone by changing the White Balance. Use an eyedropper tool to set white balance from a neutral white, gray, or black area of an image, or choose a preset Kelvin temperature from a drop-down menu. If you want a punchier or paler color, you can try the Vibrance or Saturation sliders, though I caution you not to overdo it with either unless you're specifically going for a hyperrealistic look. Otherwise, you can raise or lower the microcontrast of an image using Clarity and Texture sliders, or sharpen a hazy shot with Dehaze.
