I try to use the Clarity and Texture options very conservatively; adding too much of either gives an image an unnatural look reminiscent of the worst examples of 2000s action films, while dialing them all the way back results in a diffused, soft-focus effect. Lightroom Classic's Detail panel includes the Super Resolution and Denoise tools, which respectively increase the pixel count and remove graininess. Both are useful if you’re cropping heavily or planning to make a large print. Super Resolution does a good job of adding detail without introducing AI hallucinations, unlike the upres features on phones like the Google Pixel 11 Pro. And it beats the in-camera version Canon includes in the EOS R5 Mark II and EOS R1 in terms of detail. I cover the Denoise feature in more detail further below (it’s part of Adobe’s AI toolset). The Transform tool can correct shots that aren’t quite level or suffer from keystone distortion with a single click. I struggle with getting shots perfectly level in the field and perhaps rely on the Level button too much, but it works reliably. If you’re going for an artsy look, you can use the Effects panel to add grain or a vignette. I like the ease of adding grain, as well as the option to adjust the amount, size, and roughness of the effect. Still, Adobe’s grain tends to look about the same from image to image, and doesn’t let you emulate different film stocks like you can with the Nik Collection tools, such as Color Efex and Silver Efex. That said, I use Lightroom Classic’s grain tool far more often than Nik's, simply because it’s quicker. With the latter, I have to export a TIFF and round-trip it back to my gallery. For social posts and my web gallery, Lightroom Classic’s convenience wins out, but if I were making a large print and wanted a filmic look, I’d go with Nik. Lens Profiles also come in handy. The vast majority of lenses for mirrorless camera systems are designed to work best with digital corrections to compensate for optical distortion and a vignette. Most digital cameras apply these automatically for JPGs, but you need to do it yourself for Raws. Lightroom Classic supports the vast majority of first-party and third-party lenses on the market. If you notice barrel or pincushion distortion or darkened corners when editing a photo, the first thing to do is to check if the Lens Profile correction setting is on. I’ve tested hundreds of lenses over the years, and Adobe’s profiles typically match in-camera corrections to a tee. Lightroom puts most of its useful tools in the Develop menu, but a quick right-click on an image opens more options, including the ability to stitch together panoramas or merge bracketed exposures into an HDR image that captures more dynamic range than even the best image sensors can in a single exposure. The right-click menu also shows some organization tools, including the option to create virtual copies of an image (so you can make different edits without taking up more room on your hard drive), group photos into stacks, or add a photo to a Quick Collection. These features are also available from the top menu and via hot keys. Generative AI has earned a bad name among creators, and for good reason. Adobe is as culpable as any AI brand, since you can use Firefly to create images from a text prompt, but the company takes a far more conservative approach than most with Lightroom Classic. Essentially, the app uses AI to improve its existing photo development tools. It doesn't put them in a separate section; instead, it maintains a summary of all AI edits on an image. This works alongside the C2PA Content Credentials system that embeds an image's editing history. It's helpful for photographers entering photo contests or working with agencies that want to see some provenance for a photo. Ultimately, it’s up to you to decide which AI tools are ethical to use and which aren’t. Where you land is likely tied to the type of photography you enjoy—photojournalists and documentarians should likely avoid it altogether, while digital creators, portrait and event photographers, and landscape artists who are used to burning, dodging, and retouching are likely to approach the tools more freely. If you often photograph events, sports, or wildlife, or simply prefer to keep your camera’s drive to Hi+ at all times, the AI Culling feature is for you. Lightroom analyzes sequences of images to identify the ones with the best focus and exposure, discarding the rejects and potentially saving you hours. Modern consumer cameras take photos at rates between 20 and 40fps, and high-end sports cameras like the Sony a9 III can hit 120fps, making it a little too easy to overshoot in the field. Assisted Culling takes some time to run. For instance, it needed about 10 minutes to check a batch of 2,500 images I shot at a local air show for focus, which it winnowed down to around 750 shots. Even so, that represents a net savings in editing time, so I count Assisted Culling as a smart use of AI. Noise Reduction has long been a feature in Lightroom Classic. By default, it removes color (chroma) noise from every image during import, so I won’t blame you if you didn’t notice. Its AI-driven Denoise tool instead attacks luminance noise, and does so more effectively than the old-school Luminance slider (which remains available). Generally, the AI Denoise tool removes grain more effectively while letting detail shine through, whereas the Luminance noise slider can soften an image if used too liberally. The only downside? The Denoise process takes a while to work—I tried it on an ISO 51200 shot of my detail test target captured with the Sony RX1R III, and it took about 20 seconds to analyze and apply noise reduction. Thankfully, you can apply Denoise to a batch of images, so you can grab a cup of coffee while Lightroom churns through a gallery. Lightroom lets you select someone’s face in a photo and find other instances of the person in your catalog. AI Face Recognition can help if you're bad at tagging friends in your snapshots or want to automatically add tags to the important members of a wedding party to make sure you get all the best shots with the bride and groom in frame. To get started, go to the top text menu, select View, and click on People. It performs fine, but I wish it extended to pets. I would also like to see support for descriptive natural language searches, such as "all images of bald eagles.” Lightroom has had a sensor dust removal tool for years, but it previously required you to select another area of the photo as a source. That wasn't a big problem if your dust spot was over a clear blue sky, but for removing actual specks of dirt from a product photo or a skin blemish from a portrait, the tool often fell short. Now, the AI-powered version looks at what you’re trying to remove (or clean up) and the surrounding area. The results are impressive. I shoot a lot of product photos of cameras and lenses with flash, and despite my best efforts, I always end up finding some spots of white dust or dirt that I missed—a matte black subject is unforgiving. Lightroom Classics’s Generative Remove does an outstanding job for this type of work. The tool isn’t just for dust, either. Lightroom can also remove reflections from surfaces, so you can freely shoot through glass even if you forgot to pack a circular polarizing filter. This works well—I tried it with some images I shot through glass at a trade show, and Lightroom cleaned them up. If I hadn't seen the originals, I wouldn't have guessed the images were edited. Finally, the technology can remove people from cityscapes and landscapes, which is handy for architectural and travel photographers who don't want to see tourists. Family photographers who want to send out a holiday card without exes in group shots might use it, too. People removal works quite well for the most part. I noticed that it could occasionally miss people who were diminutive in the frame, but it's easy enough to use a brush to manually tag anything the automatic detection misses, including inanimate distractions like trash cans, for that matter. Did you ever get back home after taking a photo and wish you had used a wider aperture to get the blurry background (bokeh) look? Or wish that you could adjust the look and intensity of bokeh like you can with your iPhone? Lightroom Classic's Lens Blur tool uses the same tech as the Masking tool to identify a subject and soften the background. Even better, it gives you control over the look of the blur, so you can choose between a 5-blade aperture, anamorphic, mirror lens, modern, or soap bubble look, as well as adjust the depth of field and change highlights to cat’s eye shapes. The blur tool can take a while to analyze complex images—as long as 20 seconds in some cases—and doesn’t always get the mapping spot-on initially. If the automatic depth mapping process misses it, you can manually add blur to an area of the frame with a brush tool. I like the results with this tool in some cases. For instance, I had to use an f/11 aperture at 30mm to keep both grave markers in focus in the preceding image, resulting in a deep-focus image. The Lens Blur tool effectively softens both the background and foreground while keeping the subjects in sharp focus. Masking is a powerful tool that lets editors apply selective edits (as opposed to global edits) to photos in Lightroom Classic. In the old days, this was a manual process in Photoshop that required careful use of the Lasso tool to draw an outline over a subject. Adobe now uses its AI engine to identify subjects or objects, the sky, or the background, which you can then edit independently of the rest of the image. It’s handy to be able to apply selective color effects, brighten a subject captured against a backlight, darken a sky in a landscape image to add some drama, or turn a portrait background into nothing to mimic the look of a studio shoot. Because Lightroom Classic’s edits are nondestructive, you'll need to render and export your images for archiving, printing, or uploading. The Export window offers granular control over file naming, resolution, formats, and locations, and supports plug-ins for direct uploads to Flickr, Mylio, Smugmug, and other popular cloud photo storage options. The Export window also lets you create and save presets, which are handy for quick right-click exports of an image. It's also possible to add watermarks. As mentioned, Lightroom Classic also lets you create layouts for printing, photo books with Blurb, or web-based photo galleries. These tools aren’t available in the non-Classic flavor of Lightroom. I run Lightroom Classic on two different systems regularly, a 2022 Mac Studio M1 Max with 64GB of memory for any serious photo work, and an Intel-based 2019 MacBook Pro i9 with 64GB RAM for quick edits when I’m not in my home office. I’m generally happy with how the software performs on both. Aside from waiting for my RAID disk to spin up from sleep, I don’t see any lag when making basic edits or when using advanced tools that run locally. I’ve yet to see a Raw file that can choke Lightroom, including images from cameras like the 100MP Fujifilm GFX100S and the 66MP Sony a7R VI. That said, both of these systems have plenty of RAM. When I tried Lightroom Classic with an 8GB MacBook Neo, I noticed some delay when zooming into photos at full resolution and using the AI Denoise and dust spot removal tools. Lightroom Classic's AI features obviously perform better on newer, more powerful hardware. Michael Muchmore contributed to this article. Final Thoughts Adobe Lightroom Classic - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Lightroom Classic excels at pretty much everything you might want to do in the digital darkroom: basic retouching, granular exposure and color adjustments, effective noise reduction, and much more. And it does all this non-destructively. Moreover, we count its comprehensive keyword and sorting tools, consistent and segmented user experience, local catalog storage, and reasonably useful AI tools as major strengths. Yes, its subscription costs can add up over time, but Lightroom Classic easily delivers enough value and innovations to remain an Editors' Choice winner, alongside Lightroom, its cloud-based sibling that comes with the same subscription. Meanwhile, Photoshop, another Editors' Choice winner, is the undisputed leader in photo manipulation. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Series 11: Is the Upgrade Actually Worth It?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.65
Table of Contents Apple is going even harder on AI and health tracking with the Apple Watch Series 12, which packs a range of new features enabled by a faster S11 chip and an entirely redesigned health-sensing system. However, the Series 12 looks virtually identical to its predecessor and shares the same estimated battery life. Do these underlying updates add up to a smartwatch that actually feels new? After testing it side by side with the Series 11, here's how the two generations compare to help you decide whether it's worth the upgrade. Full Specs | Apple Watch Series 12 | Apple Watch Series 11 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S10 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 54.5 hours (tested) | 43 hours (tested) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: A Higher Premium for Larger Sizes While year-over-year pricing remains mostly unchanged, the Series 12 gets a bit pricier if you prefer a larger watch. Like the Series 11, the base 42mm aluminum GPS model starts at $399. However, jumping to the 46mm size now costs an extra $50, compared with the $30 premium on the Series 11. Upgrading to cellular remains a $100 add-on across both generations. Titanium models with cellular also keep their previous price points at $699 (42mm) and $749 (46mm). If you want something even more premium, the Series 12 introduces a new ceramic finish for $899 (42mm) and $949 (46mm). Winner: Tie Design: A New Ceramic Option and Fresh Finish Colors The two Apple Watches look nearly identical, though the aluminum and titanium Series 12 are just a millimeter wider and 1.5 grams heavier than their Series 11 counterparts. The color choices are slightly different, with the aluminum Series 12 swapping out silver and rose gold finishes for light gold and bronze, and titanium adding a radiant gold. Then there's the ceramic version, in white or blue. It adds another millimeter to the watch's height, width, and depth, and another six to eight grams in weight. Either way, you have more options with the Series 12. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 AI Features: S11 Chip Powers On-Device Audio Intelligence The Series 12 uses Apple's new S11 chip to enable Apple Intelligence features that the Series 11 lacks. The biggest addition is an upcoming feature called Audio Intelligence, which lets the Series 12 listen to everything around you all day, providing summaries of conversations and even rewinding parts to help you catch up. It can also recognize important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, and notify you if you're hard of hearing. Apple claims the S11 chip protects privacy with hardware-isolated onboard audio processing. It also says Audio Intelligence doesn't identify speakers and doesn't include identifying information in its output. If you're still uncertain, though, you can just turn the feature off. The Series 11 doesn't support Audio Intelligence at all, but it still has all the standard hands-free Siri functionality and other Apple Intelligence features. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Health and Fitness: Frequent Heart Tracking and Daily Readiness Score The Series 12 makes some big leaps in fitness and health tracking features. Apple has reworked its optical and electrical heart rate sensors, and now the watch measures your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day instead of only periodically, as the Series 11 does. The new watch also measures heart rate variability up to 24 times more often, with a new section of the Heart Rate app dedicated to the data. Apple claims it's the most accurate heart rate tracking in a wearable. Apple is also taking a more holistic approach to fitness with a new Apple Intelligence-powered readiness score that provides a number from 0 to 10 assessing your energy for the day, with a recommendation to go all-out, pace yourself, or rest and recover. The readiness score is exclusive to the Series 12, though the Series 11 offers other holistic scores for sleep and mindfulness. Outside of the improved heart rate sensors and readiness score, the Series 12 and Series 11 are equally equipped for general health and fitness. Both support on-demand blood oxygen and ECG readings, keep tabs on your sleep, and offer all the other fitness-tracking tools. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Battery Life: S11 Efficiency Yields Superior Real-World Endurance Apple is always conservative in its battery life estimates, and both the Series 11 and the Series 12 have the same 24-hour estimate. In our real-world testing, the Series 11 lasted 43 hours with the always-on display enabled. The Series 12 did even better. The new chip and health-sensing system make a big difference in efficiency, helping the Series 12 power through 54.5 hours in our testing before it needed to be plugged in. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Durability: Tougher Ceramic Shield 2 Glass for Aluminum Models The Series 12 has the same IP6X dustproof rating and is water-resistant to up to 164 feet, just like the Series 11. The aluminum version is a bit tougher, though, thanks to its new Ceramic Shield 2 glass (different from the ceramic case option), which Apple claims is 60% more durable than the Ion-X glass on the Series 11. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Connectivity: Identical Wireless Specs and Cellular Options Both models pack identical connectivity specs: dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.3, L1 GPS, and Apple's Ultra Wideband chip for precision phone tracking. Choose a cellular model, and you get the exact same 5G and LTE radios regardless of which generation you buy. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Series 12 The Series 12 delivers where it matters most, making it a far more satisfying upgrade than the Series 11 was over the Series 10. You get significantly smarter health sensors, longer battery life, and new AI tools—all without a base-price increase. Unless you find a massive discount on last year's model, the Series 12 is well worth the money.

item.title: iOS 27 Is Reportedly Freezing iPhones After a Few Quick Swipes: Here's the Fix
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.57
Apple’s iOS 27 software began rolling out last weekend, and 9to5Mac has spotted a bug that freezes iPhones after a series of quick swipes across the home screen. Not every user may experience the issue, but for those who do, the freezing occurs when you swipe down from the top left of the home screen to draw the Notification Center, and before it launches, you quickly swipe down from the top right to open the Control Center. When the screen freezes, you’ll see the Notification Center’s Camera and Torch icons stuck on top of your screen, 9to5Mac says. I couldn’t replicate the issue on my iPhone 14 running iOS 27, but if you're facing it, there’s a simple fix: force-restart your iPhone. To do so, press and quickly release the Volume Up button on the left, then do the same with the Volume Down button, and finally hold the Power button on the right until the Apple logo appears. This should reboot your iPhone and restore normalcy, the report adds. On iPhones, a force-restart is different from a regular restart, which requires you to hold the Volume Up and Power buttons together and swipe across the Power Off slider that appears. Since screen-freezing issues can prevent your taps and swipes from registering on the display, a force restart using the physical buttons is the easiest way out. iOS 27 users have also been sharing ways to freeze iPhones using a few other methods. As it happens with major iOS releases each year, they have also been complaining about battery drain after upgrading to iOS 27. Apple’s iOS 26 release drew similar reactions last year, and the company responded, saying it’s quite normal for major software updates to temporarily affect battery life. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: AOC 16T20 Review: A Workable Portable Monitor for the Very Tightest Budgets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.00
The AOC 16T20 ($69.99) is the least expensive portable monitor we've encountered in recent years. This compact, lightweight display is worth considering if you're cash-strapped and looking for a roomy auxiliary monitor for your home or for use on the road. (It's a 15.6-inch panel.) However, the trade-offs for its bargain-basement pricing include limitations in both features and performance. Its stand and navigation are primitive by portable monitor standards, and its peak brightness is low. For a bit more money (though still less than $100), you can get the Editors' Choice-award-winning MSI Pro MP165 E6, which includes a more tilt-adjustable stand and much higher brightness. Compact and lightweight, the 16T20 measures 8.8 by 14 by 0.4 inches (HWD) and weighs just 1.5 pounds, making it easy to travel with and fit in tight spaces. The 16T20's chassis has a matte-black front with fairly thin top and side bezels. These frame a 15.6-inch (diagonal) in-plane switching (IPS) screen with a resolution of 1,920 by 1,080 pixels (aka Full HD, FHD, or 1080p) and a 16:9 widescreen aspect ratio. AOC rates the vertical and horizontal viewing angles at up to 170 degrees, meaning you can view the screen from the side or above without significant degradation in brightness or color. Its refresh rate is 60Hz, typical of budget portables. The 16T20 comes with a wraparound, rigid, black protective cover, which doubles as a folding stand. The cover can be unfolded so that a strip magnetically attaches to the top of the panel's lid, while the monitor's lower edge can fit into either of two grooves in the cover's base, letting the screen rest at your choice of two tilt angles. Such "origami-style" folding stands, once common on lower-priced monitors, have largely been replaced by more rigid stands, such as the MSI Pro MP165 E6's built-in kickstand, that permit a much wider range of tilt angles. On the back of the monitor, below a large, silver AOC logo, are two holes for a 75mm VESA mount (bracket not included). At the bottom of the panel's left-hand edge are four buttons for controlling the monitor's on-screen display (OSD), along with a 3.5mm audio jack. I prefer a mini-joystick controller, such as the one found on the ViewSonic VG1655, but at the 16T20's price, I don't expect to find one. The 16T20 does have a pair of 1-watt speakers built in, but their output is unimpressive, hampered by rather tinny sound. On the right edge of the monitor are two USB-C ports, one for data and one for power, and one mini HDMI port. You may be able to use a single USB-C cable for both power and data; that worked fine in my testing with several laptops. The AOC includes one USB-C cable, but the 16T20 lacks a mini-HDMI-to-HDMI cable. Although I wouldn't call mini HDMI rare, it is atypical (except among portable monitors), so you may not have such a cable kicking around. Online retailers offer a number of them, starting at under $10, but one should have been included in the box. We tested brightness, contrast, and color coverage using a Klein K10-A colorimeter and Portrait Displays' CalMAN Ultimate 2026 software. AOC rates the 16T20's luminance at 250 nits (candelas per square meter); in our testing, it came up somewhat short, at 212 nits. The 16T20's advertised contrast ratio is 800:1; we measured it at a healthy 955:1. Most competitors have rated contrast ratios between 600:1 and 1,000:1. Lower-end IPS portable monitors generally have limited color coverage, and the 16T20 is no exception. We measured the 16T20's coverage of the sRGB color space, which is the universal color standard for websites and web-based art, at 50.7%. The panel's sRGB profile, as shown in the chromaticity (color quality and coverage) chart below, showed a pattern similar to many other sub-$200 portable monitors we have reviewed. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. In my ad hoc experiential testing of the 16T20, which includes viewing images from our photo test suite as well as selected video clips, I concluded that its image quality is typical of budget portable monitors. It will be usable for viewing web pages and office documents, as well as for casual viewing of photos and short videos. I noticed slight muting of the red tones, relative to other colors, in some of our images. (That's not uncommon with this sort of panel.) In general, the colors didn't really pop, partly due to the panel's relatively low brightness. So, although the 16T20 is not great for entertainment or photo work, it should be fine for general-purpose personal and business use. Final Thoughts AOC 16T20 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Listed at $69.99 and usually retailing for even less—at this writing, major online retailers are selling it for $49.99—the AOC 16T20 is one of the lowest-priced portable monitors we have encountered. It's a tempting choice for cash-strapped students and occasional business travel, but as you would expect from a display at its price, it comes with some trade-offs. Its feature set is basic; it uses a button-driven OSD; and its origami-style folding stand limits you to two tilt angles. Its screen is, in most ways, typical of budget monitors, with limited sRGB color coverage and modest brightness. And although it has both USB-C and mini HDMI ports, it doesn't include a mini HDMI-to-HDMI cable, which you probably don't have and will need to buy if you want to use that connection. Among under-$100 portable monitors, the 16T20 sells for about $10 less than the AOC 16T30. They are largely the same, except that the 16T30 replaces the 16T20's origami-style stand with a built-in kickstand, giving users much more flexibility in tilt angles, and it has slightly higher rated brightness and contrast. Listing at $95 but often retailing for less ($74, as of this writing), the Editors' Choice-winning MSI Pro MP165 E6 has a tilt-adjustable kickstand and a full-size HDMI port (with an included cable to match), but what really puts it over the top is its screen's brightness, well in excess of its rated luminance and more than twice as bright as the 16T20's panel. The MP165 E6 is our preferred sub-$100 monitor, but the AOC 16T20 will do in a pinch, especially if you're on a very tight budget. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: How Did AI Send 1M Scams in 3 Days? 7 Brutal Security Stories Making Headlines This Week
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.90
There are two rules when it comes to cybersecurity news. First, there’s always something to talk about. Second, those things are often so irritating that you just want to go back to bed. Take this week, for example, when we reported on three different campaigns that compromised legitimate, trusted names to spread malware. Perhaps the biggest was that an HBO Max Reddit account was hijacked and began directing users to an app that was actually infostealer malware in disguise. Hot on the heels of that attack were the Iranian-affiliated hackers who used known security brands like Norton and KeePass to trick users into installing spyware. In this case, you may not need to worry about it as much, since the campaign is designed to target political dissidents, journalists, and activists opposed to the Iranian government. Even so, targeted malware attacks usually don’t stay targeted for long. For example, cybersecurity company Kaspersky published a warning this week that iTorrents.org, a public torrent repository, had been hijacked and was instead spreading malware, including a malware-laden version of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey that we mentioned a few weeks ago. As of right now, the site remains compromised. It’s not all bad news, though. I love sharing security-related wins when we find them, and this week we reported on law enforcement taking down one of the web’s most long-running DDoS sites. The site, NightmareStresser, posed as a legitimate tool that allowed users to stress test websites for reliability, but of course, for a modest fee, you could stress test hard enough to disrupt a site that didn’t belong to you, and that was the primary business model. Similarly, this week Bastille Networks, a security startup specializing in wireless intrusion detection, announced it had developed tools to detect nearby smart glasses, specifically for businesses and government agencies that want to keep them out of sensitive areas. Considering the reputation that pervert glasses have, we can only hope the tech becomes available to consumers soon, too. Now then, let’s take a look at what else is going on in the infosec world this week. Threat Actor Uses AI to Generate 1M Personalized Fraud Emails in 3 Days When we talk about how AI is a hacker’s favorite tool and how it supercharges malware campaigns, this is what we mean. Dark Reading reports that researchers at Microsoft tracked a phishing campaign in which an unknown threat actor sent over 1 million highly personalized phishing emails in less than three days, targeting payroll and accounts payable departments at companies worldwide with fake ServiceNow invoices and demanding payment for overdue bills. Even worse, because the threat actor used AI to draft the emails, they were often personalized with the actual names and roles of the target employees at the impacted companies, along with information about each company’s management. The emails even looked like they were part of a threaded conversation with other company representatives, making the email look like it was originally addressed to a company leader, who then directed the scammer to contact accounting to have the bill paid. Attacks like this play on the human element of security, creating a false sense of urgency and authority to encourage overworked, stressed-out employees to just do what the email asks rather than stop to verify its claims. It’s certainly creative, if not scary, and AI is making it easy for scammers to scale up such spear-phishing campaigns. Copyright Scammers Get Instagram Accounts Suspended and Demand Payment This isn’t so much a strict security story as it is a warning for anyone with an Instagram account they’d actually like to hold on to, and another example of social media platforms’ lax policy enforcement and overreliance on automated tools for reporting and moderation. Both the BBC and the Malwarebytes blog shared an alarming story about copyright scammers on Instagram weaponizing the platform’s automated reporting tools and “suspend first, verify later” approach to moderation by filing repeated false copyright strikes against accounts, getting them suspended, and then demanding payment via cryptocurrency to have the complaints withdrawn so the owner can get their accounts back. As with any ransom-style attack, there’s no guarantee that paying the ransom will actually get the attacker to withdraw the complaint, and even if they do, there’s no guarantee that Meta, the parent company of Instagram (and Facebook and WhatsApp), will restore the account. Malwarebytes reported that similar attacks have been occurring since 2023, and the platform hasn’t found a way to handle them. Meta says it restored the accounts the BBC reported, but let’s be honest: It shouldn’t take a media campaign to get a platform to listen to its users and to fight people who use its own tools to scam others. EFF: Privacy Considerations With AI Tools We’ve discussed before that AI and privacy don’t really go hand in hand, and we've even tested the most popular chatbots ourselves to see which ones store the most personal data. Since they’re so widely used, we also have tips to limit what ChatGPT and what Google Gemini know about you. But the folks over at the Electronic Frontier Foundation published a broad guide to AI privacy last month that dives much deeper, going into the differences between cloud-based AI and on-device AI, and reminding people that “do not train using my data” is not the same thing as “do not access my data and use it for other things,” which is easy to overlook. Opting out of one method of data handling doesn’t mean you’re successfully keeping your data private, unfortunately. The EFF guide also has specific links to disable AI training for individual tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and others. Additionally, it reminds people to consider how these services would handle law enforcement requests and if that should matter in your use case. Whether you’re an AI skeptic or a regular user, it’s worth bookmarking, if only as a reminder of how these platforms handle your data, from your prompts and queries to everything else they’re capable of collecting about you just based on your usage habits. Ask Our Expert: If Your Phone Is Stolen, Are Your Passkeys at Risk? Do you have a question about online privacy or security? I'm here to help! You can submit your question here, and I may answer it in an upcoming SecurityWatch column and newsletter. If you're not subscribed to the newsletter, head here to sign up, and check back each week for the latest updates from PCMag's security team. Now, on to this week's question! Sam F asks: “Can using passkeys on a phone be at risk if your unlocked phone is snatched out of your hand?” Hi Sam! Thanks for your question. If you’ve been nagged by pop-ups every time you log in to Amazon, PayPal, or even your bank lately to create a passkey for the site and stop using passwords (usually the messages say “sign in faster next time!”), you’re not alone. On the one hand, passkeys do make signing in to websites and services faster: They create a unique key pair, with the public key on the website to identify you and the private key on your device to verify that it’s really you logging in to your account. The downside is that while you don’t have to remember a passkey (and you can store them in a password manager), they’re susceptible to other kinds of attacks, like cookie hijacking and session stealing. To get to your question, though, if someone snatches your phone out of your hand and it’s unlocked, yes, whoever has your phone probably has your passkeys as well and can use them, assuming you don’t have your password manager or whatever tool you use to store the passkeys set to ask you to authenticate every time you use one. For example, I use Proton Pass for all of my passwords, and before I can log in to an app or website, I have to authenticate to unlock my vault. Still, just like my vault’s master password and those passkeys, it’s not like the burglar can use them after I’ve changed them or taken steps to disable them. A thief who runs off with my phone may have access to some open sessions before the phone locks itself (or before I lock and wipe it remotely, which you should do as soon as possible if your phone gets stolen). But when someone has physical access to your unlocked device, all bets are off, really. That’s not the fault of passkeys any more than it’s the fault of saved passwords or any other security measure that relies on your device to work. So don’t think of it as a limitation of passkeys—just remember that there’s a reason security experts admit there’s only so much you can do if someone has physical control of your device. About Our Expert I've been writing and editing stories for almost two decades that help people use technology and productivity techniques to work better, live better, and protect their privacy and personal data. As managing editor of PCMag's security team, it's my responsibility to ensure that our product advice is evidence-based, lab-tested, and serves our readers. I've been a technology journalist for close to 20 years, and I got my start freelancing here at PCMag before beginning a career that would lead me to become editor-in-chief of Lifehacker, a senior editor at The New York Times, and director of special projects at WIRED. I'm back at PCMag to lead our security team and renew my commitment to service journalism. I'm the author of Seen, Heard, and Paid: The New Work Rules for the Marginalized, a career and productivity book to help people of marginalized groups succeed in the workplace.

item.title: How to Stop AI Hacking? Some Companies Say the Answer Is More AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.58
With all the talk of automated AI hacking and alignment fears reaching a new level, a number of companies have proposed solutions to some of the booming technologies' biggest issues. Unsurprisingly, it's to add more AI to the loop, as TechCrunch reports. A number of startups are using AI defenses to address rogue agents. Apollo Research introduced its Watcher AI, which monitors a coding agent's work to ensure the tasks it's performing aren't malicious, that it avoids leaking any data, and that it doesn't delete anything important without explicit permission. Apollo's Watcher system then layers AI monitors. The first gives everything a quick pass, and if it spots any concerning behavior, it flags it and escalates it to a more capable monitor that can analyze it further. Only after that step does a human enter the loop to officially approve or reject the suggested actions. Meanwhile, rival company Goodfire offers another solution that examines an AI's internal activations rather than its output to detect whether it's engaged in nefarious activity. Following the Hugging Face attack, the CEO of Goodfire took to X to highlight how his company was doubling down on interpreting AI via the reasoning summary. He noted that it was specifically targeting improvements in AI safety in key areas, such as cybersecurity and bioengineering. Reasoning paths and summaries are techniques some AI developers have used in distillation attacks, in which a model maker trains their technology on another model's outputs. However, to counter such attacks, some AI developers are now making the reasoning summary less legible, making it harder to extract its true meaning. Not everyone believes AI is the solution to these problems. Other non-AI systems include more robust logs of agentic activities, which can then be interpreted using more traditional, non-AI tools, much as cybersecurity professionals have done for years. While security monitoring with AI might be easier, perhaps looping in some more traditional safety systems might be the smarter plan than relying on unproven automation. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 vs. Ultra 3: How Much 'Ultra' Do You Actually Get for $799?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.36
Table of Contents Apple didn't change the design of the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but what’s under the hood is a whole different story. Thanks to a new S11 chip, upgraded heart sensors, and impressive 74-hour battery life, the newest Ultra makes a serious case for your wrist. But with the Ultra 3 holding its ground, is it actually worth making the jump? If you're deciding between buying new or keeping your current watch, here's everything that actually changed. Full Specs | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | Apple Watch Ultra 3 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S10 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.9 inches | 1.9 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer, Pulse Oximeter | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 74 hours (tested) | 63 hours (tested) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: Still Starts at $799 No changes here. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in one size (49mm), one casing material (titanium), and one wireless configuration (GPS and cellular) for $799, the same as the Ultra 3. That's for the Ultra 4 with an Alpine Loop, Trail Loop, or Ocean Band. If you want to be fancy, you can get the Ultra 4 with a Titanium Milanese Loop for $899, or spend anywhere from $1,499 to $3,149 for an Apple Watch Hermès Ultra 4, with an Hermès band and exclusive Hermès watch faces. Winner: Tie Design: Identical Look and Feel The Ultra 4 is nearly identical to its predecessor, with the exact same shape and measurements for its titanium body, and the same choice of natural titanium or black finishes. It's 1.5 grams heavier than the Ultra 3, but I implore you to notice the difference of a twentieth of an ounce on your wrist. In other words, they look and feel like the same watch. Winner: Tie Health and Fitness: Smarter Sensors and Readiness Scores Apple introduces its new S11 chip as the brains of the Ultra 4 and the Series 12, adding new AI and health features that the S10-equipped Ultra 3 lacks. For fitness, the Ultra 4 introduces a new holistic readiness score that assesses your overall state on a scale of 0 to 10 and offers a recommendation on how hard you should push yourself. An upcoming redesign of the iPhone Health app will have a Longevity tab for evaluating your Health Age, and tests to measure your balance, flexibility, and strength. The app will also let you incorporate new lab data from Quest Diagnostics for $119. Aside from the readiness score, the new app-based features will likely work on the Ultra 3 as well. In addition, Apple says that the S11 gives the Ultra 4 the most accurate step tracking of any smartwatch, with machine-learning algorithms that enable more precise distance measurements. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is also better at monitoring your heart rate thanks to upgraded optical and electrical heart sensors. Like the Series 12, the Ultra 4 can measure your heart rate every five seconds and checks heart rate variability (HRV) 24 times more often than the previous generations. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 AI Features: Audio Intelligence and Always-On Processing The S11 adds some new AI tricks to the Ultra 4 beyond holistic health tracking. It enables an upcoming Audio Intelligence feature, which lets the Ultra 4 and Series 12 listen throughout your day to provide AI summaries and guidance. It can recognize sounds and alert you to alarms and doorbells if you're hard of hearing, give you a Live Rewind text summary of the last 15 seconds of your conversation, and provide full recaps of those conversations after the fact. Apple claims that Audio Intelligence has several privacy measures to protect your data, including a dedicated hardware compartment on the S11 that processes audio internally. Apple also says it doesn't identify or attribute speakers in conversations and cuts out sensitive personal information. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Durability: Equally Equipped for Adventure No surprises here. The Ultra 3 is already a practically bulletproof smartwatch with a titanium body and a sapphire crystal display, tested to MIL-STD-810H standards. It comes with an IP6X dustproof rating, EN13319 diving certification, and depth capability up to 131 feet, and general water resistance up to 328 feet. The Ultra 4 offers all of those assurances, too. Winner: Tie Connectivity: Equal Signal Strength Everywhere This is another area where the Ultra 4 and Ultra 3 are equally well-equipped. Whichever generation you pick, you get dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, 5G, and LTE cellular connectivity, satellite connectivity, and precision L1/L5 dual-frequency GPS. Both watches also have Apple's ultra-wideband chip for precisely locating your phone nearby. Winner: Tie Battery Life: A Weekend-Ready Endurance Bump Apple is usually conservative in its battery life estimates; it claims the Ultra 3 can last up to 42 hours, but in our tests, it lasted 63 hours with the always-on display enabled. The Ultra 4 has an estimated battery life of up to 50 hours, and it similarly exceeded Apple's estimate, running for 74 hours before needing a charge. It hit that number without any kind of help from a power-saving mode, so you can safely take the Ultra 4 on a weekend trip and leave your charger behind. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 And The Winner Is... Apple Watch Ultra 4 The Apple Watch Ultra 4 delivers substantial under-the-hood upgrades without raising the price, making it a strong value for serious athletes and outdoor adventurers. If you already own an Ultra 3, you can safely hold off unless you crave every extra hour of battery life or cutting-edge health tracking. Otherwise, the Ultra 4 is the clear, undisputed champion.

item.title: September's Best Laptops Deals From Apple, Dell, Lenovo, and More Will Save You Hundreds

If you've spent any time laptop shopping recently, you must have realized that prices are out of control. Skyrocketing demand for RAM has made prebuilt PCs more and more expensive, but we're here to help. The PCMag Deals team spends every day finding you the best offers on all kinds of tech, comparing specifications, real-world use cases, and historical prices to ensure that the laptop we recommend is worth every penny you pay for it. Below you'll see ten portable PCs that have been extensively tested and vetted by our experts using rigorous benchmarks, with detailed reviews that explain why each one is worth your time and money. I update this rundown regularly, so check back if you don't see the perfect machine for you right now. We've found the best laptops from all the major brands. These machines have clear screens, long battery life, and high-speed connectivity. Check out the latest discounts on laptops. If you're not as concerned about portability, check our list of the best desktop deals we've found for the month. Best Budget Laptop Deals These budget laptops cost less than $1,000 and can easily handle daily tasks. We focused on capable PCs that will last a while, avoiding underpowered e-waste. Our top budget laptop picks are a low-cost Dell with a good-sized screen and an affordable Lenovo that we've reviewed positively. If money's tight and you need an ultra-budget option, we'd recommend this Lenovo portable, which is currently on sale for $137 off at Best Buy, the lowest price we've seen all year. This is a great choice for students, as it has a fairly large 15-inch FHD display and a full-size keyboard for comfortable typing. Under the hood, you get a capable and price-conscious Intel Core i3 processor, coupled with 8GB of RAM. In our review, we were impressed by the light weight and good value for the money, although the 128GB of internal UFS storage is pretty skimpy. Use that money you'll save for an external flash drive. Best Buy has a super-deep discount on this Dell portable that makes it absolutely dominate the budget category. You'll have a hard time finding a laptop with a full 2K resolution touchscreen at this price, and it maintains a sleek, lightweight design despite the solid component loadout. While it's not suited for resource-intensive gaming or creative work, it'll more than handle daily productivity tasks, Web surfing, and video streaming without breaking a sweat. Also of note is its solid battery life, with Express Charge support letting you top it off quickly when it starts to run down. We wouldn't expect this machine to last long at this price, so if it fits your needs, snatch it up. Acer also makes reliable budget machines, and the Aspire Go 15 is a really solid unit at a nice price. You can read our extensive review to hear how it performs, but in short: even with less than cutting-edge components, it still knocked it out of the park in our productivity benchmarking, and the all-plastic build feels relatively sturdy. The FHD screen is decently sized, with Acer's BlueLight Shield eye protection for long periods of use. Best Gaming Laptop Deals If you want to play your favorite PC games on the go, you need to invest in a machine with a dedicated GPU and pumped-up cooling. One of the best deals out there on a versatile 2-in-1 comes with the OmniBook Flip, HP's midrange performer that checks off all the boxes we want. Under the hood, the silicon loadout is solid for the price, with a 2026 AMD Ryzen AI 5 processor delivering speedy performance on most programs, and battery life was acceptable, coming in at just under 10 hours on a single charge. This discount drops it down to budget-laptop levels, and it's a far better machine than that would indicate. For a portable that's off the beaten path, this $200 discount on the Zenbook Duo deserves your attention. Your eyes don't deceive you: this is a laptop with a pair of screens for expanded vertical working area, multitasking, and more, with a detachable keyboard to give you even more flexibility. In our review, it easily earned an Editors' Choice award, with PCMag expert Matthew Buzzi gushing that the unit was "a brilliantly executed two-screen convertible laptop with little compromise, gorgeous OLED displays, fast performance, and ultra-long battery life to enhance your productivity." A solid component loadout, including an "Intel Panther Lake" processor and a generous 32GB of RAM, made it dominate our benchmarking tests, and dual batteries let it run all day without a charge. Laptop prices will range based on features. Basic but full-featured models can cost as little as $500, while gaming juggernauts can run you over $2,000. The most important factors to remember are the components and specs you need most, as the price range will determine what you’re getting—and what you’re sacrificing. For example, a low-budget laptop will have less storage space and RAM than a higher-priced laptop. It will be suitable for casual use, but only if you're not multitasking or running CPU-demanding programs. What’s the Best Low-Priced Laptop? The 2025 Asus Chromebook Plus CX14 was named the best extreme budget Chromebook overall and comes in at $329.99. What we loved, other than the price tag is this model's, "decent productivity performance, satisfactory battery life, and well-chosen port selection." What Is the Best Laptop Under $800? You can get a lot of computing power nowadays for under $800. PCMag’s current top-rated budget laptop is the brand-new-to-market Apple MacBook Neo, which according to our experts, "rewrites the budget laptop playbook." We're talking a higher-end build, a more advanced screen, longer battery life, and faster speeds that similar models in this range. Which Laptop Is the Best (So Far) in 2026? Laptops come in many flavors. Do you need a gaming PC? A portable, convertible 2-in-1? Maybe you’re a macOS fan. We have top-rated laptops in each category, but some of our top-rated overall laptops include the HP OmniBook 5 14 (Snapdragon), the Apple MacBook Air 13-Inch (2026, M5), and the MSI Raider 18 HX AI for gaming. How Long Should My Laptop Last? A computer can last a few years if you treat it well. This means using malware protection when browsing the web, using a dedicated surge protector to protect your hardware from electrical damage, managing battery health, and more. You can find longevity-boosting tips for your laptop at the link, too. If you have battery life in mind, that generally varies based on usage. Laptops with 4K displays running demanding games that test the limits of your GPU will naturally drain more quickly than a laptop just used to surf the web, all else being equal. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. After starting my career at PCMag as an intern more than a decade ago, I’m back as one of its editors, focused on managing laptops, desktops, and components coverage. With 15 years of experience, I have been on staff and published in technology review publications, including PCMag (of course!), Laptop Magazine, Tom’s Guide, TechRadar, and IGN. Along the way, I’ve tested and reviewed hundreds of laptops and helped develop testing protocols. I have expertise in testing all forms of laptops and desktops using the latest tools. I’m also well-versed in video game hardware and software coverage. When she isn't perusing online stores for deals, Jade enjoys playing video games (mostly JRPGs and roguelikes), sorting board game components neatly into containers, and building Gundam models. Her love of electronics has persisted through her youth and has resulted in a collection of gaming peripherals including keyboards and controllers, scale figures, and art work. Jade lives in blissful harmony with her wife, cat, and two chinchillas—as well as a host of houseplants.

item.title: MSI Pro MP165 E6 Review: The Sub-$100 Portable Monitor to Beat
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.13
The MSI Pro MP165 E6 ($94.99), a 15.6-inch portable monitor, sells at a budget price and offers both USB Type-C and HDMI connectivity—indeed, it is one of the few portable monitors we have seen that integrates a full-size HDMI port. The MP165 E6 is small and lightweight, and comes with a carry bag made of stiff fabric. It has a built-in, tilt-adjustable kickstand that integrates a tripod socket, and its IPS screen offers good contrast and brightness. My extensive testing suggests that it is best for workaday tasks, rather than photo editing or movie watching. Still, it offers a lot for its price, and earns our Editors' Choice award as the best portable monitor for people on the tightest of budgets. The MP165 E6 has typical specs for a sub-$100 portable monitor, sporting a 15.6-inch full HD (1,920-by-1,080-pixel) in-plane switching (IPS) screen, which is aided by a matte, antiglare coating. The screen has a 16:9 aspect ratio, making it best for use with widescreen laptops. The panel is housed in a matte-black frame. On the monitor's left-hand edge are the ports: two USB-C and one HDMI. This is one of the few full-size HDMI ports I have seen on a portable monitor—many instead have mini HDMI ports, which are easier to fit in a thin frame. MSI includes both a USB-C cable and an HDMI cable in the box. You can connect the MP165 E6 to a power adapter via one of the USB-C ports, but in testing, it worked fine when it was bus-powered, drawing power solely from my laptop over the same USB-C connection it uses to transfer data via the DisplayPort Over USB Alternate Mode's protocol. On the right edge of the MP165 E6 are the power button, a three-way rocker switch for the on-screen display (OSD), and a 3.5mm headphone jack. The rocker works in tandem with the power button to let you navigate the OSD, though I found the controls awkward to manipulate. I would have preferred a mini-joystick controller, such as the one found on the Editors' Choice-winning ViewSonic VG1655. The MP165 E6 has dual built-in 1-watt speakers that are reasonably loud but of mediocre sound quality, which is about what we expect at this price. The MP165 E6 has a narrow built-in kickstand, which gives you fine control over the monitor's tilt angle. The stand also has a 0.25-inch threaded hole to fit a tripod. You'll also find holes in the back to support a 75mm VESA mount (bracket not included). We did our color and brightness testing using a Klein K10-A colorimeter and Portrait Displays' CalMAN Ultimate 2026 software. MSI rates the MP165 E6's peak luminance at 250 nits (candelas per square meter); in our testing, it was considerably brighter, tallying 335 nits. This should be fine for use in rooms with substantial ambient light, especially since the screen has an anti-glare matte finish. The MP165 E6's advertised contrast ratio is 1,000:1; we measured it at a slightly better 1,142:1. Sub-$100 portable monitors generally have rated contrast ratios ranging between 600:1 and 1,000:1, so this is good. As is the case with most sub-$200 IPS portable monitors, the MP165 E6 has limited color coverage. We measured its coverage of the sRGB color space, which is the universal color standard for websites and web-based art, at 51.7%. The panel's sRGB profile, as shown in the chromaticity (color quality and coverage) chart below, showed a pattern similar to many other budget portable monitor panels we have reviewed. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. In my ad hoc experiential testing, in which I view images from our photo test suite and some selected video clips, I concluded that the MP165 E6's color coverage is typical of a low-priced portable display. The overall impression? It's suitable for viewing web pages and office documents, as well as casual viewing of photos and short videos. I noticed that the red tones in some of our test images appeared a bit muted, which we frequently see with budget portable monitors. On the plus side are its high brightness and solid contrast. Final Thoughts MSI Pro MP165 E6 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. As a sub-$100 portable monitor, the MSI Pro MP165 E6 includes a basic feature set plus a couple of surprises: a full-size HDMI port and brightness well in excess of MSI's rating. Plus, its kickstand gives precise control over the panel's tilt angle. It's considerably brighter than the bargain-basement AOC 16T20, has a more functional stand, and includes all necessary cables. It's the best we've reviewed in its price range, and earns our Editors' Choice nod for budget portable monitors. For between $150 and $500, you could get a portable monitor with features such as a hinged stand, high refresh rate, stunning color coverage, a touch screen, a built-in battery, and even an OLED panel. But with the MP165 E6, you can both save cash and get a capable monitor. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: Apple iPhone 13 vs. iPhone 18: How Performance and Features Have Changed in 5 Years
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.10
Table of Contents Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max deliver more power, take better photos, and last longer than ever. They also push your aging iPhone another rung down the ladder. The iPhone 13, released in 2021, remains the most widely used iPhone worldwide in 2026. That got me wondering: What exactly are iPhone 13 owners missing out on? Has Apple introduced enough meaningful upgrades to trigger serious FOMO, or are the changes unimportant to the average person? To figure this out, I did a deep dive into what five years of iPhone upgrades really get you. One caveat: The iPhone 13 is an entry-level model, while Apple only unveiled Pro models this year, so this isn’t exactly your typical apples-to-apples spec comparison. That aside, let's look at how much the iPhone has evolved over the past five years—and what you're sacrificing by holding on to your iPhone 13. Full Specs | Apple iPhone 18 Pro | Apple iPhone 13 | | |---|---|---| | Operating System | | | | Operating System | iOS 27 | iOS 15 | | CPU | | | | CPU | Apple A20 Pro | Apple A15 | | Dimensions | | | | Dimensions | 5.91 by 2.83 by 0.34 inches | 5.78 by 2.82 by .3 inches | | Screen Size | | | | Screen Size | 6.3 inches | 6.1 inches | | Screen Resolution | | | | Screen Resolution | 2622 by 1206 pixels | 2,532 by 1,170 pixels | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | | | | Camera Resolution (Rear; Front-Facing) | 48MP, 48MP, 48MP, 25MP | 12MP, 12MP; 12MP | | Battery Life (As Tested) | | | | Battery Life (As Tested) | TBD | 15 hours | Design: 5 Years Later, It Still Holds Up Slap a case on it, and the iPhone 13 still looks and feels like it could be from 2026. Similar to the new iPhone 18 series, it’s got that iconic, squared-off silhouette, MagSafe support, and IP68 water-resistance rating. The iPhone 13 has an aluminum frame with a glass back, while the iPhone 18 Pro models feature an aluminum unibody design. The iPhone 13 has a 6.1-inch screen compared with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s larger 6.3- and 6.9-inch displays, respectively. All three phones use Apple's Ceramic Shield, though the latest iPhones step it up to Ceramic Shield 2. But the biggest changes start to show up once you turn the screen on. As a phone tester for six years, I vividly remember Apple boasting about the iPhone 13's "20% notch reduction" and feeling duped when I saw it for myself. It was narrower side to side but taller, meaning it dipped farther into the display. I wasn't a fan, so I'm relieved that we've moved on to the Dynamic Island, which debuted on the iPhone 14 Pro models. Designed to capture live, motion-rich information at a glance, the Dynamic Island is now smaller than ever on the iPhone 18 Pros (25% shorter than the 17 Pros). It still keeps you informed about what's going on in the background, whether you're navigating with Apple Maps, tracking your Uber driver's ETA, or keeping an eye on your Spotify playlist—it just stays more out of your way. What's nice is that it now supports up to three live activities, instead of just two. No, Dynamic Island isn't a must-have feature, but it’s a nice-to-have convenience. Is it going to change your life? Probably not. It’s definitely not a reason to ditch your iPhone 13, but having useful, glanceable information floating at the top of your screen is more useful than staring at an intrusive black box. You can also stick this one on the "not upgrade worthy" list, but Apple has been shaving down the bezels over the past five years. For example, when the iPhone 16 Pro models launched, Apple boasted that they featured the thinnest borders of any Apple product, a claim it later made again with the iPhone 17 and iPhone 17 Air. The iPhone 18 series continues to sport an ultra-slim display frame, allowing for more screen real estate. However, if you prefer more bezel space to rest your thumbs, this may not matter much to you. Apple's stubborn insistence on keeping base iPhones at 60Hz while budget Android phones offer zippier refresh rates has always baffled me. After the iPhone 13 series launched, it took Apple four product generations to finally expand ProMotion to its base models. The iPhone 17 lineup was the first to feature a 120Hz variable refresh rate at a lower price. If 60Hz is all you’ve ever known, you probably won’t miss what you’ve never seen. Speaking from experience, higher refresh rates make scrolling smoother, animations more fluid, and the entire phone feel snappier. The screens are also brighter than ever. Cameras: The Biggest Hardware Gap Between Generations Sorry, but your iPhone 13's camera is aging fast. The entire iPhone 13 lineup, including the Pro models, has a lower-res 12MP main camera. That's not even close to the phones of 2026. The iPhone 18 models feature Apple's best camera system to date. Their 48MP main cameras now have a showstopping variable aperture feature, which means the lens can adjust its light-gathering capabilities based on the shooting conditions. For example, in low light, it's supposed to soak up as much light as possible. However, in bright sunlight, photos should show reduced glare and blown-out highlights if the aperture is stopped down. The iPhone 13’s 12MP selfie camera is pretty dated, too. You're missing out on the higher-res 18MP front-facing camera for sharper, more detailed pictures. Moreover, the latest iPhones have a square selfie camera sensor that lets you take portrait or landscape selfies without rotating the phone. The iPhone 13 has a 12MP ultrawide camera, and while it's solid, it cannot tackle macro work. The latest iPhones can focus on ultra-close objects using the 48MP ultrawide lens. Further, the iPhone 13 lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, so you're missing the iPhone 18 Pro's ability to get 8x closer to distant subjects without relying on digital cropping. If you're a content creator, you're limiting yourself. The iPhone 13 lacks features such as Action Mode and 4K Cinematic Mode, and it also lacks support for ProRAW and ProRes, which are needed for advanced video editing. New to the iPhone 18 Pro models, you’re also missing smart-focus tracking, an AI feature that locks onto moving subjects, and Pro Controls, which lets you customize the camera app for quicker access to your most-used settings. Serious video shooters are missing out big time. Ports: Ditching Lightning for Universal USB-C Convenience Perhaps the most convincing case for upgrading comes down to ports. The iPhone 13 is locked to Apple’s proprietary Lightning ecosystem. USB-C is now the global standard, so holding onto a Lightning port is self-sabotage. If you ever need to borrow a charger these days, you'll likely be handed a USB-C cable, not a Lightning cable, leaving you high and dry. Plus, when traveling, you need to bring an extra cable just to accommodate your iPhone 13. Why do this to yourself when you can juice up all your devices with a single cord? You don’t need to purchase a $1,199 iPhone 18 Pro to ditch the Lightning port, but you should at least consider a refurbished or used model from the iPhone 15 series, the first lineup to make the leap to USB-C after Apple was forced to change course. Your iPhone 13 is missing the Action Button, a customizable shortcut key that replaced the age-old mute switch. Making its debut in the iPhone 15 lineup, the Action Button lets you assign quick shortcuts to your favorite features. For example, you can map it to trigger the flashlight, launch the camera app, record a voice memo, run custom Apple Shortcuts, and more. It's incredibly helpful. Your iPhone 13 also lacks the Camera Control feature that was introduced on the iPhone 16. This capacitive button gives you instant access to the camera to snap photos, capture video, or tweak settings such as exposure, depth of field, and zoom. Meanwhile, on your iPhone 13, you have to use the screen to execute these actions. Although I find the Action Button useful for firing up Shazam when I hear an unfamiliar song, I still haven’t gotten used to Camera Control beyond launching the Camera app. For actions like zooming, I find the on-screen controls easier and more intuitive. iPhone 13 owners narrowly escaped Apple’s SIM tray purge. When Apple launched the iPhone 14 lineup, it killed off the physical SIM slot on US iPhones, leaving eSIM as the only option. As a frequent traveler, I miss the old-school approach. I’d buy a SIM abroad, pop it into my phone, and be on my way with a local number and cell service. Setting up an eSIM without solid Wi-Fi is a nightmare. Trust me; I know from experience. The iPhone 13 supports both eSIM and physical SIM. If you're in the US, the latest iPhones remain eSIM-only. Processor and Software Features: A20 Pro Speed Gains and Apple Intelligence Support The iPhone 13 launched during a much simpler time: The AI craze hadn't hit yet. The 13's A15 Bionic chip doesn't have to handle much beyond running apps and some photo and video processing. The iPhone 18 Pro models are running the most advanced version of Apple Intelligence (Apple's AI suite). The A20 Pro chip, engineered on a 2nm process, has more memory bandwidth to support Apple's ballooning AI ambitions, including the new-and-improved Siri. The A20 Pro chip has a dedicated vapor chamber to improve thermal performance under demanding workloads, giving it a leg up for AI. Even though it can run iOS 27, the iPhone 13 does not support Apple Intelligence, which may be a plus for users with AI fatigue. Day-to-day performance has also jumped. When we tested the iPhone 13 five years ago, it blew competitors away with Geekbench scores of 1,721 (single-core) and 4,629 (multi-core). The iPhone 18 Pro models are running 3x faster than that. Battery Life: You Gain 14 Hours and Fast 60W Charging The iPhone 13, packed with a 3,227mAh battery, ran for 19 hours in our battery tests; it barely lasts an entire day. Fast forward to 2026, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max ran for 34 hours and 31 minutes in testing. You're starving yourself of potentially 14 hours of extra battery life by holding on to the iPhone 13. That's a huge deal. Moreover, the iPhone 13 charges at a slow 20W rate. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max charges at 60W. It can reach a 50% charge in just 15 minutes, which we confirmed in testing. Whoa! You're missing out, iPhone 13 users. Verdict: Is It Finally Time to Trade in Your iPhone 13? Yes, it’s finally time to retire that iPhone 13. Upgrading to the iPhone 18 Pro gets you off the Lightning leash, gives you hours of extra battery life, and puts a vastly superior camera system in your pocket. Plus, you can get some good carrier incentives on a trade-in. If you don't want to drop $1,200 (or more) on the latest Pro model, you should at least aim for an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. This will unlock Apple Intelligence, USB-C, upgraded cameras, and the freedom to roam without a portable battery.

item.title: See ChatGPT, Claude, and Other AIs Handle the Same Prompt With a $55 Tool
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.00
TL;DR: ChatPlayground AI puts multiple AI models in one place, so you can compare their responses to the same prompt. A lifetime subscription is currently on sale for $54.97. Getting a useful AI answer often means checking it against another model. Instead of opening several different AI tools and copying the same prompt back and forth, ChatPlayground AI lets you run multiple models side by side and compare the results in one place. A lifetime subscription is currently $54.97 (MSRP $619). ChatPlayground AI sends any prompt to several models at once and lines up the responses in one window, so you can see how they differ and pick what works best. The platform supports more than 25 models, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek, Llama, and Perplexity. That means you can use the same workflow for chat, coding help, content drafts, or image ideas and compare model output without copying and pasting everywhere. You can tweak a prompt, run it again, and see how each model changes the answer. Prompt engineering tools help you refine and reuse effective prompts. ChatPlayground AI also lets you upload images and PDFs, then ask questions about them, so you can check how different models handle the same document or screenshot. Saved chat history keeps longer projects and useful prompts easy to revisit. The Unlimited Plan is a lifetime subscription with unlimited messages each month. It’s aimed at prompt engineers, startups, and teams that test or use AI heavily and need room to experiment. You can use it on any desktop that runs a recent version of Chrome, Edge, or Firefox, with no set limit on how many devices you sign in from. Until September 20, get a ChatPlayground AI lifetime subscription on sale for $54.97. Prices subject to change. PCMag editors select and review products independently.
