item.title: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11 Review: A Snapdragon Workhorse With Just a Little Sizzle
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.72
The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x won't blow you away, but it offers something hard to find right now: a decent everyday laptop with helpful features and potent enough silicon for less than $1,000 ($969.99 as tested). As you'd expect, it comes up short against the competition in some spots, such as underwhelming graphics capabilities and a lackluster design. The machine also packs a Snapdragon Arm processor, so you may encounter edge-case compatibility issues with x86-based apps. All told, the IdeaPad Slim 5x strikes a mostly successful balance between performance and affordability, while including some nifty upgrades that don't cost a fortune. Still, if you’re looking for a more premium design for a close or sometimes lower price, check out the HP OmniBook 5 14, our Editors' Choice pick for midrange ultraportable laptops. I tested the IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11's base configuration, which runs $969.99 and comes with an Arm-based six-core/six-thread Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus (X2P-42-100) processor with integrated Qualcomm Adreno (X2-45) graphics, 16GB of LPDDR5x memory, a 512GB solid-state drive, a 15.3-inch display, and a 54.7-watt-hour battery. The IPS panel has a native resolution of 1,920 by 1,200 pixels (1200p), and it supports up to 120Hz refresh and touch input. You can double the RAM for $300 more and boost the storage to 1TB for another $200, while an extra $30 will score you a 2,560-by-1,600-pixel 165Hz OLED display (without touch support)—a feature you should absolutely grab if given the choice. Same with the $10 upgrade that will boost the battery capacity to 70 watt-hours. Selecting all of these options brings you to $1,509.99, still relatively midrange but entering MacBook Air and Dell XPS territory. The IdeaPad Slim 5x isn’t designed for a premium market, so the build quality isn’t necessarily top-notch. I could tell in the seams of the build as I held it, and in the feel of the diving-board touchpad. First, the laptop measures 0.61 by 9.3 by 13.4 inches and weighs 3.28 pounds, so it’s less portable than a 14-inch device, even though the screen-space difference here isn’t all that significant. The hinges are fairly stiff, as well, so opening it up with one hand is a challenge, though the webcam lip on the lid helps. The only real embellishment you'll see on the outside of the laptop is a Lenovo logo. Likewise, Lenovo sells only one color, Cloud Grey, which is about as exciting as it sounds. The IdeaPad's IPS display simply can’t compete with an OLED panel, so, as I said before, definitely consider upgrading to the sharper and more colorful screen. It's only $30! The IPS comes limited to 1200p, and while the 120Hz refresh is welcome, it doesn’t have anywhere near the color vibrancy of OLED laptops you can find for about the same price (like this one). The larger footprint on the IdeaPad Slim 5x gives it room for two 2-watt Dolby Audio-certified up-firing speakers flanking the keyboard. They deliver some booming audio for a laptop in this price range. (Just don’t expect miracles in the bass department.) The IdeaPad Slim 5x serves up a spacious keyboard. Unlike some other laptops at this size, it doesn't come with a 10-key number pad, which might be a drawback for some. However, I prefer this setup since it allows for better top-firing speakers and more room for the main key layout. The keyboard provides deep enough travel and makes for comfortable typing over extended periods. The buttonless touchpad works well enough. It's wide and spacious, with minimal flex when left- and right-clicking. However, it might take some getting used to, since it isn’t quite centered below the keyboard, but on the space bar. For the webcam, Lenovo supplies a 1080p IR camera with a physical privacy shutter for extra security. It supports Windows Hello and can record video at 30 frames per second at 1080p. The image quality is surprisingly high, and for most users, it’ll be more than enough for video calls with friends and family, not to mention job interviews. Lenovo served up two 5Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, with one always-on connection for device power delivery, on the right side. The laptop's left side includes two 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C ports with up to 65-watt power delivery and DisplayPort 1.4 video output. Finally, Lenovo installed an HDMI 2.1 port and a 3.5mm audio/mic combo jack on the left side, along with a Micro SD card reader on the right. For connectivity, the laptop includes Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 hardware, giving the laptop an edge over a lot of last-generation devices. The laptop lacks a wired Ethernet port, but that's a rare one these days, anyway. To gauge the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x’s performance on specific tasks, such as content creation and common productivity apps, I’ve compared it with several competing ultralights to see how it measures up. These include the Apple MacBook Air 13-inch ($1,299 as tested, $1,499 for a 15-inch with the same specs), followed by our $1,419.99 Dell 14S review configuration. Next, we have our current Editors' Choice pick for best Windows laptop for most people, the $899.99 HP OmniBook 5 14, as well as the Intel "Wildcat Lake"-based Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i 15 (tested at $1,299, but down to just under $1,000 in places). Our first group of tests represents workloads such as content creation, office productivity, and raw CPU speeds. Our go-to overall productivity and storage test, PCMark 10, is not yet Snapdragon-compatible, so we focused on core-stressing tests and media tasks. The three primary tests presented below are CPU-centric or processor-intensive. Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the transcoding freeware HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Additionally, we have encountered issues with Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators Adobe Photoshop 25 test on systems with Qualcomm Arm processors, so we’ve skipped it here until we resolve the issues. In testing, the IdeaPad Slim 5x outperformed much of its competition in both multi-core and single-core performance, as measured in Cinebench 2024 and Geekbench 6.3. It couldn't keep up with the M5 MacBook Air, though, lagging well behind it across all tests. Considering the MacBook's steep pricing—and even more for the 15-inch version—the IdeaPad turned in respectable results for the price. All of this comes with one big caveat, though. The Snapdragon X2 Plus turned in generally fast processor performance when running native Arm apps, but that may not hold when running x86-based apps through Windows’ Prism emulation. Most Windows apps were originally developed for x86 microcode-based processors made by Intel and AMD, and this code can't run on an Arm-based processor like Qualcomm’s Snapdragon line. To get around this, Windows 11 uses an x86 emulation layer called Prism, which translates an app’s x86 code into Arm code in real time. This allows these apps to run on Arm chips, but this added layer introduces latency into the code that can affect an app’s performance, sometimes significantly. However, distinguishing between the Arm and x86 versions of an app can be challenging, leading to unforeseen performance hits. In Cinebench 2024, for example, running the x86 version of the app through emulation drastically reduces performance compared with running the Arm version, with up to 39% lower multi-core performance and up to 34% lower single-core performance. That’s not to say every x86 app will have that kind of performance loss, but it shows how significant this performance hit can be, so it’s essential to always make sure you are downloading the Arm version of an app wherever possible to see the best performance out of this laptop. We challenge all systems’ graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The IdeaPad 5x turned in fairly weak graphics performance, but not the worst on the list. It especially struggled with ray tracing, as you can see in 3DMark’s Solar Bay benchmark. So, if you're involved in computer gaming or advanced creative work, the MacBook Air 13-inch or 15-inch will be a much better choice. While we wouldn't directly compare the two, a similarly priced gaming laptop will perform much better for gaming, regardless. Specific game compatibility with Arm processors should also factor into your decision here if you're a gamer. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with display brightness at 50% and audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we also use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). On our endurance test, Qualcomm's well-documented Snapdragon X power efficiency came through once again, giving the IdeaPad 5x just shy of a full day’s worth of juice (23 hours and 56 minutes). That beat the latest MacBook Air 13-inch by several hours, but the Dell 14S took the crown here with an astounding 38 hours and 29 minutes. The Lenovo's IPS panel, though, was strictly middling. It features 100% sRGB color-gamut coverage, which is important for web and general app color coverage, and a shiny 424 nits of max brightness. However, its measurements of 78% for Adobe RGB and 79% for DCI-P3 color coverage—essential for photo editing and watching movies, respectively—can’t keep up with the competition. If you’re looking at buying this laptop, opt for the OLED panel. It’s well worth the extra $30, which still keeps the price just under $1,000. Final Thoughts Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Weak graphics performance, a lackluster design, and a ho-hum display are significant drawbacks for the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x Gen 11. However, the laptop’s upsides are hard to ignore, thanks to fast native Arm app performance (which covers most apps most people use every day), plentiful ports, and all-day battery life. For the price, this IdeaPad strikes an effective balance between performance and value, something that’s difficult to find in the laptop market right now. However, we've already found an even better-presented version of this package in the HP OmniBook 5 14, our Editors' Choice pick in the midrange laptop category. About Our Expert John (he/him) is a programmer, gamer, activist, and Brooklyn College alum currently living in Brooklyn, New York. Named by the CTA as a CES 2020 Media Trailblazer for his science and technology reporting, John specializes in all areas of computer science, including industry news, hardware reviews, and PC gaming. He's also well-versed in general science writing and the social impact of the tech industry. John has a Bachelor’s degree in English and a Master’s degree in Computer Science. You can usually find him on Bluesky, where you’ll get his hot takes on stuff, as well as his reposts of content that is almost as good as the worst stuff you used to be able to find on Vine. Beyond PC gaming, he spends his evenings building digital circuits, multiboxing Linux kernels, and coding shell scripts.

item.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Review: This Battery Beast Lasts Longer Than Ever
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.71
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 takes everything that makes the Series 12 great and houses it inside a 49mm titanium fortress built for extremes. While it keeps the rugged adventuring credentials of its predecessor, this generation packs a faster S11 chip for rapid Siri AI responses, an overhauled sensor suite for continuous heart-rate tracking, and an astounding 74-hour real-world battery life. The $399 Series 12 remains our Editors' Choice smartwatch for most iPhone users, but for outdoor adventurers and power users demanding ultimate endurance, the $799 Ultra 4 is in a class of its own. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a single 49mm titanium build in either a black or natural finish for $799. You can pick from several bands in a variety of materials and colors to round out the look. Like the Ultra 3, it looks and feels large. I tested the natural model with a Sand Trail Loop band. I’m a bigger guy, so it works well on my wrist, but not everyone will like the size. The Apple Watch Series 12 has more size and case options to fit a wider range of buyers. Measuring 49 by 44 by 12mm and weighing 2.22 ounces, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is slightly heavier than the Ultra 3, which has the same dimensions but weighs 2.17 ounces. The always-on Retina screen is the same as on the Ultra 3. It's an LTPO3 wide-angle OLED with a 1,245mm display area, a 422-by-514-pixel resolution, and a flat sapphire crystal cover for durability. It reaches up to 3,000 nits of brightness and can automatically adjust based on ambient light down to a single nit. The physical controls are the same as the last generation as well. The Ultra 4 has a physical crown that you can press to bring up your apps or to return home from another screen. The side button beneath the crown opens a control center with options for battery life and modes (such as airplane and do not disturb). A third, orange button on the other side of the case is a customizable Action button; I set mine to open the Exercise app. A great appeal of the Ultra line comes from its durability, and the Ultra 4 has the same credentials as its predecessor. It features an IP6X dustproof housing, WR100 water resistance down to 328 feet, and EN13319 certification for scuba diving up to 131 feet. Tested to MIL-STD-810H standards, it easily shrugs off extreme temperature swings, blowing sand, intense shock, and severe vibration. The Series 12 has the same dust rating, but is water resistant to a lesser depth of 164 feet, and isn’t suited for scuba diving, high-velocity water sports, or extreme environmental conditions. Samsung’s rugged watch, the $699.99 Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, has scuba and high-velocity water sport certifications, matching the Ultra 4. Inside, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 features the same new S11 silicon as the Series 12, with a faster CPU, GPU, and neural engine than the S10 in the Ultra 3. The 64-bit dual-core processor helps the Ultra 4 seamlessly move between apps and run advanced AI-powered tasks more efficiently. It maintains 64GB of storage and the same impressive connectivity as the previous generation, including 5G cellular support, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, ultra-wideband for precise device location tracking, and dual frequency GPS. When out of cellular range, it can use satellite communication to call for help or text your location. The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 uses LTE and lacks emergency satellite connectivity. Under the hood, familiar sensors like the depth gauge, compass, and water temperature sensor return, but the bottom of the watch tells a brand-new story. The Ultra 4 debuts a completely revamped heart rate tracking array. Also featured on the Series 12, this redesigned health sensor represents one of the most significant architectural upgrades in this generation of Apple Watches. The inner ring still has LEDs of multiple colors to shine against your skin, but the green ones are now larger and more power-efficient. The photodiodes surrounding the LEDs are more densely arranged to better capture heart rate data. Redesigned electrodes fill the outermost sensor ring and are more densely packed to increase skin contact and ECG accuracy. This new system allows the watch to take heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) readings with greater accuracy and frequency. The Ultra 4 measures your heart rate once every five seconds, up from once every five minutes on the Ultra 3, and it checks your HRV once every five minutes instead of once every two hours. As a result, the Heart Rate app now shows more detailed charts alongside your heart rate range, resting heart rate, and average heart rate while walking. It also displays your recovery HRV, a distinct type of HRV that monitors for stress and fatigue. Like previous Apple Watches, it tracks overall HRV to assess cardiovascular health and detect warning signs such as irregular rhythms. The Vitals app, which makes it easy to check your metrics for deviations, is now more robust, with HRV included in the overnight view and a new daytime view that can alert you to signs of illness during waking hours. The new health-sensing system also allows the Ultra 4 to provide a holistic readiness score that encapsulates your activity, overnight vitals, and sleep on a scale from 0 to 10. Readiness is meant to provide general guidance on how hard to push your training for the day, and Apple Intelligence includes a summary and advice alongside the score. Readiness takes about a week to establish a baseline. As you can see in the photo above, Apple gave me a 5 out of 10 with a status simply called "ready." It docked me for a rough night of sleep, but my vitals were still within my normal range, and lots of recent activity counted as a positive for the fitness subcategory. Devices with Fitbit software, including the $399 Google Pixel Watch 5, have long offered a holistic health metric called Readiness, while the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 has a similar Energy Score. Apple’s version updates throughout the day when it meaningfully changes, such as after a workout or a nap. The scores from Google and Samsung are static, but both companies offer a separate workout-specific metric that updates as you complete activities. The new chip and more efficient health-sensing system make a big difference in battery life for both the Ultra 4 and the Series 12. In real-world testing with the always-on display enabled, one tracked workout with GPS per day, and otherwise typical use, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lasted for 74 hours. Under similar conditions, the Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 lasted 69.5 hours and the Series 12 lasted 54.5 hours. Impressively, the Ultra 4 lasts long enough to leave the charger behind on a weekend trip. Keep in mind, it lasted 74 hours without any power-saving features turned on. Apple estimates it could last up to 84 hours in low-power mode. It recharges relatively quickly as well. In testing, it reached 100% after 94 minutes on the included charging puck and my own 18W power brick. The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 took 110 minutes to reach 100% under the same conditions, while the Series 12 took 55 minutes to reach 100%. The main feature of watchOS 27 is a more conversational and contextually aware generative assistant called Siri AI. The Siri AI app is available on any Apple Watch running watchOS 27, but it works extra quickly on the Ultra 4 and the Series 12 thanks to their new processor. You can chat with Siri AI by holding the crown, saying the “Hey Siri” wake words, or opening the Siri AI app. The AI can respond to general information questions, and proved helpful when I asked about events near me in Chicago for the coming weekend. When I asked follow-up questions about the listed festivals, it told me the headlining performers and schedule, and then provided directions from my place when I asked for them. In addition to general info, Siri AI can pull from personal context to answer questions and build on past responses. It can also search apps on the watch to quickly surface details such as flight information or your driver's license number from an email. You can even ask about your progress on your activity rings for the day. Past conversations can be found in the Siri AI app, though my conversation history isn't showing up on the watch app yet. Given that watchOS 27 just launched, I expect this bug to be fixed soon. When you press the crown, instead of the full app drawer, you now see a circle of suggested and recently used apps with Siri AI in the center. Tap the bottom icon on this screen, or rotate the crown, to open the full app drawer. watchOS 27 adds new widgets to the Smart Stack, including a Shazam music recognition widget that uses Apple's Audio Intelligence to automatically display the title of the song being played. You can now open Smart Stack widgets with an easier gesture, a single tap of your thumb and forefinger. The existing double-tap gesture is still active, but scrolls through widgets instead. The AI-powered Workout Buddy has also improved with watchOS 27. It still offers encouraging words and metrics updates during certain exercises, but now works without your phone if you have a cellular signal on your watch, and provides more detailed personal context. Cycle tracking gets an upgrade with watchOS 27 as well, adding support for perimenopause and menopause. As before, Apple’s wearable software offers a class-leading variety of first- and third-party apps, with tons available for download via the App Store. On the lifestyle front, you can use the watch to check notifications, send texts, make phone calls, get directions, listen to music, make mobile payments through Apple Pay and Wallet, and get live translations. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also carries over all of its predecessor’s health and safety features, including atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat) detection, crash and fall detection, a depth app for swimming, hypertension notifications, and sleep apnea detection. On the Horizon: Health Age and Audio Recaps Software updates slated to arrive before the end of the year will reorganize the Health app on iPhones to show long-term wellness with a Health Age metric based on your HRV, sleep, and VO2 Max (the maximum volume of oxygen that your body can use during a workout, a key indicator of cardio fitness). The app can also guide you through fitness assessments and track various aspects of your well-being over time, such as activity, sleep, and stress. Another update will add several Audio Intelligence features. By double-tapping the crown, Live Rewind lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation. Siri Recap takes high-level notes of your conversations throughout the day and creates bulleted summaries. Sound Recognition can alert the hard-of-hearing to common sounds, such as blaring alarms and barking dogs. While features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap raise potential privacy concerns, the data will be stored in a Secure Exclave within the S11 chip, encrypted when sent to your iPhone, and processed locally, so the audio is never shared with Apple. I tested the Ultra 4's new health-sensing system during several workouts, including a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session, an hour of pickleball, a run, and a walk. During most of these workouts, I wore the Pixel Watch 5 on my other wrist, and for the run and HIIT session, I also wore the Wahoo Trackr Heart Rate chest strap. The Ultra 4 offered impressive performance during the intense parts of my HIIT session and my run. During the run, it stayed within 2 to 3 beats per minute (bpm) of the chest strap's reading the entire time, even when I sprinted in intervals, causing spikes and dips in my heart rate. After the run, its average heart rate matched the chest strap’s exactly, and their maximum heart rate readings were within 1bpm. Its chart of my heart rate throughout the run lined up perfectly with Wahoo's. The Ultra 4 also kept up with the chest strap during casual walks and pickleball. During my guided HIIT session, the Ultra 4's heart rate readings spiked appropriately when my trainer made me do a circuit filled with burpees, and both its average and maximum heart rate values again matched those of the chest strap. Throughout the intense parts of my run and HIIT workouts, the Ultra 4 stayed closer to the chest strap's readings than the Pixel Watch 5 by a couple of bpm. Like the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 captures more details during a run than during exercises like HIIT and pickleball. For the latter two, it shows time, calories, heart rate, and a chart of heart rate over time. During running workouts, the Ultra 4 also captures form metrics such as cadence, ground contact time, and vertical oscillation. During sleep, the Ultra 4 monitors heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and recovery HRV. It charts the duration and depth of your sleep, breaking it down by time in each sleep cycle. It also scores your sleep on a scale from 0 to 100 based on bedtime, duration, and total number of interruptions. Those features carry over from the Ultra 3, but with its new heart rate sensor, the Ultra 4 takes overnight heart readings more frequently. I tested it over several nights while wearing the Pixel Watch 5 on my other wrist. Both devices showed similar sleep duration and cycle lengths. Even the sleep charts lined up to a reasonable degree. Apple’s sleep score also matched my anecdotal experience. It was lower after a night of tossing and turning, and as high as 90 when I got a good amount of deep sleep and woke up feeling refreshed. I appreciate the clarity Apple provides with this score; tapping it offers a breakdown of how each contributing factor adds up to the total. Final Thoughts Apple Watch Ultra 4 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 doesn't reinvent the wheel, but it perfects the engine. By pairing the Series 12's smartest features—the faster S11 chip, instant Siri AI responses, and drastically improved heart rate sensing—with an astounding 74 hours of real-world battery life, Apple has built an absolute endurance machine. While the Series 12 is our Editors' Choice for most iPhone users thanks to its versatile sizing and incredible value, the Ultra 4 is worth the splurge if you need a relentless, dive-ready smartwatch that can survive a full weekend off-grid without touching a charger. SHOULD I UPGRADE? Yes, if you own an Ultra 2 or older—or if battery anxiety is your main concern. The leap to the S11 chip, the massive bump to 74 hours of real-world battery life, and five-second heart rate sampling make the Ultra 4 a genuinely meaningful generational upgrade. Faster Siri AI processing and continuous HRV tracking alone elevate daily usability. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Make Movie Nights Spectacular With September's Best Projector Deals
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.64
Updated September 17: The days of home theater setups being just for the ultra-wealthy are long gone. You can spend a couple hundred bucks and get a solid projector that casts big, sharp images that approach cinema-quality. Modern projectors are a breeze to set up, with automatic image adjustments, lots of built-in streaming services, and long-lasting bulbs. We've found the best digital projectors from our favorite brands at the best prices. At PC Labs, we've been testing projectors for many years, working up a clear series of benchmarks to compare and contrast them. Whether you're interested in a high-end model with vivid hues and crisp contrast that's fast enough for high-speed gaming, or something more affordable and easy to move around with slightly lower specs, major companies have top-quality projectors available at sizable discounts. Here are September's eight best projector deals. The Best Portable Projector Deals We called the Nebula Cosmos 4K SE the best room-to-room portable projector in its price range in our review, giving it an Editors' Choice award for exceptional brightness and clarity. With a hybrid LED/laser light source, impressive 4K resolution and automated image adjustment that saves you time when you move it to a new location, it excels across the board. The fully integrated Google TV system lets you connect through Wi-Fi for streaming, and it also has two HDMI ports and a USB port. The rectangular form factor also includes a pair of 15-watt speakers that support Dolby Audio and Dolby Digital Plus. Get a 31% price cut now. For a budget option, the Vankyo Leisure 470 Pro is a capable little unit that even comes with a carrying bag to tote it around. In our review, contributing editor M. David Stone declared the projector "offers a watchable image that's acceptable for movies in the backyard or for ad hoc setup indoors." With just 1080p resolution and 170 lumens of brightness, it can't compete with ambient light, but once the sun is down, it handles itself well enough. The built-in speakers have surprisingly good sound quality and volume, it's a breeze to set up, and it supports Android and iOS screen mirroring. For $130, you'll have a hard time finding a better deal. Modern portable projectors are breaking through the 4K barrier at reasonable prices, and this unit from Chinese company Dangbei is a great value in an easy-to-carry form factor. Using a hybrid light engine that combines a traditional triple-laser array with a bright LED bulb means you get incredible contrast and sharp edges, eliminating the fuzziness that can plague portable projectors at large sizes. It also delivers great color coverage, with 11% of the BT.2020 gamut, and solid audio with a pair of 12-watt speakers. It's also super versatile, with a stand that lets you tilt to 135 degrees and rotate freely. The built-in Google TV streaming platform has all of the major services pre-installed, so you can plug it in, hook up to your Wi-Fi and be good to go. Save $300 at Amazon. Ever wish you could visit Roku City for real? The purple-hued screensaver is a popular meme in the home entertainment world, and Aurzen is cashing in by producing a portable projector that's shipped with Roku onboard. The easy-to-use streaming platform is one of the biggest draws of this unit, which we reviewed positively and praised for its good value for the price in terms of image brightness and clarity. While its 330 ANSI lumen brightness can't compete with more expensive units, it blows other budget models out of the water, and autofocus and automatic four-corner keystone correction add to its appeal. This spectacular portable unit delivers such exceptional picture quality that you could just install it permanently in your home theater and nobody would know any better. The Anker Nebula X1 received an Editors' Choice award in our review, with PCMag expert M. David Stone saying "it has genuinely impressive automated setup features for image size and geometry after moving it from one room to another, and specs that boast high brightness and a level of color accuracy usually reserved for dedicated home theater models." He did notice that it was a bit heavy for a portable unit, and fairly pricey, but this Amazon discount drops it to the lowest we've ever seen it on sale. With tons of connectivity options, a liquid cooling system to reduce fan noise, and a luxe 14-element all-glass lens, the Nebula X1 is worth every penny. The Best Non-Portable Projector Deals It's a spendy one, but the EpiqVision Ultra LS800 is a great pick for a TV replacement, as it delivers top-tier performance across all of the important metrics. We gave it an Editors' Choice award in our review, raving over its ultra-bright laser-phosphor light source that pumps out 4,000 ANSI lumens, more than enough to use it easily in a well-lit room. The three-chip LCD delivers rich, realistic colors without any rainbow artifacts, and the input lag is some of the lowest we've tested, hitting just 11.7ms at 1080p resolution. You can snag a $1,500 discount right now. This massive discount on a top-flight Awol Vision projector will be the cornerstone of your home entertainment system. The LTV-3000 is a marvel of lens construction, able to blast out an 80-inch image on the diagonal from just six inches away. It doesn't skimp on picture quality, either, with full 4K resolution, support for Dolby Vision and HDR10+, and solid colors thanks to a tri-laser light source rated for over 25,000 hours of use. It's not the most user-friendly projector on the market, with a relatively obtuse Android TV install powering it, but the image looks good right out of the box, and you have multiple connectivity options, including three HDMI ports and great 3D performance. Walmart has the best price anywhere on this excellent all-in-one home entertainment box that combines a rippingly high-quality 4K projector that looks great on screens up to 130 inches in diameter with a TV tuner and built-in Android TV streaming. In our review, it easily took home an Editors' Choice award, as we loved the impressive 2,200-lumen light source using Hisense's TriChroma laser engine, sharp focus, and good color accuracy. Connectivity is also extensive, with support for high-speed HDMI, a pair of HDMI 2.1 inputs, and eARC. If you dislike rainbow artifacts in your projected images, they're barely noticeable thanks to the speed with which the three colored lasers alternate. Our only real complaint was that there's no native Netflix app installed. More Projector Deals - Anker Nebula Capsule 3 Laser 1080p Wi-Fi Mini Projector — $599.99 ($749.99) Save $150.00 - Anker Nebula Mars 3 Air 1080p Portable Projector — $519.99 ($599.99) Save $80.00 - Epson EpiqVision Flex CO-FH02 1080p Smart Portable Projector — $449.99 ($499.99) Save $50.00 - Optoma Photon Life PK31 4K LED Portable Projector — $534.99 ($1,099.00) Save $564.01 - Aurzen Eazze D1R 1080p USB-C Smart Portable Roku T... — $149.97 ($239.99) Save $90.02 - Get the Best Prices On Projectors — Download Our Free Price Comparison Tool $0 What Are the Different Types of Projectors? Digital projectors create images using three primary types of technology. The most basic, DLP (which stands for digital light processing), has an array of minute mirrors inside the lens to transform white light into other colors. 3LCD projectors use a trio of LCD screens, one for each primary subtractive color. Liquid crystal on silicon, or LCoS, uses an active-matrix display on a silicon backplate for the most accurate colors, although it is significantly more expensive. What Should I Look for in a Projector? The two most important metrics for a projector are brightness and resolution. Brightness is measured in lumens, with a larger number being better. However, projectors typically have two distinct brightness numbers, one for white light and one for color. Images may appear dull if the color rating is lower than the pure white rating. Resolution determines the number of pixels the projector uses to create the image. 1080p high definition is the most common. For best results, match your projector resolution to the image source. What Is the Best and Cheapest Projector? We've put together a robust rundown of the best projectors on the consumer market, covering a wide range of uses, from large units to anchor a home theater to portable models for movies on the go. That frequently updated rundown lists our current top pick, but there's no single best and cheapest projector for everyone. You should look for one that is fast enough for casual gaming, is bright enough for movies, and has decent built-in speakers if you won't attach it to an external sound system. We've also seen some excellent projectors from Xgimi, Epson, LG, and many other brands sell for their low prices, too. Mini projectors are also a cheaper option most often due to the compromises in bulb brightness. Check out In our rundown of the best portable projectors to learn more. Do I Need a Screen for My Projector? In general, although you can cast an image from a projector on any wall or surface, it's not going to look as good as if you use a nonreflective white screen designed for that purpose. There are many different types of screens on the market, some for permanent installs, and even some that are inflatable for easy setup and storage. While they're not strictly required, they definitely make your viewing experience better. Here's our handy guide for how to choose the right screen for your projector. How Do We Test Projectors? The short answer? Thoroughly. When we test projectors, be they data projectors, home entertainment projectors, or home theater projectors, we give the units a 30-minute warm-up time while running through preliminary setup steps before performing extensive picture quality tests. And that's just the start! Dive into any of our reviews to see how deep we go. About Our Experts K. Thor Jensen is a writer and cartoonist living in the Pacific Northwest. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. I’m a managing editor at PCMag.com focused on PC hardware. Reading this during the day? Then you've caught me testing gear and editing reviews of Wi-Fi routers, printers, laptops, and tons of other personal tech. (Reading this at night? Then I’m probably dreaming about all those cool products.) I’ve covered the consumer tech world as an editor, reporter, and analyst since 2015. I've covered most major consumer tech events, including CES, Computex, Google I/O, and IFA. I've also appeared on CBS News, in USA Today, and at many other outlets to offer analysis on breaking technology news. Before I joined the tech-journalism ranks, I wrote on topics as diverse as Borneo's rainforests, Middle Eastern airlines, and Big Data's role in presidential elections. A graduate of Middlebury College, I also have a master's degree in journalism and French Studies from New York University.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 Review: A New Era of Wrist-Based AI Has Arrived
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.52
The Apple Watch Series 12 delivers one of the line's biggest generational leaps in years and ushers in a new era for Apple wearables. Armed with an entirely redesigned health array that tracks heart rate data every five seconds, a faster S11 chip driving context-aware Siri AI, and a massive jump to 54 hours of real-world battery life, it addresses longstanding user complaints while delivering more flagship features. Starting at the same $399 price as its predecessor, the Series 12 is a better value than ever, making it our Editors' Choice smartwatch for most iPhone users. The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399 for the base 42mm aluminum model (Bluetooth-only), maintaining the same entry price as the Series 11. Upgrading to the larger 46mm case costs $449, which is $20 higher than last year's size differential. Regardless of size, adding 5G cellular service costs an extra $100. The aluminum Series 12 is available in Black, Dark Bronze, Light Gold, or Space Gray. Like the Series 11, the Series 12 comes in a titanium case if you're looking for a sturdier build. The titanium model comes in a Natural or Radiant Gold finish and starts at $699 for 42mm or $749 for 46mm, each with built-in cellular service by default. New to this generation, you can also get a Series 12 with a ceramic case, for an extra-premium look and feel. The Ceramic models also have built-in cellular service and start at $899 for 42mm or $949 for 46mm. Ceramic is available in Night Blue or Pearl White. The line tops off with an Hermès version in titanium with exclusive band styles, priced at $1,399 for 42mm or $1,499 for 46mm. The Series 12 launches alongside the Apple Watch Ultra 4, which comes in a single 49mm titanium build with cellular connectivity for $799. While Apple has held the line on the Series 12's $399 starting price, its biggest competitors have raised their prices this year. Google bumped the Pixel Watch 5 by $50, bringing it to an identical $399 base price as Apple's entry model. Samsung's Galaxy Watch 9 remains the cheapest of the three, but a $30 price hike brings its new baseline to $379.99—narrowing the price gap between Apple and Android wearables considerably. For the most part, the Apple Watch Series 12 mirrors its predecessor in look and feel. I tested the 46mm aluminum model, which features an upgraded Ceramic Shield front cover—a display Apple claims is 60% tougher than the Series 11's Ion-X glass. Otherwise, durability remains unchanged: Both generations carry an IP6X dust-resistance rating and WR50 water resistance (submersible down to 164 feet). By comparison, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 matches the Series 12 in dust protection but doubles its water resistance, adds EN13319 dive certification, and has a MIL-STD-810H rating for extreme environments. By the numbers, the Series 12 is slightly bigger than the Series 11. Specifically, the 42mm Series 12 measures 37mm by 9.7mm (WD) and weighs 1.1 ounces, while the 46mm Series 12 measures 40mm by 9.7mm and weighs 1.4 ounces. Different variations of the watch change the measurements slightly, with titanium models increasing the weight, and ceramic further upping it to as much as 1.9 ounces for the 46mm in Night Blue (interestingly, the same size in Pearl White weighs slightly less at 1.8 ounces). Ultimately, the design differences from the last generation are so small that I barely noticed them, even when examining the models side by side, and I couldn't feel a weight difference. Otherwise, all versions of the Series 12 have the same LTPO3 wide-angle OLED Retina screen as the Series 11. It reaches 2,000 nits of adaptive brightness, with a minimum of 1 nit. Display area and pixel count remain unchanged from the last generation: 970mm with 374 by 446 pixels for the 42mm model, and 1,196mm with 416 by 496 pixels for the 46mm model. Using the Series 12 or updating an older Apple Watch to watchOS 27 requires an iPhone 11 or later running iOS 27. Apple’s latest smartwatch makes using Siri smoother and faster than ever, thanks to its new S11 chip with a 64-bit dual-core processor. The chip has upgraded CPU and GPU power as well as a better neural engine. The Series 12 has the same 64GB storage capacity as the Series 11. Apple’s artificial intelligence is a key part of the Series 12’s upgrades. The Siri AI app is front and center in watchOS 27. Pressing the crown no longer pulls up the entire app drawer. Instead, it shows a small circle of recommended and recently used apps with Siri AI always in the middle. Hit the bottom icon or rotate the crown to see the rest of your apps. The Siri AI app tracks past conversations, both for real-time reference and to build context for future inquiries. The Siri AI app on my iPhone 17 successfully showed my conversation history, pulling in all my questions and responses, even from interactions I had on my watch. The Siri AI app on my watch didn’t show the same conversations as it’s supposed to, but hopefully, this is a minor bug that can be patched soon. You can access Siri by holding down the digital crown or simply by saying the “Hey Siri” wake words. The AI-enabled version of Apple’s digital assistant is more conversational than ever. It can answer general knowledge questions and use personal context from compatible apps. You can ask about progress on your activity rings, for example, or have it search your email for flight information or your driver’s license number. I used it to make weekend plans by asking what was going on in my home city of Chicago, and then for further details about the festivals and events it listed that I found interesting. Siri told me the dates and times for Riot Fest at Douglass Park, the headliners for each night, and then showed me directions from my place. Besides Siri AI, watchOS 27 adds new widgets to the customizable Smart Stack, such as one from Shazam that will automatically pull up the name of any song playing in the background. You can browse these widgets by scrolling up on the crown, and you can select one with a single tap of your thumb and your forefinger. The previous double-tap gesture now scrolls the Smart Stack. The AI-powered Workout Buddy, which offers encouraging words during certain exercises, has also improved with watchOS 27. It now works without your phone if you have a cellular signal on your watch, and provides more detailed personal context. Cycle tracking gets an upgrade with watchOS 27 as well, adding support for perimenopause and menopause. On paper, Apple has kept the Series 12's battery estimate steady at 24 hours, maintaining the baseline jump introduced with the Series 11 (up from the historical 18-hour standard). But Apple has a habit of underpromising on stamina, and the Series 12 continues to quietly overdeliver in testing. In real-world use, with the always-on display enabled and one tracked exercise with GPS each day, the Series 12 lasted an impressive 54.5 hours. The Series 11 lasted 43 hours under the same conditions. It almost matches the Pixel Watch 5, which lasted 56.5 hours between charges under similar conditions. Both models are well ahead of the Galaxy Watch 9, which lasted just 26 hours in testing. The Series 12 charges more quickly than its predecessor, returning to 100% in 55 minutes using the included magnetic puck and my own 18W brick. The Series 11 needed 77 minutes to recharge under the same circumstances. Flip the Series 12 over, look closely, and you can see a handful of small visual changes from the Series 11 resulting from the entirely redesigned health sensing system. From the inside out, the green LEDs are larger, yet more power-efficient. Denser photodiodes surround these LEDs to capture more data than before. The electrodes on the outermost ring have similarly increased in density to provide greater surface area within roughly the same footprint, allowing for better skin contact and more accurate ECG readings. This system takes both heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV) readings significantly more frequently over the course of the day compared with the last generation's sensors. For heart rate, the Series 12 takes a reading every five seconds, up from once every five minutes. For HRV, it now collects data every five minutes instead of every two hours. Heart Rate App: Real-Time Stress Tracking and Recovery HRV The Heart Rate app on the watch provides richer data than before. The main page shows your current value, and a two-minute history of measurements on a line graph. Scroll down for your heart rate range for the day, and a chart of those values over time. The next two pages show graphs of your average resting heart rate and average heart rate while walking for the day. The last page shows HRV details. Here, you'll see your recovery HRV, a metric that monitors stress and fatigue. Prior Apple Watches focused more on overall HRV, a similar but slightly different metric used to assess cardiovascular health and monitor for irregular rhythms. I enjoyed perusing this app after a Sunday of watching football. I went for a run that morning and saw similar heart rate spikes during the stressful parts of an overtime game my favorite team played in. New watch complications let you add a heart rate widget to your watch face and check your real-time beats per minute (bpm) with a quick glance at your wrist. During the football game, this provided a handy visual reminder that I needed to calm down. Vitals App: All-Day Trend Monitoring to Catch Illness Early More frequent HRV readings also enable new features and metrics in the Vitals app. The overnight view shows how your trends compare with an established baseline as before, but recovery HRV is now one of the included metrics along with heart rate, respiratory rate, and wrist temperature. You can now switch to a daytime view, as the watch takes enough measurements to update your trends throughout the day. This helps keep you up to date earlier if you start showing signs of stress, burnout, or illness. The daytime view shows overall trends, heart rate, recovery HRV, and a new metric called Readiness. Readiness Score: Dynamic Daily Guidance That Adapts as You Move Readiness takes seven nights of sleep to establish a baseline, then provides a score from 0 to 10 each morning based on your activity, overnight vitals, and sleep score. In addition to appearing in the Vitals app, Readiness has its own app and is designed to help you plan the intensity of your workouts based on your current well-being. Google, Samsung, and others have long had similar scores that assess your readiness for the day, with recommendations for workout intensity. One differentiator is that Apple’s score adapts throughout the day in response to meaningful shifts, so it can drop after an intense workout to signal that you should take it easy, or rise if you become more rested after a nap. Similar scores from Google and Samsung remain static throughout the day, but both companies provide a separate workout-specific metric that updates as you complete activities. Apple also provides an assessment based on your readiness and vitals. For instance, I received a score of 5, and the app identified my short night's sleep as the main negative factor. Given that my fitness and vitals otherwise contributed positively, it determined that I was "ready" for the day. While Apple’s AI assessments are simple, they are offered at no additional cost. Google's wearables provide health scores and tracking for free, but the company's highly advanced AI Health Coach comes with a $9.99 monthly premium. Aside from the new heart rate tracking system, the Series 12 maintains its predecessor's sensor array, which includes an accelerometer, an altimeter, an ambient light sensor, a blood oxygen sensor, a compass, a depth gauge, a gyroscope, and a water temperature sensor. It also has a built-in single-frequency GPS. I tested the Series 12's exercise tracking during a walk around my neighborhood, a 30-minute run, and a 60-minute high-intensity interval training (HIIT) session, with the Fitbit-powered Google Pixel Watch 5 on my other wrist and the Wahoo Trackr Heart Rate strapped to my chest. During the first five minutes of the HIIT exercise on my second day of testing, the Series 12's heart rate numbers were low by 10 to 20bpm, and grayed out at one point, which made it seem like it was having trouble getting a reading. After five minutes, the Series 12 started to show accurate heart rate values. The issue reoccurred during the run but lasted only 30 seconds instead of a few minutes, so it's likely a calibration issue or a glitch in watchOS 27. Regardless, I don’t think it’s a major concern, as it didn’t meaningfully skew the data from the rest of the workout or the assessments and charts afterward. During my run, the Series 12 stayed right in line with the readings from my chest strap, deviating by no more than 2 to 3bpm, even when I sprinted during intervals. Afterward, its maximum heart rate was closer to the chest strap reading and differed by about 5bpm from the Pixel Watch 5, while all three showed a similar average heart rate. The Apple Watch Series 12 can track a wide range of different sports and activities, but for HIIT, it only shows time, calories burned, and average heart rate, along with a chart of my heart rate throughout the workout. For running, it also shows advanced form metrics such as cadence, ground contact time, stride length, and vertical oscillation. During the night, the Apple Watch Series 12 tracks heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and recovery HRV. It also measures the amount and depth of your slumber, and charts your sleep cycles over time. The watch gives you a sleep score from 0 to 100, with a clear breakdown of how duration, bedtime, and interruptions affected it. I tested the Series 12 over several nights of sleep while wearing the Pixel Watch 5 on my other wrist. Its sleep cycle numbers roughly matched both my anecdotal experience and the values from Google's watch. Its sleep score also mostly lined up with my expectations, falling to 79, or "fair," one weekend after I went to bed and then got up much later than usual. Otherwise, it was low after a rough night, and as high as 90 on other nights when I stuck to my schedule and got a decent amount of rest. Some of the Series 12's coolest features are still on the way. Audio Intelligence: Live Rewinds, Meeting Recaps, and Privacy Safeguards Powered by the S11 chip, Audio Intelligence comprises four new capabilities. By double-tapping the crown, Live Rewind lets you see a transcript of your last 15 seconds of conversation. Siri Recap takes high-level notes of your conversations throughout the day and creates bulleted summaries. Sound Recognition can alert hard-of-hearing individuals to sounds such as blaring alarms and barking dogs. The Shazam widget mentioned above also uses Audio Intelligence, and that feature is live now. Live Rewind and Siri Recap both raise privacy concerns, but Apple says all audio is stored and processed in a Secure Exclave on the S11 chip. The audio is protected with end-to-end encryption when sent to the iPhone for Siri Recaps, and is not saved as audio, only as the AI-processed files, and is never shared with Apple. Live Rewind overwrites audio as the 15 seconds elapse unless the feature is triggered, and Siri Recap can be programmed to activate only during certain times or at certain locations, like your workplace. It won't attribute any audio to individual speakers; instead, it just focuses on the information relayed. All aspects of Audio Intelligence will be opt-in, so you’ll have to manually enable them, meaning you can easily leave them off if you’re not comfortable with the privacy implications. I’m excited to try them since I sometimes struggle to understand fast speakers, and I’d find it useful to have bullet points summarizing my meetings during the workday. iPhone Health App: Dynamic Insights and the New Longevity Tab The existing Health app on iPhone will be overhauled later this year. The main Insights tab will be more dynamic, surfacing relevant tiles throughout the day to the top of the page. A new Longevity tab will show your Health Age compared with your actual age based on your HRV, sleep, and VO2 Max (the maximum volume of oxygen that your body can use during a workout, a key indicator of cardio fitness). It can guide you through fitness assessments and provide information on how to improve your Health Age, along with a pie chart showing how different aspects of your well-being have changed over time, such as activity, sleep, and stress. I look forward to testing these new features and changes, and will update this review once I do. Final Thoughts Apple Watch Series 12 - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Apple Watch Series 12 isn't just an incremental update; it's a definitive leap forward. Even with headline features like Audio Intelligence still on the horizon, the core experience is noticeably transformed by context-aware Siri AI, lightning-fast S11 performance, and sensor upgrades that track your heart rate every five seconds. The ultra-durable Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a compelling alternative for extreme outdoor adventurers, but with an impressive 54-hour battery life and an unchanged $399 base price, the Series 12 comfortably claims our Editors' Choice award as the undisputed top pick for most iPhone users. SHOULD I UPGRADE? If you're on a Series 11, it depends, but for almost everyone else, absolutely. While the design remains familiar, the jump to 50-plus hours of real-world battery life completely changes how you use the watch. Between the faster S11 chip driving smart, contextual Siri AI and redesigned sensors that capture heart rate data every five seconds instead of every five minutes, the Series 12 offers meaningful daily utility that older models simply can't match. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Get a daily iPhone briefing with one simple Apple AI prompt
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.99
The long-awaited Siri AI revamp finally landed this week with the arrival of iOS 27—but aside from the new Siri, iPhone users got another Apple Intelligence-enabled superpower. I’m talking about the Shortcuts app, a longstanding iOS feature that lets users create powerful automations capable of doing everything from making GIFs and kicking off timers to marking up images and controlling smart home devices. But with its modular building blocks and myriad options, the Shortcuts app is—or was—notoriously tough to use. I’ve tried tinkering with it in the past only to give up after a few broken workflows. The whole process always seemed more oriented toward coders than everyday users. Now with iOS 27, the Shortcuts app has gained a much-needed feature: the ability to create and edit Shortcuts using natural-language prompts, courtesy of the same Apple Intelligence models that now power Siri. With its new prompting abilities, you simply tell your iPhone the shortcut you want to create and the model does the rest, quickly constructing your workflow and allowing you to edit it afterwards. Unlike ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, which could theoretically let you build pretty much anything, the iOS Shortcuts app is limited by the actions, scripts, controls, and functions in its bag of tricks. So while you can arrange the Shortcuts app’s collection of Tinkertoy-like blocks in a wide variety of ways, you can’t create new ones from scratch. Still, with its new prompting abilities, you can use the Shortcuts app to create repeatable iPhone workflows that chain multiple actions together, and we’re going to start with an easy one: a one-tap daily digest. Just fire up the Shortcuts app, tap the “+” button at the bottom of the screen, and type (or say) this prompt: Give me a daily digest of the weather, my calendar events and reminders, and triage my email and messages. After a minute or so, the app will come back with a freshly minted Daily Digest shortcut that’ll fetch a weather report, assemble your daily agenda, and summarize the emails and text messages you’ve recently received. Ben Patterson/Foundry Tap the Edit button to see the building blocks of your new shortcut, which you previously would have had to put together yourself. Here, you can tweak the options that Apple Intelligence has picked for you (such as changing the number of emails or messages it summarizes), or you can tap the Apple Intelligence button in the top-right corner of the screen to request changes using a prompt. One thing you’ll notice in the shortcut is that Apple Intelligence only comes into play for the penultimate step, where it summarizes the details gathered by the previous shortcuts blocks. In other words, there won’t be swarms of AI agents scouring everything in your Calendar, Mail, and Messages apps. Ben Patterson/Foundry Speaking of the Apple Intelligence block, you can switch out the model used for that action by tapping Cloud. The options are “On Device,” “Cloud” (Apple’s cloud-based model), “Cloud Pro” (which offers enhanced reasoning capabilities at the cost of limited usage), and “ChatGPT.” In my tests, Cloud Pro delivered the most polished results while Cloud did the job with a few rough edges. On Device choked the shortcut entirely (“The request exceeded the maximum allowed length”) while ChatGPT appeared confused, spitting out a template rather than the digest itself. Once you’re all set, tap the Share button to add your new shortcut to the home screen, then tap it whenever you want your daily digest. You can also add it as a home screen widget.

item.title: Microsoft spreads its version of DLSS to more Intel laptops
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.76
There’s more than one kind of optimized upscaling for games. Nvidia does it (DLSS), AMD does it (FSR), Intel does it (XeSS). And you might be surprised to hear that Microsoft does it, right there in Windows. Auto Super Resolution has been quietly spreading out to more and more hardware, and this week it comes to laptops and desktops with the latest chips. That’s not just a big deal for Core Ultra Series 3 laptops, which are the newest and coolest thing on a Best Buy shelf that no one can afford. It’s a big deal for the Arc G3 series, which are the chips in the coolest handheld gaming PCs that no one can afford, like the Predator Atlas 8. The majority of these devices are coming with Windows, so while FSR and XeSS are both options, it’s interesting to get an upscaling tool from the native operating system. It’s also enhanced by NPUs, so finally they can do something if you’re not trying to generate slop. Microsoft says that you can try out Auto SR with any game using DirectX 10 or later, but it’ll shine on “texture-heavy games at higher resolutions and graphics settings.” Interestingly, the promotional page is pushing users to bump up the settings quality and get the same or slightly better framerate, rather than going for a pure performance win. While only still images are shown, an Assassin’s Creed Shadows image shows more foliage on an Ultra High setting with approximately the same framerate. Auto SR also has some growing pains. It’s still trained on very specific input and output performance targets capping out at 1080p, and might get wonky at other resolutions. It also upscales the entire image, so even Microsoft says that “text & fine line UI detail appear ‘fainter.'” In fact it’s still recommending XeSS and other upscalers when the game explicitly supports them. If you’re on a Panther Lake laptop or handheld, you can download the Auto Super Resolution package to try it out.

item.title: Asus Zenbook 14 review: A $799 laptop that feels pricier than it is
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.74
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Good office performance - Lightweight, stylish - Great OLED screen and good sound - The price! Cons - Modest battery life - Only available with a 256 GB SSD Our Verdict Asus strikes the right balance with the ZenBook 14, delivering a laptop that feels premium without costing a fortune. A small SSD and a small battery bring the rating down slightly. But if you use the laptop wisely, these drawbacks are less of an issue. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $799 Best Prices Today: Asus Zenbook 14 UX3480Q Last spring, Asus launched the ZenBook A14, a compact laptop with a stylish design, excellent build quality, a superb OLED screen, good sound, snappy performance, and long battery life. I crowned it the world’s best laptop at 2.20 pounds. There was just one problem with it… it was over a grand at launch. What if you could get the same experience in a laptop for just half the price? Now you can. Or at least come close. The Zenbook 14 (sans the A) is a new Snapdragon-based laptop with a 14-inch OLED screen and a starting price of $799. It boasts the same sleek design and high build quality as the ZenBook A14, along with many of its best features. Fortunately, the things holding it back are relatively minor. Asus ZenBook 14: Premium design in new colors Asus hasn’t compromised on build quality to keep the price down. The chassis is durable and ergonomically designed, with rounded edges, a well-built and thoughtfully designed keyboard with clear backlighting, a smooth-action screen hinge and a large touchpad with precise control. Asus They call the material “Ceraluminium” — aluminum with a ceramic-like finish. Once again, the laptop is available in the sandstone-like color Zabriskie Beige. There are now also two other colors to choose from: a grey-blue and a coral-colored pink variant. All three are really stylish. You get the same expected array of external ports on the sides: two USB-C 4 ports with DisplayPort support, one USB-A, one HDMI port and a headphone jack. One area where Asus has cut corners is Wi-Fi. You won’t get Wi-Fi 7 support here, but you do get Wi-Fi 6e, which is good enough in the vast majority of situations. Asus ZenBook 14: Slower, but still fast The areas where Asus has cut corners the most to keep the price down are performance and storage capacity. You get the previous-generation Snapdragon X instead of the Snapdragon X2 Elite found in the ZenBook A14; as mentioned, you get 16 GB of RAM instead of 32, and a 256 GB SSD with no option for more – at least at the time of this writing. Memory and storage are expensive, and this is where Asus is saving a lot of money. Mattias Inghe The SSD is also of the PCIe 3.0 type rather than PCIe 4.0, which is found in most top-of-the-range models at the moment (including the 512 GB model of this laptop, apparently). This means a read speed of around 3,500 MB/s, whereas the best drives today offer speeds of between 6,000 and 7,000 MB/s. The performance is still perfectly adequate. Asus markets this as a good student laptop, and I can only agree. It’s more than capable of handling all everyday tasks, such as working in office software, browsing the web, emailing, taking part in webcam meetings, and streaming video. You can also easily do some basic photo editing and video editing, though not quite at a professional level, and it’s not really a gaming laptop. Simple, light games work fine, but nothing more demanding. The laptop never gets more than marginally warm, and even under heavy CPU load, I’m not particularly bothered by the fan noise. Asus ZenBook 14: Beautiful screen and great sound You still get an excellent 1920×1200 OLED screen, with the superb contrast and color reproduction typical of OLED technology. It isn’t quite as bright as the ZenBook A14, with a typical brightness of around 300 cd/m² instead of 400 cd/m², and the HDR effect isn’t quite as intense, even though the display technically supports HDR mode. Mattias Inghe The screen is completely glossy, with a clear mirror image on the surface if you’re viewing a dark image, but this is something it has in common with many more expensive laptops, and it’s hardly a major distraction. On the underside of the chassis are two grilles with speaker units behind them, and they sound surprisingly good. Detailed, well-balanced, and with clear bass. The webcam and microphone also perform well, though not quite flawlessly. The image is a little washed-out in terms of color reproduction, and the microphone is noisier than expected. But this can be remedied. In the My Asus app, the manufacturer offers a range of features like controlling fan speed, changing the colors on your screen, and activating an AI noise filter on your microphone. You can also switch between fan and performance modes using a hotkey on the keyboard, either to maximize performance or efficiency. But even when the fans are spinning away, it remains relatively quiet. Asus ZenBook 14: Smaller battery, but more energy-efficient Battery is where the ZenBook 14 suffers (if only slightly). It’s a modest 50 Wh and, unfortunately, it doesn’t last nearly as long as the ZenBook A14, which comes with a 70 Wh battery. What the Snapdragon X excels at, however, is its high efficiency during active use. Mattias Inghe Although the maximum battery life under light use isn’t quite as impressive this time round, working under more normal loads yields really good results. I can push the processor to its limits for over five hours, meaning the laptop lasts a full working day without me having to hunt for a power socket. The relatively low screen brightness also helps with this. Nevertheless, this laptop weighs slightly more than the ZenBook A14. It’s still a very light machine, weighing just 2.43 pounds. But, clearly, Asus has kept costs down in some subtle ways. A simpler internal chassis and perhaps older, bulkier components. Whatever the case, it’s not something you’d notice from the outside. This is a stylish, well-built, and comfortable quality laptop with almost the same premium feel as its twice-as-expensive sibling, with brisk performance and specifications well-suited to office work. You’ll have to make do without a large SSD, extra RAM, and a more powerful processor, but everything else is almost as good. Which is still very good indeed. Asus ZenBook 14: Specifications Product name: Asus ZenBook 14 UX3480QA-U1155W Tested: September 2026 Manufacturer: Asus Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon X1-26-100, 8 Oryon cores at 3 GHz NPU: Hexagon, 45 tops Graphics: Adreno X1-45, 1250 MHz Memory: 16 GB LPDDR5x Storage: 256 GB SSD Display: 14-inch glossy OLED, 1920×1200 pixels, 60 Hz, approx. 300 cd/m² Webcam: 1080p with IR Ports: 2 x USB-C Gen 3, Port 2 with DisplayPort, USB-A Gen 3, HDMI, headphone jack Wireless: Wi-Fi 6e, Bluetooth 5.3 Operating system: Windows 11 Home Other: Backlit keyboard Noise level: 0–37 dBa Battery: 50 Wh. 5 hours 10 minutes (heavy use, high brightness), approx. 14 hours (light use, low brightness) Dimensions: 31.11 x 21.58 x 1.69 cm Weight: 2.43 lbs Price: Starting price, $799 Rating: 4 out of 5 Performance Cinebench 2026, multi-threaded CPU: 2,958 points Cinebench 2026, single-threaded CPU: 398 points Geekbench 6, CPU multi-core: 10,662 points Geekbench 6, single-core CPU: 2,151 points Geekbench 6, GPU: 13,751 points

item.title: iFixit now has a dozen guides for repairing your Steam Machine
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.30
In summary: - PCWorld reports that iFixit has launched over a dozen detailed repair guides for the Steam Machine, covering components like RAM, storage, and the faceplate. - Replacement parts for the device are expected to arrive soon, making maintenance and upgrades more accessible for owners. - Highlights include a recommended single-DIMM RAM upgrade and a custom e-ink faceplate mod for dedicated hobbyists looking to personalize their hardware. If you look at the Steam Machine as a game console, it’s remarkably open and repairable. With a little bit of knowledge and research, you can mod both the hardware and software down to the bones. But if you look at it as a PC, it’s suddenly more intimidating. Even by the standards of a small form factor device, this thing is tiny and complicated. iFixit is here to help. The right-to-repair gurus have put together a series of more than a dozen guides on removing and replacing just about every component, from the faceplate (just pull it off, it’s magnetic!) to the RAM and storage, to the itty-bitty microSD card reader. For the truly dedicated, there’s even a guide from community contributors on how to build and set up that e-ink faceplate mod. None of this is rocket science. (Okay, the e-ink thing might be, at least by my standards.) But as someone who prefers to keep things nice and easy with an ATX PC build, I appreciate the hell out of it. Especially since the Steam Machine’s single-DIMM RAM setup makes a memory boost one of the most obvious upgrades to make, and the device’s layers-in-a-shell setup isn’t obvious if you’re not forewarned. As usual iFixit’s guides are concise and clear, with wonderful photos and helpful tips. According to an iFixit representative, parts for the Steam Machine are coming soon.

item.title: Asus ProArt KD300 review: A tiny keyboard with big features
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.26
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - A high-quality feel - Smart touch control - Smooth and flexible with settings - Good battery life Cons - Cramped key layout - Unclear what the ‘professional’ angle is Our Verdict I’ve no idea what makes the ProArt a keyboard specifically for professionals, and the extra-compact layout won’t be to everyone’s taste. But it’s backed by a smart and user-friendly system, and the quality is undeniable. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $165 Best Prices Today: Asus Proart KD300 It’s hard to find good mechanical keyboards that aren’t marketed as “gaming keyboards,” but this one from Asus is just that. ProArt is their brand for creative gear, primarily monitors and laptops, but also this keyboard and a mouse that I’ve also tested. When I look at what Asus says about the ProArt KD300 online, I’m met with phrases such as “inspires boundless creativity” and “expressive control.” What exactly is particularly expressive and inspiring about the keyboard is, in fact, rather unclear. One of the noteworthy features is said to be its format. This is an extra-compact keyboard with a so-called 65 percent layout, which means it’s small in size and lacks some keys. There’s no numeric keypad on the side, nor even a row of function keys above. Mattias Inghe Cramped but well-built Everything is very well built and the chassis is sturdy, but it’s lighter than many competing keyboards, even compared to similarly small ones. The keys are low-profile, but with full travel and linear switches without a mechanical click. They trigger early when pressed, allowing you to type quickly. There is some clicking sound when pressing and releasing the keys, but it’s not excessively noisy. The point of the compact design is supposedly to free up more desk space for other things, such as a graphics tablet, mouse, cameras, and a microphone. I’m not sure if it’s worth it — I’ve never felt short of desk space — but that’s up to you. For some reason, this type of more compact keyboard is popular. Personally, I always prefer more keys. It’s not that the functions are inaccessible. There are F1 to F12 functions, media controls, window management in Windows, screenshot, and brightness and volume controls, but all via Fn combinations. These functions and more are printed on the front edge of the keys. They’re hard to see without good lighting in the room, but they’re there. The backlight doesn’t illuminate them, only the main characters in the center of the top row. Mattias Inghe Lots of features, plenty of flexibility You can also access other features this way, such as controlling the RGB backlighting with colors and effects, a macro function, and switching between paired devices. You can connect up to five devices, using a combination of Bluetooth, a USB receiver, and USB-C. In addition to the buttons on the top, there’s also a touch strip along the back edge of the keyboard. This gives you quick control over things like volume, screen brightness, the media player, and customizable swipe and click gestures. These are configured in Gearlink, Asus’s web-based interface. You simply browse to it from the computer that you’re connected to, so you don’t need to install any app. Here, you can change the function of absolutely every button and save your settings in different profiles. You get easier access to the backlight and control over power consumption. There are plenty of options for customization for both productivity and gaming, but it’s entirely manual — you’ll need to design your own setups. Mattias Inghe Can last for weeks It’s all powered by a 4,000mAh rechargeable battery, which, according to Asus, should last for “up to 16 months” without backlighting and 100 days with it. But of course, that depends on how much you use it during that time. In any case, you won’t need to hunt for a charging cable straight away. During my week-long test, the battery level dropped by 5 percent. But then I was using the laptop and keyboard rather sporadically. That’s still very good, though. If you appreciate an extra-compact keyboard — perhaps because you want to be close to your mouse or your desk is a bit cramped — this is one of the better ones you can buy. It offers surprisingly high functionality, a nice sense of quality, and precise keystrokes. The angle, specifically marketed as a keyboard for creative work, feels rather contrived. It’s a somewhat limiting solution as a text-input device and typing tool, and it doesn’t offer anything extra in terms of control for creative software. But that doesn’t stop it from being really good, if you’re comfortable with the format.
